item.title: Genie 4 把声音也一起生成了：Gemini 3.8 Flash 在环内拆步骤、审帧、验成败，世界边跑边被语言改 ｜ Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
item.description:
一句话：首个原生生成音频的实时世界模型；Gemini 在环内当导演，把目标拆成步骤喂给生成器。

要点：

  • 原生多模态：音乐、环境音与可交互对话和画面同时生成，是 DeepMind 第一个原生出音频的实时世界模型
  • 实时可控：键盘控导航与相机、文本改天气/换人/加物件；两次输入之间 Gemini 持续监控并纠偏，防止世界失去连贯
  • 复杂事件靠 Gemini 3.8 Flash 在环内当导演——观察场景、把目标拆成步骤、审帧验证每步成功，例子是 Gemini 4 Argon + Genie 4 模拟 Apollo 人形机器人下跳棋

为什么值得看：这条把「世界模型当引擎」推到端到端那一端：状态与因果由规划＋生成共同承担。看完要问的三个工程问题很具体——已有资产怎么喂进去、同一动作能否复现、延迟怎么摊进可交互预算。与 BoxWorld（引擎算状态、生成器只渲染）正好是对照组。

中文摘要：Genie 4 是 DeepMind 于 10 月 27 日发布的新一代世界模型，核心变化是原生多模态：音乐、环境音以及可交互的人声对话，与画面同时生成。它把四项能力叠在一起。第一是实时用自然语言改世界：键盘控导航与相机，文本换天气、移相机、加人或物件，Gemini 会把提示改写为贴合场景的指令，并在两次输入之间持续监控纠偏。第二是物理与人物真实度：空气动力、碰撞可模拟，人物移动自然且能被实时操控。第三是音频，包括环境音与实时对话。第四是用 Gemini 当导演：Gemini 3.8 Flash 在环内观察画面、把目标拆步骤、审帧验证，世界一变就改写计划，示例是 Gemini 4 Argon 与 Genie 4 合作模拟 Apptronik Apollo 人形机器人下跳棋。发布节奏是先做 research preview，再向 AI Ultra 订阅者与 Gemini API 早期伙伴开放。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：DeepMind Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-27

本期推送：2026-10-28

DeepMind 在 10 月 27 日发布 Genie 4，定位是「新一代世界模拟」。与前三代最大的不同不是画质，而是原生多模态：声音（音乐、环境音、可交互对话）与画面同时生成。

四个能力，逐一拆开

一、实时用自然语言改世界

用户用键盘做导航与相机控制，用文本提示就地改变世界——换天气、移相机、加入新的人或物。关键细节是 Gemini 会先把提示「翻译」成贴合当前场景的指令，并在两次输入之间持续监控、纠偏，让世界往前推进而不是停住。

二、物理与人物真实度的跃升

官方口径是基于对世界的先进物理理解：空气动力、碰撞这类场景能模拟；人物则「移动自然、对环境有反应、且能被实时操控」。对人形角色来说，这一条比画质更值钱——过去视频世界模型最明显的破绽就是人一动就穿帮。

三、原生音频与实时对话

Genie 4 是 DeepMind 第一个原生生成音频的实时世界模型：每个世界自带环境音（风吹树叶、海浪）。更前沿的是人声——角色能实时对话、并跟着你的输入或世界里的事件改变反应。

四、用 Gemini 当「导演」模拟复杂事件

实时生成的背后有一个 in-the-loop 的引导 agent：Gemini 3.8 Flash 持续观察画面、把目标拆成步骤、审查每一帧、验证每步是否成功；世界一变或用户介入就改写计划。官方给的两个例子是「Argon 把任务拆成步骤、以文字 caption 形式插进 Genie 的生成过程」，以及「Gemini 4 Argon + Genie 4 一起模拟 Apptronik 的 Apollo 人形机器人下跳棋」。

发布节奏

先在受信测试者中做 research preview，随后向 Google AI Ultra 订阅者（Project Genie）以及 Gemini API / Google AI Studio 的早期合作伙伴开放，排队入口在官方页面。

对引擎开发者意味着什么

这条路线里，引擎不再是唯一的状态权威：状态、因果与「下一步该发生什么」由 Gemini 侧的规划与 Genie 的生成共同承担。真正的工程问题因此变成三个：怎么把已有内容的资产与规则喂进去（而不是从视频里重新学）、怎么保证同一动作的结果可复现、以及怎么把延迟摊到可交互的预算里。对比同一天收录的 BoxWorld（引擎算状态、生成器只负责出画面），这条是「端到端生成」的另一端，两条路线今年会正面撞上。

（正文为编辑整理的官方博客要点，原文链接见文末。）

item.title: 让引擎算状态、让生成器只管画：BoxWorld 用 coding agent 现造一个规则引擎，20.7 FPS 还能在线改规则 ｜ BoxWorld: Let World Engines Control and Video Generators Render
item.description:
一句话：交互推理与生成渲染分离：引擎吐 layout 盒与状态变量，生成器把这串状态渲染成视频。

要点：

  • 按用户给的规则，一个 coding agent 现场造出 Box World Engine：判定交互结果，并通过「layout 盒 + 持久对象属性 + 动态状态变量」这层轻接口暴露状态，外观与物理效果全交给生成渲染
  • Box-State Generative Renderer 自回归地把状态流渲染成视频，支持在线改物体运动、状态切换与条件事件；难点是既要实时响应对象级更新，又要与已生成的历史保持一致
  • 同 20.7 FPS 下画质与 LongLive 相当，VBench Semantic 76.47→79.54、VBench-Long 75.82→77.67；消融显示状态接口是命门——去掉空间 mask，mIOU 从 0.572 掉到 0.291，把动态状态换成静态描述，Trigger 92.2%→42.5%、OnTime 91.2%→16.1%

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生引擎」最工程化的一种解：规则与状态留在可读、可改、可验证的引擎里，模型只负责像素。它顺便回答了「agent 该怎么生成引擎」——不是让模型直接吐画面，而是让 agent 造一个小引擎并通过结构化接口驱动生成器。

中文摘要：现在的端到端视频世界模型把交互动力学学进生成器里，于是「物体级规则怎么指定、后果怎么推理」变得很难。BoxWorld 把交互推理与生成渲染拆开：给定用户规则的描述，一个 coding agent 现场生成 Box World Engine，由它判定交互结果，并以轻量接口输出 layout 盒、持久对象属性与动态状态变量；外观与物理效果交给 Box-State Generative Renderer 自回归渲染成视频。渲染这串状态流并不轻松：既要实时响应对象级状态更新，又要和已生成历史保持连贯，作者为此引入相应机制。结果是在 20.7 FPS 下画质与 LongLive 相当而语义分数更高，消融进一步说明状态接口是命门——去掉空间 mask 或把动态状态改成静态描述，指标会大幅塌陷。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-10-28

BoxWorld: Let World Engines Control and Video Generators Render

Abstract

We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page:boxworld-web.github.io.

1 Introduction

Building models that can understand, simulate, and interact with the physical world has long been an ambitious goal of artificial intelligence [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018)]. Recent progress in video generation [(Team Wan et al., 2025; Google DeepMind, 2025; Team Seedance et al., 2026)] has given this goal a concrete instantiation: interactive video worlds, where users can act in a generated world and experience it unfolding over time in response to their actions [(Brooks et al., 2024; Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Ball et al., 2025)]. We are interested in real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors, where users also specify how the world responds to their actions. For example, a user may specify that a flower blooms only when nurtured (Figure 1(top)), or that a door opens only if the cat has collected the key (Figure 1(bottom)). Realizing such behaviors requires the world to track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the consequences as users act.

A prevailing approach learns interactive video worlds end to end, mapping visual history and user actions directly to future frames with a video generator that generalizes across diverse scenes [(Bruce et al., 2024; Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] (Figure 2(a)). However, the generator must then handle all three tasks implicitly, reasoning about whether rules are satisfied and what consequences should follow, which makes object-level rules and their consequences difficult to specify and control. A complementary direction instead conditions video generation on explicit states, ranging from trajectories [(Li et al., 2025a)] and layouts [(Feng et al., 2025b)] to physical priors [(Zhang et al., 2025)], 3D caches [(Ren et al., 2025)], and full simulators [(Xie et al., 2025)] (Figure 2(b)). These states provide finer control, but grow heavier and more domain-specific as control becomes finer, making them expensive to construct and simulate, and difficult to obtain from videos at scale.

Taken together, these lines of work reveal a trade-off between generalization and fine-grained control in interactive video worlds. This motivates separating interaction reasoning from generative rendering: interaction rules are applied explicitly outside the generator, while the generator retains its broad visual priors and focuses on faithfully rendering the resulting object states. The two sides are connected by an explicit-but-minimal Object-Centric State Interface, which exposes only the variables needed for object-level interaction while remaining simple to specify, update, and apply across diverse scenes. Crucially, these state variables should be identifiable from videos with off-the-shelf perception models, so that learning the renderer is not restricted to predefined simulators or scarce action-paired interaction data.

Following this design, we present BoxWorld, a framework for real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine, which applies these rules to user actions, determines the resulting interaction outcomes, and updates object states. The engine exposes these states through the Object-Centric State Interface, composed of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving texture, lighting, style, and physical effects such as smoke and splashing water to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events (Figure 2(c)).

However, rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. First, states arrive online, so generation must be few-step and causal, whereas existing layout-to-video methods rely on multi-step bidirectional generation over the entire layout sequence [(Li et al., 2025a; Lian et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025b)]. Second, an update makes part of the generated history outdated, so the renderer must distinguish what to preserve from what to change. Third, the renderer must synthesize the new state of the affected object, such as a door swinging open. Existing video editing methods achieve similar localized changes, but rely on precise masks, costly inversion, or per-video optimization [(Jiang et al., 2025; Mou et al., 2024; Ku et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2026a)], making them unsuitable for online rendering from coarse boxes.

To address these challenges, we build the Box-State Generative Renderer on an autoregressive video generator [(Yang et al., 2025a)] and train it in three stages, each with a training scheme matched to its role (Sec. 3.3). The first stage, Masked Layout Grounding, learns frame-wise object grounding on open-domain videos [(Tan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b)] with Diffusion Forcing [(Chen et al., 2024)], whose independent per-frame noise levels make grounding hold regardless of the noise level of the temporal context. The second stage, State Dynamics Adaptation, learns state transitions on gameplay videos with teacher forcing, whose clean history depicts the preceding state, so that the renderer learns to change the affected object while continuing the rest of the scene. The third stage, Rollout Distillation, distills the renderer on its own rollouts with Self-Forcing-style distribution matching [(Huang et al., 2025b)], restoring few-step generation while adapting it to the self-generated histories encountered at inference. The state annotations are extracted by off-the-shelf perception models [(Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024b)], requiring no action-paired interaction logs (Sec. 3.4).

We further introduce PairedStateBench, which evaluates user-defined behaviors through paired branches with distinct intended outcomes, measuring whether generated videos realize specified consequences and suppress unspecified ones. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models on PairedStateBench, and remains competitive in short- and long-horizon video quality on VBench and VBench-Long [(Huang et al., 2024)], and layout-to-video generation on YouTube-VIS [(Yang et al., 2021)], while running in real time. Our key contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose BoxWorld, a framework for real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors, in which a Box World Engine created by a coding agent determines interaction outcomes and a Box-State Generative Renderer realizes them through the Object-Centric State Interface.

  • •

    We introduce a three-stage training strategy with distinct roles: Masked Layout Grounding and State Dynamics Adaptation learn object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and Rollout Distillation restores few-step generation on the renderer’s own rollouts.

  • •

    We propose PairedStateBench for fine-grained interaction control, on which BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models while remaining competitive on public benchmarks for video quality and layout-to-video generation.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive Video World Models. Early controllable world models showed that playable dynamics can be learned directly from video [(Menapace et al., 2021)] or prompt-conditioned game loops [(Menapace et al., 2024)]. This line then scaled to tokenized or latent world models [(Wu et al., 2024; Bruce et al., 2024; Bar et al., 2025)] and larger video corpora [(Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Ball et al., 2025)], and more recently to interactive simulators built from powerful video generators with action [(Valevski et al., 2025; Che et al., 2025)], camera [(Huang et al., 2025a)], and navigation control [(Yu et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025)]. Recent extensions further target open environments, character-centered interaction, and longer-horizon memory [(Sun et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025)]. In parallel, stronger backbones [(HaCohen et al., 2024; Team Wan et al., 2025)] together with causalization and distillation [(Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025a)] are beginning to enable real-time interactive systems [(Shin et al., 2026)]. These works show strong visual interaction, but scene dynamics and intervention logic still largely reside in the generator [(Valevski et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025a)], making object-level rules and their consequences difficult to specify and control.

    State-Conditioned Generation. Another line exposes explicit state and conditions image or video generation on it. Early grounded generation uses layouts and regions for object-level control [(Li et al., 2023; Dou et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2023)], while ControlNet-style methods extend explicit conditioning to dense signals such as edges, depth, segmentation, and pose [(Zhang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Zavadski et al., 2025)]. Later methods extend this idea to planning [(Lin et al., 2024)], trajectories and tracklets [(Yin et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026)], camera and motion control [(Wang et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2023)], and more compositional object guidance [(Li et al., 2025b; Feng et al., 2025b; Mei et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a)]. Recent physics-aware and simulator-grounded variants further improve consistency by injecting physical priors or planning [(Zhang et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025b)], or by conditioning generation on richer state such as simulators, depth, geometry, and 3D caches [(Xie et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025)]. Together, these methods show that explicit conditioning improves controllability, but they typically generate a complete clip offline, using multi-step bidirectional denoising given the full condition sequence in advance [(Li et al., 2025a; Feng et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024)], or depend on heavier state and supervision [(Xie et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025)]. In contrast, BoxWorld renders in real time, consuming object states as they arrive with few-step causal generation, and realizes state changes during the rollout while remaining coherent with the generated history.

    3 Method

    BoxWorld assigns interaction reasoning to a Box World Engine and generative rendering to a Box-State Generative Renderer, which communicate through the Object-Centric State Interface. We describe the engine and interface in Sec. 3.1, the renderer in Sec. 3.2, and how the renderer is trained in three stages (Sec. 3.3) on video-derived annotations (Sec. 3.4).

    3.1 Box World Engine and Object-Centric State Interface

    At time step t, the Object-Centric State Interface describes the scene as Sₜ={(b_t,i,cᵢ,d_t,i)}ᵢ₌₁^Nₜ over Nₜ active objects. For object i, the layout box b_t,i gives its 2D location in frame coordinates, the persistent attribute cᵢ describes its identity and appearance, and the dynamic status variable d_t,i describes its current status.

    Given user-specified rules, a coding agent implements a Box World Engine from a shared engine template before interaction (Appendix B). During interaction, the engine maintains its internal scene variables and updates them with each user action. It applies the rules to decide whether and when each object changes state, and projects the resulting object states into Sₜ, which is published to a state buffer read asynchronously by the renderer.

    Since Sₜ can be recovered from videos with off-the-shelf perception models (Sec. 3.4), the renderer can be trained without engines or action-paired interaction logs, and at inference time it can be driven by any engine that publishes the same interface (Sec. 4.2).

    3.2 Box-State Generative Renderer

    Frame-wise state grounding.

    The Box-State Generative Renderer generates the latent video autoregressively, modeling p_θ(xₜ|x_3). At frame t, the states of all objects are encoded into grounding tokens Eₜ∈ℝ^(NₜL)×D with L tokens per object, and their boxes define a mask Mₜ∈{0,1}^HW×(NₜL) that lets each visual token attend only to the objects covering it. We reshape the flattened visual tokens h∈ℝ^B×(THW)×D into per-frame tokens h̃∈ℝ^(BT)×(HW)×D and apply masked cross-attention to each frame:

    Yₜ=Softmax(((h̃ₜW_Q)(EₜW_K)^⊤)/(√D)+Φ(Mₜ))EₜW_V,

    		(1)

    where Φ(Mₜ) is 0 for allowed entries and -∞ otherwise. The per-frame outputs Yₜ are reshaped back into the video-token sequence Ȳ and injected through a gated residual:

    h^′=h+λ\tanh(γ)Ȳ,

    		(2)

    where λ is a control scale and γ is a learnable gate initialized to zero. Temporal coherence across frames is left to the causal self-attention of the backbone.

    Asynchronous streaming rendering.

    At inference, the Box World Engine and the renderer run as asynchronous processes connected by the state buffer. The engine continuously receives user actions, updates its internal scene variables according to the rules, and publishes the resulting state Sₜ through the interface. Meanwhile, the renderer reads the latest state from the buffer whenever it generates new frames and renders them autoregressively from the generated history. A state update is therefore reflected in the next generated frames, while the engine keeps simulating the scene in parallel.

    3.3 Three-Stage Training

    We initialize the renderer from LongLive [(Yang et al., 2025a)], a few-step autoregressive video generator distilled from Wan2.1 [(Team Wan et al., 2025)], and train it in three stages: the first two learn object grounding and state transitions, respectively, and the third restores few-step generation by distilling on its own rollouts. In each stage, θ denotes the trainable parameters of that stage.

    Stage 1: Masked Layout Grounding.

    This stage learns object grounding, binding each object to its layout box and persistent attribute, and trains on open-domain videos [(Tan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b)] whose diversity supports grounding across scenes. We freeze the backbone and train only the State Grounding Module. To bind every frame to its own state, we follow Diffusion Forcing [(Chen et al., 2024)], which assigns independent noise levels to the latent frames, so the module learns grounding regardless of the noise level of its temporal context. The objective is

    L_S1(θ)=𝔼_x₀,t,τ[w_S1(τₜ)∥v_θ(x_τₜ,t,τₜ,x_τ_

    		(3)

    where each frame is noised independently with levels τ=(τ₁,…,τ_T), so the history x_τ_

    Stage 2: State Dynamics Adaptation.

    This stage learns state transitions, which open-domain videos rarely contain, so we train on gameplay videos. We freeze the Stage 1 renderer and train LoRA adapters [(Hu et al., 2022)] in its linear layers, as LongLive [(Yang et al., 2025a)] shows that LoRA adaptation of a distilled streaming generator approaches the quality of full fine-tuning. To learn how a status change alters the video, we use teacher forcing, in which the renderer denoises the current frame given the clean ground-truth prefix. When a status changes, the prefix depicts the preceding status and the target depicts the new one, so the adapters learn to change the affected object while continuing the rest of the scene. The objective is

    L_S2(θ)=𝔼_x₀,t,τ[∥v_θ(x_τ,t,τ,x_0,

    		(4)

    where the history x_0,

    Stage 3: Rollout Distillation.

    The denoising objectives of the first two stages shift the renderer away from its distilled few-step distribution, and teacher forcing trains it on clean prefixes, whereas inference conditions on self-generated ones. This stage therefore restores few-step generation by distilling the renderer on its own rollouts. We freeze the Stage 2 renderer and train an additional LoRA adapter θ with Self-Forcing-style distribution matching distillation (DMD) [(Yin et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025b)], using the Stage 2 renderer as the teacher and state sequences from both open-domain and gameplay annotations. The student generates few-step autoregressive rollouts x̂ and is updated with

    ∇_θL_S3=𝔼_τ,ε[w(τ)(s_fake(x̂_τ,τ,S_1:T)-sᵣₑₐₗ(x̂_τ,τ,S_1:T))^⊤(∂x̂)/(∂θ)],

    		(5)

    where x̂_τ is the rollout re-noised to level τ, sᵣₑₐₗ and s_fake are the scores of the teacher and of a critic initialized from it, and w(τ) is the normalizer following DMD. Sec. 4.4 evaluates its effect on long-horizon generation.

    For efficient inference, we merge the LoRA adapters of LongLive and of Stages 2 and 3 into the backbone weights [(Hu et al., 2022)], so that the adapters add no runtime cost.

    3.4 Video-to-Structure Annotation

    We recover Sₜ from open-domain and gameplay videos with off-the-shelf perception models: LLaVA-NeXT-Video [(Zhang et al., 2024b)] for clip descriptions, Grounding DINO [(Liu et al., 2025)] for initial layout boxes, SAM 2 [(Ravi et al., 2025)] for tracking, and object-level captioning for persistent attributes. Open-domain videos cover diverse objects and scenes but contain few status changes, whereas gameplay videos contain frequent actions and triggered events. For both sources, we crop each tracked object across frames and describe its current status and action with emphasis on status changes, so that the per-frame descriptions form d_t,i and expose status transitions. Appendix A provides details and examples.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Implementation Details

    We train Stage 1 on filtered open-domain videos from VideoGen-1M [(Tan et al., 2024)] and 4DNeX [(Chen et al., 2025b)], Stage 2 on 4,000 short gameplay clips collected online, and Stage 3 on state sequences from both sources. The three stages run for 20K, 10K, and 400 iterations, with rank-16 LoRA adapters in Stage 2 and a rank-64 adapter in Stage 3. At inference, the renderer uses four denoising steps at 832×480, and the State Grounding Module is active only at noise levels above 0.8. The Box World Engines in our experiments are created by Kimi K2.5 [(Kimi Team et al., 2026)] from user-specified rules (Appendix C.1).

    4.2 Fine-Grained Interaction Control

    We evaluate fine-grained interaction control on PairedStateBench, whose cases range from directional motion and object handling to credential-dependent doors, charging, and multi-stage interactions. Each case specifies the intended state evolution, event conditions, and temporal windows, and paired cases share the initial scene but differ in the intended outcome. We compare against the end-to-end world models LingBot-v1 [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] and LingBot-v2 [(Gao et al., 2026b)], each with an oracle variant that additionally receives the interaction consequences as text, and against LongLive [(Yang et al., 2025a)], the backbone of our renderer. The metrics measure whether required events appear (Trigger), forbidden consequences remain absent (Suppress), both branches of a pair succeed (Paired-CF), state windows and event onsets match the specification (State-Fid, OnTime), and complete multi-stage tasks succeed (Task). Appendix C.2 provides the full benchmark details.

    Quantitative Results. As shown in Table 1, BoxWorld realizes both the occurrence and the suppression of specified consequences, reaching 92.2% Trigger and 90.5% Suppress, and satisfies both branches in 97.3% of pairs, whereas no baseline exceeds 16.2% Paired-CF. The end-to-end models tend to produce the likely event regardless of the branch condition (Figure 4), and supplying the resolved outcome as text does not close this gap: both oracle variants remain at 16.2% Paired-CF. LongLive reaches only 13.5%, indicating that the specified outcomes are realized through state grounding. BoxWorld also completes 83.9% of the full multi-stage tasks, compared with at most 25.3% for the baselines, and the Task gap widens with difficulty: on hard cases, BoxWorld retains 94.7% Paired-CF and 80.6% Task, whereas the baselines reach at most 15.8% and 8.3%, respectively. These results show that fine-grained interaction consequences, which end-to-end models struggle to infer from visual history, are straightforward for an explicit engine to determine, and that the Box-State Generative Renderer faithfully realizes them once they are expressed as object-level states.

    Qualitative Results. Figure 4 compares branches that differ in whether the precondition is met, such as nurturing the flower or collecting the key. BoxWorld renders the event only once the precondition holds, whereas LingBot-v1 renders it before the precondition is met, even with oracle text. Figure 5 further shows rollouts from six engines, each rendered in two visual worlds. The same interaction, such as picking up, carrying, and placing an object, is realized consistently across scenes and styles, indicating that one engine can drive diverse visual worlds through the Object-Centric State Interface.

    4.3 Public Benchmarks

    Video Quality. We evaluate how much of the pretrained visual prior the renderer retains on VBench and 30-second VBench-Long [(Huang et al., 2024)]. As shown in Table 3 (Appendix C.3), BoxWorld achieves video quality comparable to LongLive at the same 20.7 FPS while improving the Semantic score from 76.47 to 79.54 on VBench and from 75.82 to 77.67 on VBench-Long, suggesting that object-level states strengthen compositional control.

    Layout-to-Video Generation. Following BlobGEN-Vid [(Feng et al., 2025b)], we test on YouTube-VIS 2021, where ground-truth tracks provide layout boxes and per-track descriptions provide object attributes. As shown in Table 4 (Appendix C.4), BoxWorld is the only real-time method, yet it achieves the lowest FVD (62), the highest regional text and image alignment (rCLIPt 0.291, rCLIPi 0.837), and the highest regional cross-frame consistency (rCFC 0.965) among all compared methods. Its mIOU of 0.572 is second only to BlobGEN-Vid (0.598), whose blob representation offers finer spatial support than boxes.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Training Stages. As shown in Table 2, the Total score on VBench and VBench-Long increases with each stage, and Stage 3 brings the largest gain on VBench-Long, from 81.82 to 83.00, showing that rollout distillation benefits long-horizon generation. On PairedStateBench, Stage 2 raises Suppress from 60.3% to 85.7% and Task from 49.4% to 64.4%, indicating that gameplay adaptation teaches the renderer to change an object only when its status changes. Stage 3 further raises Paired-CF from 67.6% to 97.3% and Task to 83.9%, indicating that rollout distillation keeps state changes faithful over self-generated histories. Appendix C.5 reports all metrics and further compares Stage 2 adapter variants.

    State Interface. On YouTube-VIS, removing the spatial mask lets every visual token attend to all objects and reduces mIOU from 0.572 to 0.291, which supports routing each object’s state to its own region, and replacing all object attributes with the generic word “object” reduces mIOU to 0.323, showing that attributes identify objects beyond their box geometry. On PairedStateBench, replacing dynamic status with static descriptions lowers Trigger from 92.2% to 42.5% and OnTime from 91.2% to 16.1%, since dynamic status specifies whether and when each object changes.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering for real-time interactive video worlds. A Box World Engine, created by a coding agent from user-specified rules, determines interaction outcomes and exposes them through the Object-Centric State Interface of layout boxes, persistent attributes, and dynamic status variables. A Box-State Generative Renderer, trained in three stages on automatically annotated videos, then renders the resulting state stream into video in real time. On PairedStateBench, BoxWorld realizes fine-grained interaction consequences that end-to-end world models struggle to produce, while retaining video quality comparable to its backbone. These results suggest a practical path for controllable interactive video worlds: let a world engine decide what changes, and let a video generator render how those changes appear.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Video-to-Structure Annotation

    A.1 Data Preparation

    This section describes how we collect, filter, and annotate the training videos.

    A.1.1 Collection and Filtering

    Collection: We collect videos from two sources:

  • •

    Online Datasets: We rely on two large-scale datasets: VideoGen-1M [(Tan et al., 2024)] and 4DNeX [(Chen et al., 2025b)], which capture diverse objects, environments, and interactions.

  • •

    Gameplay Data: We collect diverse gameplay videos from online sources, which provide structured object behaviors and interactions.

    • Filtering: Once videos are collected, we apply a filtering process to ensure only high-quality, relevant videos are included in the dataset:

  • •

    Resolution and Quality Filtering: We only select videos with a minimum resolution of 720p, 16 FPS, and 81 frames.

  • •

    Content Relevance: We keep only videos in which objects are identifiable and in motion.

    • A.1.2 Data Annotation

    Our data labeling process follows a three-stage approach: Video Content Extraction, Object Detection and Tracking, and Object Captioning. For gameplay data, we implement an additional dedicated stage: Structural Video Description with Element Breakdown. Figures 7 and 8 show two representative examples of our annotation results, drawn from the online dataset and the gameplay dataset, respectively.

    Video Content Extraction. In the initial stage of labeling, we extract high-level content from each video using LLaVA-NeXT-Video [(Zhang et al., 2024b)]. This model processes the entire video and performs two main tasks:

  • •

    Object Identification: The model identifies the main objects present in each video to provide an initial list of visual entities appearing in the scene, such as humans, vehicles, animals, and inanimate objects.

  • •

    Full Video Description and Background Generation: The model then generates a high-level description of the video, capturing not only the main objects but also the overall context of the scene. This includes background descriptions that characterize the environment, lighting, and any static elements in the scene that remain unchanged throughout the video.

    • Object Detection and Tracking. Once objects have been identified by the video captioning model, we proceed to detect and track the position of these objects across video frames.

  • •

    Initial Object Detection: Grounding DINO [(Liu et al., 2025)] detects the identified objects in the first frame and produces their initial bounding boxes.

  • •

    Object Tracking: After the initial detection, we use SAM 2 [(Ravi et al., 2025)] to track these objects across subsequent frames. SAM 2 allows us to maintain temporal consistency by tracking the same object across frames, even if it undergoes motion, partial occlusion, or appearance changes due to lighting or viewpoint shifts.

    • Object Captioning. In the final labeling step, we crop each tracked object and caption it frame by frame with an image captioning model.

  • •

    Object Descriptions: Each caption describes the object’s identity and appearance (e.g., “a red car”), which forms its persistent attribute.

  • •

    Temporal Captioning: Each caption also describes the object’s current status and action, with emphasis on status changes, which forms its dynamic status. For example, the red car might be described as “a red car driving down the road” in one frame and “a red car stopping at a traffic light” in another.

    • Structural Video Description with Element Breakdown. For gameplay datasets, we enhance the standard video description by including additional elements that are specific to game environments and interactions. This breakdown captures both the visual aspects and the dynamic game mechanics. Specifically, we expand on the following key elements:

  • •

    Spatial Layout: Descriptions of how objects are spatially arranged in the frame, such as their relative positioning and proximity to other objects or the camera. For example, “The racing car is positioned in the center of the track, ahead of the player’s car”.

  • •

    Action and Interaction Descriptions: These provide detailed information about how objects interact with each other. We annotate the relationship between the primary player-controlled entity and the adversaries or objectives. This captures the behavioral logic of a game, where the player’s actions directly influence the target’s state and vice-versa. For example, “The racing car aggressively closes the gap with the lead vehicle”.

  • •

    Background Descriptions: Beyond individual object interactions, broader scene descriptions are generated, focusing on the environment or setting where the objects exist. For example, “An urban street with tall skyscrapers, neon signs, and a crowd of pedestrians walking.”

一句话：交互推理与生成渲染分离：引擎吐 layout 盒与状态变量，生成器把这串状态渲染成视频。

要点：

  • 按用户给的规则，一个 coding agent 现场造出 Box World Engine：判定交互结果，并通过「layout 盒 + 持久对象属性 + 动态状态变量」这层轻接口暴露状态，外观与物理效果全交给生成渲染
  • Box-State Generative Renderer 自回归地把状态流渲染成视频，支持在线改物体运动、状态切换与条件事件；难点是既要实时响应对象级更新，又要与已生成的历史保持一致
  • 同 20.7 FPS 下画质与 LongLive 相当，VBench Semantic 76.47→79.54、VBench-Long 75.82→77.67；消融显示状态接口是命门——去掉空间 mask，mIOU 从 0.572 掉到 0.291，把动态状态换成静态描述，Trigger 92.2%→42.5%、OnTime 91.2%→16.1%

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生引擎」最工程化的一种解：规则与状态留在可读、可改、可验证的引擎里，模型只负责像素。它顺便回答了「agent 该怎么生成引擎」——不是让模型直接吐画面，而是让 agent 造一个小引擎并通过结构化接口驱动生成器。

中文摘要：现在的端到端视频世界模型把交互动力学学进生成器里，于是「物体级规则怎么指定、后果怎么推理」变得很难。BoxWorld 把交互推理与生成渲染拆开：给定用户规则的描述，一个 coding agent 现场生成 Box World Engine，由它判定交互结果，并以轻量接口输出 layout 盒、持久对象属性与动态状态变量；外观与物理效果交给 Box-State Generative Renderer 自回归渲染成视频。渲染这串状态流并不轻松：既要实时响应对象级状态更新，又要和已生成历史保持连贯，作者为此引入相应机制。结果是在 20.7 FPS 下画质与 LongLive 相当而语义分数更高，消融进一步说明状态接口是命门——去掉空间 mask 或把动态状态改成静态描述，指标会大幅塌陷。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-10-28

BoxWorld: Let World Engines Control and Video Generators Render

Abstract

We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page:boxworld-web.github.io.

1 Introduction

Building models that can understand, simulate, and interact with the physical world has long been an ambitious goal of artificial intelligence [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018)]. Recent progress in video generation [(Team Wan et al., 2025; Google DeepMind, 2025; Team Seedance et al., 2026)] has given this goal a concrete instantiation: interactive video worlds, where users can act in a generated world and experience it unfolding over time in response to their actions [(Brooks et al., 2024; Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Ball et al., 2025)]. We are interested in real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors, where users also specify how the world responds to their actions. For example, a user may specify that a flower blooms only when nurtured (Figure 1(top)), or that a door opens only if the cat has collected the key (Figure 1(bottom)). Realizing such behaviors requires the world to track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the consequences as users act.

A prevailing approach learns interactive video worlds end to end, mapping visual history and user actions directly to future frames with a video generator that generalizes across diverse scenes [(Bruce et al., 2024; Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] (Figure 2(a)). However, the generator must then handle all three tasks implicitly, reasoning about whether rules are satisfied and what consequences should follow, which makes object-level rules and their consequences difficult to specify and control. A complementary direction instead conditions video generation on explicit states, ranging from trajectories [(Li et al., 2025a)] and layouts [(Feng et al., 2025b)] to physical priors [(Zhang et al., 2025)], 3D caches [(Ren et al., 2025)], and full simulators [(Xie et al., 2025)] (Figure 2(b)). These states provide finer control, but grow heavier and more domain-specific as control becomes finer, making them expensive to construct and simulate, and difficult to obtain from videos at scale.

Taken together, these lines of work reveal a trade-off between generalization and fine-grained control in interactive video worlds. This motivates separating interaction reasoning from generative rendering: interaction rules are applied explicitly outside the generator, while the generator retains its broad visual priors and focuses on faithfully rendering the resulting object states. The two sides are connected by an explicit-but-minimal Object-Centric State Interface, which exposes only the variables needed for object-level interaction while remaining simple to specify, update, and apply across diverse scenes. Crucially, these state variables should be identifiable from videos with off-the-shelf perception models, so that learning the renderer is not restricted to predefined simulators or scarce action-paired interaction data.

Following this design, we present BoxWorld, a framework for real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine, which applies these rules to user actions, determines the resulting interaction outcomes, and updates object states. The engine exposes these states through the Object-Centric State Interface, composed of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving texture, lighting, style, and physical effects such as smoke and splashing water to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events (Figure 2(c)).

However, rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. First, states arrive online, so generation must be few-step and causal, whereas existing layout-to-video methods rely on multi-step bidirectional generation over the entire layout sequence [(Li et al., 2025a; Lian et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025b)]. Second, an update makes part of the generated history outdated, so the renderer must distinguish what to preserve from what to change. Third, the renderer must synthesize the new state of the affected object, such as a door swinging open. Existing video editing methods achieve similar localized changes, but rely on precise masks, costly inversion, or per-video optimization [(Jiang et al., 2025; Mou et al., 2024; Ku et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2026a)], making them unsuitable for online rendering from coarse boxes.

To address these challenges, we build the Box-State Generative Renderer on an autoregressive video generator [(Yang et al., 2025a)] and train it in three stages, each with a training scheme matched to its role (Sec. 3.3). The first stage, Masked Layout Grounding, learns frame-wise object grounding on open-domain videos [(Tan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b)] with Diffusion Forcing [(Chen et al., 2024)], whose independent per-frame noise levels make grounding hold regardless of the noise level of the temporal context. The second stage, State Dynamics Adaptation, learns state transitions on gameplay videos with teacher forcing, whose clean history depicts the preceding state, so that the renderer learns to change the affected object while continuing the rest of the scene. The third stage, Rollout Distillation, distills the renderer on its own rollouts with Self-Forcing-style distribution matching [(Huang et al., 2025b)], restoring few-step generation while adapting it to the self-generated histories encountered at inference. The state annotations are extracted by off-the-shelf perception models [(Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024b)], requiring no action-paired interaction logs (Sec. 3.4).

We further introduce PairedStateBench, which evaluates user-defined behaviors through paired branches with distinct intended outcomes, measuring whether generated videos realize specified consequences and suppress unspecified ones. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models on PairedStateBench, and remains competitive in short- and long-horizon video quality on VBench and VBench-Long [(Huang et al., 2024)], and layout-to-video generation on YouTube-VIS [(Yang et al., 2021)], while running in real time. Our key contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose BoxWorld, a framework for real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors, in which a Box World Engine created by a coding agent determines interaction outcomes and a Box-State Generative Renderer realizes them through the Object-Centric State Interface.

  • •

    We introduce a three-stage training strategy with distinct roles: Masked Layout Grounding and State Dynamics Adaptation learn object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and Rollout Distillation restores few-step generation on the renderer’s own rollouts.

  • •

    We propose PairedStateBench for fine-grained interaction control, on which BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models while remaining competitive on public benchmarks for video quality and layout-to-video generation.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive Video World Models. Early controllable world models showed that playable dynamics can be learned directly from video [(Menapace et al., 2021)] or prompt-conditioned game loops [(Menapace et al., 2024)]. This line then scaled to tokenized or latent world models [(Wu et al., 2024; Bruce et al., 2024; Bar et al., 2025)] and larger video corpora [(Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Ball et al., 2025)], and more recently to interactive simulators built from powerful video generators with action [(Valevski et al., 2025; Che et al., 2025)], camera [(Huang et al., 2025a)], and navigation control [(Yu et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025)]. Recent extensions further target open environments, character-centered interaction, and longer-horizon memory [(Sun et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025)]. In parallel, stronger backbones [(HaCohen et al., 2024; Team Wan et al., 2025)] together with causalization and distillation [(Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025a)] are beginning to enable real-time interactive systems [(Shin et al., 2026)]. These works show strong visual interaction, but scene dynamics and intervention logic still largely reside in the generator [(Valevski et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025a)], making object-level rules and their consequences difficult to specify and control.

    State-Conditioned Generation. Another line exposes explicit state and conditions image or video generation on it. Early grounded generation uses layouts and regions for object-level control [(Li et al., 2023; Dou et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2023)], while ControlNet-style methods extend explicit conditioning to dense signals such as edges, depth, segmentation, and pose [(Zhang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Zavadski et al., 2025)]. Later methods extend this idea to planning [(Lin et al., 2024)], trajectories and tracklets [(Yin et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026)], camera and motion control [(Wang et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2023)], and more compositional object guidance [(Li et al., 2025b; Feng et al., 2025b; Mei et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a)]. Recent physics-aware and simulator-grounded variants further improve consistency by injecting physical priors or planning [(Zhang et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025b)], or by conditioning generation on richer state such as simulators, depth, geometry, and 3D caches [(Xie et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025)]. Together, these methods show that explicit conditioning improves controllability, but they typically generate a complete clip offline, using multi-step bidirectional denoising given the full condition sequence in advance [(Li et al., 2025a; Feng et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024)], or depend on heavier state and supervision [(Xie et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025)]. In contrast, BoxWorld renders in real time, consuming object states as they arrive with few-step causal generation, and realizes state changes during the rollout while remaining coherent with the generated history.

    3 Method

    BoxWorld assigns interaction reasoning to a Box World Engine and generative rendering to a Box-State Generative Renderer, which communicate through the Object-Centric State Interface. We describe the engine and interface in Sec. 3.1, the renderer in Sec. 3.2, and how the renderer is trained in three stages (Sec. 3.3) on video-derived annotations (Sec. 3.4).

    3.1 Box World Engine and Object-Centric State Interface

    At time step t, the Object-Centric State Interface describes the scene as Sₜ={(b_t,i,cᵢ,d_t,i)}ᵢ₌₁^Nₜ over Nₜ active objects. For object i, the layout box b_t,i gives its 2D location in frame coordinates, the persistent attribute cᵢ describes its identity and appearance, and the dynamic status variable d_t,i describes its current status.

    Given user-specified rules, a coding agent implements a Box World Engine from a shared engine template before interaction (Appendix B). During interaction, the engine maintains its internal scene variables and updates them with each user action. It applies the rules to decide whether and when each object changes state, and projects the resulting object states into Sₜ, which is published to a state buffer read asynchronously by the renderer.

    Since Sₜ can be recovered from videos with off-the-shelf perception models (Sec. 3.4), the renderer can be trained without engines or action-paired interaction logs, and at inference time it can be driven by any engine that publishes the same interface (Sec. 4.2).

    3.2 Box-State Generative Renderer

    Frame-wise state grounding.

    The Box-State Generative Renderer generates the latent video autoregressively, modeling p_θ(xₜ|x_3). At frame t, the states of all objects are encoded into grounding tokens Eₜ∈ℝ^(NₜL)×D with L tokens per object, and their boxes define a mask Mₜ∈{0,1}^HW×(NₜL) that lets each visual token attend only to the objects covering it. We reshape the flattened visual tokens h∈ℝ^B×(THW)×D into per-frame tokens h̃∈ℝ^(BT)×(HW)×D and apply masked cross-attention to each frame:

    Yₜ=Softmax(((h̃ₜW_Q)(EₜW_K)^⊤)/(√D)+Φ(Mₜ))EₜW_V,

    		(1)

    where Φ(Mₜ) is 0 for allowed entries and -∞ otherwise. The per-frame outputs Yₜ are reshaped back into the video-token sequence Ȳ and injected through a gated residual:

    h^′=h+λ\tanh(γ)Ȳ,

    		(2)

    where λ is a control scale and γ is a learnable gate initialized to zero. Temporal coherence across frames is left to the causal self-attention of the backbone.

    Asynchronous streaming rendering.

    At inference, the Box World Engine and the renderer run as asynchronous processes connected by the state buffer. The engine continuously receives user actions, updates its internal scene variables according to the rules, and publishes the resulting state Sₜ through the interface. Meanwhile, the renderer reads the latest state from the buffer whenever it generates new frames and renders them autoregressively from the generated history. A state update is therefore reflected in the next generated frames, while the engine keeps simulating the scene in parallel.

    3.3 Three-Stage Training

    We initialize the renderer from LongLive [(Yang et al., 2025a)], a few-step autoregressive video generator distilled from Wan2.1 [(Team Wan et al., 2025)], and train it in three stages: the first two learn object grounding and state transitions, respectively, and the third restores few-step generation by distilling on its own rollouts. In each stage, θ denotes the trainable parameters of that stage.

    Stage 1: Masked Layout Grounding.

    This stage learns object grounding, binding each object to its layout box and persistent attribute, and trains on open-domain videos [(Tan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b)] whose diversity supports grounding across scenes. We freeze the backbone and train only the State Grounding Module. To bind every frame to its own state, we follow Diffusion Forcing [(Chen et al., 2024)], which assigns independent noise levels to the latent frames, so the module learns grounding regardless of the noise level of its temporal context. The objective is

    L_S1(θ)=𝔼_x₀,t,τ[w_S1(τₜ)∥v_θ(x_τₜ,t,τₜ,x_τ_

    		(3)

    where each frame is noised independently with levels τ=(τ₁,…,τ_T), so the history x_τ_

    Stage 2: State Dynamics Adaptation.

    This stage learns state transitions, which open-domain videos rarely contain, so we train on gameplay videos. We freeze the Stage 1 renderer and train LoRA adapters [(Hu et al., 2022)] in its linear layers, as LongLive [(Yang et al., 2025a)] shows that LoRA adaptation of a distilled streaming generator approaches the quality of full fine-tuning. To learn how a status change alters the video, we use teacher forcing, in which the renderer denoises the current frame given the clean ground-truth prefix. When a status changes, the prefix depicts the preceding status and the target depicts the new one, so the adapters learn to change the affected object while continuing the rest of the scene. The objective is

    L_S2(θ)=𝔼_x₀,t,τ[∥v_θ(x_τ,t,τ,x_0,

    		(4)

    where the history x_0,

    Stage 3: Rollout Distillation.

    The denoising objectives of the first two stages shift the renderer away from its distilled few-step distribution, and teacher forcing trains it on clean prefixes, whereas inference conditions on self-generated ones. This stage therefore restores few-step generation by distilling the renderer on its own rollouts. We freeze the Stage 2 renderer and train an additional LoRA adapter θ with Self-Forcing-style distribution matching distillation (DMD) [(Yin et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025b)], using the Stage 2 renderer as the teacher and state sequences from both open-domain and gameplay annotations. The student generates few-step autoregressive rollouts x̂ and is updated with

    ∇_θL_S3=𝔼_τ,ε[w(τ)(s_fake(x̂_τ,τ,S_1:T)-sᵣₑₐₗ(x̂_τ,τ,S_1:T))^⊤(∂x̂)/(∂θ)],

    		(5)

    where x̂_τ is the rollout re-noised to level τ, sᵣₑₐₗ and s_fake are the scores of the teacher and of a critic initialized from it, and w(τ) is the normalizer following DMD. Sec. 4.4 evaluates its effect on long-horizon generation.

    For efficient inference, we merge the LoRA adapters of LongLive and of Stages 2 and 3 into the backbone weights [(Hu et al., 2022)], so that the adapters add no runtime cost.

    3.4 Video-to-Structure Annotation

    We recover Sₜ from open-domain and gameplay videos with off-the-shelf perception models: LLaVA-NeXT-Video [(Zhang et al., 2024b)] for clip descriptions, Grounding DINO [(Liu et al., 2025)] for initial layout boxes, SAM 2 [(Ravi et al., 2025)] for tracking, and object-level captioning for persistent attributes. Open-domain videos cover diverse objects and scenes but contain few status changes, whereas gameplay videos contain frequent actions and triggered events. For both sources, we crop each tracked object across frames and describe its current status and action with emphasis on status changes, so that the per-frame descriptions form d_t,i and expose status transitions. Appendix A provides details and examples.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Implementation Details

    We train Stage 1 on filtered open-domain videos from VideoGen-1M [(Tan et al., 2024)] and 4DNeX [(Chen et al., 2025b)], Stage 2 on 4,000 short gameplay clips collected online, and Stage 3 on state sequences from both sources. The three stages run for 20K, 10K, and 400 iterations, with rank-16 LoRA adapters in Stage 2 and a rank-64 adapter in Stage 3. At inference, the renderer uses four denoising steps at 832×480, and the State Grounding Module is active only at noise levels above 0.8. The Box World Engines in our experiments are created by Kimi K2.5 [(Kimi Team et al., 2026)] from user-specified rules (Appendix C.1).

    4.2 Fine-Grained Interaction Control

    We evaluate fine-grained interaction control on PairedStateBench, whose cases range from directional motion and object handling to credential-dependent doors, charging, and multi-stage interactions. Each case specifies the intended state evolution, event conditions, and temporal windows, and paired cases share the initial scene but differ in the intended outcome. We compare against the end-to-end world models LingBot-v1 [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] and LingBot-v2 [(Gao et al., 2026b)], each with an oracle variant that additionally receives the interaction consequences as text, and against LongLive [(Yang et al., 2025a)], the backbone of our renderer. The metrics measure whether required events appear (Trigger), forbidden consequences remain absent (Suppress), both branches of a pair succeed (Paired-CF), state windows and event onsets match the specification (State-Fid, OnTime), and complete multi-stage tasks succeed (Task). Appendix C.2 provides the full benchmark details.

    Quantitative Results. As shown in Table 1, BoxWorld realizes both the occurrence and the suppression of specified consequences, reaching 92.2% Trigger and 90.5% Suppress, and satisfies both branches in 97.3% of pairs, whereas no baseline exceeds 16.2% Paired-CF. The end-to-end models tend to produce the likely event regardless of the branch condition (Figure 4), and supplying the resolved outcome as text does not close this gap: both oracle variants remain at 16.2% Paired-CF. LongLive reaches only 13.5%, indicating that the specified outcomes are realized through state grounding. BoxWorld also completes 83.9% of the full multi-stage tasks, compared with at most 25.3% for the baselines, and the Task gap widens with difficulty: on hard cases, BoxWorld retains 94.7% Paired-CF and 80.6% Task, whereas the baselines reach at most 15.8% and 8.3%, respectively. These results show that fine-grained interaction consequences, which end-to-end models struggle to infer from visual history, are straightforward for an explicit engine to determine, and that the Box-State Generative Renderer faithfully realizes them once they are expressed as object-level states.

    Qualitative Results. Figure 4 compares branches that differ in whether the precondition is met, such as nurturing the flower or collecting the key. BoxWorld renders the event only once the precondition holds, whereas LingBot-v1 renders it before the precondition is met, even with oracle text. Figure 5 further shows rollouts from six engines, each rendered in two visual worlds. The same interaction, such as picking up, carrying, and placing an object, is realized consistently across scenes and styles, indicating that one engine can drive diverse visual worlds through the Object-Centric State Interface.

    4.3 Public Benchmarks

    Video Quality. We evaluate how much of the pretrained visual prior the renderer retains on VBench and 30-second VBench-Long [(Huang et al., 2024)]. As shown in Table 3 (Appendix C.3), BoxWorld achieves video quality comparable to LongLive at the same 20.7 FPS while improving the Semantic score from 76.47 to 79.54 on VBench and from 75.82 to 77.67 on VBench-Long, suggesting that object-level states strengthen compositional control.

    Layout-to-Video Generation. Following BlobGEN-Vid [(Feng et al., 2025b)], we test on YouTube-VIS 2021, where ground-truth tracks provide layout boxes and per-track descriptions provide object attributes. As shown in Table 4 (Appendix C.4), BoxWorld is the only real-time method, yet it achieves the lowest FVD (62), the highest regional text and image alignment (rCLIPt 0.291, rCLIPi 0.837), and the highest regional cross-frame consistency (rCFC 0.965) among all compared methods. Its mIOU of 0.572 is second only to BlobGEN-Vid (0.598), whose blob representation offers finer spatial support than boxes.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Training Stages. As shown in Table 2, the Total score on VBench and VBench-Long increases with each stage, and Stage 3 brings the largest gain on VBench-Long, from 81.82 to 83.00, showing that rollout distillation benefits long-horizon generation. On PairedStateBench, Stage 2 raises Suppress from 60.3% to 85.7% and Task from 49.4% to 64.4%, indicating that gameplay adaptation teaches the renderer to change an object only when its status changes. Stage 3 further raises Paired-CF from 67.6% to 97.3% and Task to 83.9%, indicating that rollout distillation keeps state changes faithful over self-generated histories. Appendix C.5 reports all metrics and further compares Stage 2 adapter variants.

    State Interface. On YouTube-VIS, removing the spatial mask lets every visual token attend to all objects and reduces mIOU from 0.572 to 0.291, which supports routing each object’s state to its own region, and replacing all object attributes with the generic word “object” reduces mIOU to 0.323, showing that attributes identify objects beyond their box geometry. On PairedStateBench, replacing dynamic status with static descriptions lowers Trigger from 92.2% to 42.5% and OnTime from 91.2% to 16.1%, since dynamic status specifies whether and when each object changes.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering for real-time interactive video worlds. A Box World Engine, created by a coding agent from user-specified rules, determines interaction outcomes and exposes them through the Object-Centric State Interface of layout boxes, persistent attributes, and dynamic status variables. A Box-State Generative Renderer, trained in three stages on automatically annotated videos, then renders the resulting state stream into video in real time. On PairedStateBench, BoxWorld realizes fine-grained interaction consequences that end-to-end world models struggle to produce, while retaining video quality comparable to its backbone. These results suggest a practical path for controllable interactive video worlds: let a world engine decide what changes, and let a video generator render how those changes appear.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Video-to-Structure Annotation

    A.1 Data Preparation

    This section describes how we collect, filter, and annotate the training videos.

    A.1.1 Collection and Filtering

    Collection: We collect videos from two sources:

  • •

    Online Datasets: We rely on two large-scale datasets: VideoGen-1M [(Tan et al., 2024)] and 4DNeX [(Chen et al., 2025b)], which capture diverse objects, environments, and interactions.

  • •

    Gameplay Data: We collect diverse gameplay videos from online sources, which provide structured object behaviors and interactions.

    • Filtering: Once videos are collected, we apply a filtering process to ensure only high-quality, relevant videos are included in the dataset:

  • •

    Resolution and Quality Filtering: We only select videos with a minimum resolution of 720p, 16 FPS, and 81 frames.

  • •

    Content Relevance: We keep only videos in which objects are identifiable and in motion.

    • A.1.2 Data Annotation

    Our data labeling process follows a three-stage approach: Video Content Extraction, Object Detection and Tracking, and Object Captioning. For gameplay data, we implement an additional dedicated stage: Structural Video Description with Element Breakdown. Figures 7 and 8 show two representative examples of our annotation results, drawn from the online dataset and the gameplay dataset, respectively.

    Video Content Extraction. In the initial stage of labeling, we extract high-level content from each video using LLaVA-NeXT-Video [(Zhang et al., 2024b)]. This model processes the entire video and performs two main tasks:

  • •

    Object Identification: The model identifies the main objects present in each video to provide an initial list of visual entities appearing in the scene, such as humans, vehicles, animals, and inanimate objects.

  • •

    Full Video Description and Background Generation: The model then generates a high-level description of the video, capturing not only the main objects but also the overall context of the scene. This includes background descriptions that characterize the environment, lighting, and any static elements in the scene that remain unchanged throughout the video.

    • Object Detection and Tracking. Once objects have been identified by the video captioning model, we proceed to detect and track the position of these objects across video frames.

  • •

    Initial Object Detection: Grounding DINO [(Liu et al., 2025)] detects the identified objects in the first frame and produces their initial bounding boxes.

  • •

    Object Tracking: After the initial detection, we use SAM 2 [(Ravi et al., 2025)] to track these objects across subsequent frames. SAM 2 allows us to maintain temporal consistency by tracking the same object across frames, even if it undergoes motion, partial occlusion, or appearance changes due to lighting or viewpoint shifts.

    • Object Captioning. In the final labeling step, we crop each tracked object and caption it frame by frame with an image captioning model.

  • •

    Object Descriptions: Each caption describes the object’s identity and appearance (e.g., “a red car”), which forms its persistent attribute.

  • •

    Temporal Captioning: Each caption also describes the object’s current status and action, with emphasis on status changes, which forms its dynamic status. For example, the red car might be described as “a red car driving down the road” in one frame and “a red car stopping at a traffic light” in another.

    • Structural Video Description with Element Breakdown. For gameplay datasets, we enhance the standard video description by including additional elements that are specific to game environments and interactions. This breakdown captures both the visual aspects and the dynamic game mechanics. Specifically, we expand on the following key elements:

  • •

    Spatial Layout: Descriptions of how objects are spatially arranged in the frame, such as their relative positioning and proximity to other objects or the camera. For example, “The racing car is positioned in the center of the track, ahead of the player’s car”.

  • •

    Action and Interaction Descriptions: These provide detailed information about how objects interact with each other. We annotate the relationship between the primary player-controlled entity and the adversaries or objectives. This captures the behavioral logic of a game, where the player’s actions directly influence the target’s state and vice-versa. For example, “The racing car aggressively closes the gap with the lead vehicle”.

  • •

    Background Descriptions: Beyond individual object interactions, broader scene descriptions are generated, focusing on the environment or setting where the objects exist. For example, “An urban street with tall skyscrapers, neon signs, and a crowd of pedestrians walking.”

item.title: 单卡跑 37.5 分钟不断片：WorldPager 把世界模型的 KV 摆到 NVMe 三层上，靠相机位姿提前预取做到零停顿 ｜ WorldPager: Zero-Stall Tiered Memory for Long-Horizon World Models on a Single Consumer GPU
item.description:
一句话：瓶颈是容量不是带宽，而访问集合在算之前就已知——因为相机位姿是输入。

要点：

  • 先量墙：Matrix-Game 2.0 的 KV 在 bf16 下 45 秒就吃满 32 GiB 主机内存，int4 也只撑到 2.8 分钟；模型自身的位置视野上限是 4.3 分钟
  • 关键观察有两条：这个记忆是容量受限而非带宽受限；访问集合在计算之前就能知道，因为相机位姿是输入而不是输出
  • 据此把 int4 KV 放进 GPU / DRAM / NVMe 三层而不是重算，按外推位姿预取下一块、miss 时从不等、后台回写；配 training-free 的位置处理，单张 4090 连续生成 37.5 分钟

为什么值得看：长时程世界模型的「记忆」问题，本质是显存/内存分层与预取调度，这类问题在引擎里已经解过很多遍（虚拟纹理、几何流送）。这篇的价值在于指出「访问集合可预测」——有了这条，KV 也能像资源一样被流送。

中文摘要：交互式世界模型会把过去 chunk 的 KV 当作检索记忆，好让 revisit 的地方保持一致。但在单张消费级机器上（一张 RTX 4090、32 GiB 主机内存、一块 NVMe SSD），长会话会撞两堵墙：容量上，Matrix-Game 2.0 的 KV 在 bf16 下 45 秒耗尽主机内存、int4 也只能到 2.8 分钟；视野上，模型的位置上限是 4.3 分钟。作者观察到这段记忆是容量受限而非带宽受限，而且访问集合在计算前就已知——因为相机位姿是输入。据此 WorldPager 把 int4 KV 放进 GPU/DRAM/NVMe 三层而不是重算，按外推位姿预取、从不等 miss、后台回写，配合 training-free 的位置处理，在单卡上连续生成 37.5 分钟。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-10-28

WorldPager: Zero-Stall Tiered Memory for Long-Horizon World Models on a Single Consumer GPU

Abstract

Interactive world models keep the KV of past chunks as retrieval memory so that revisited places stay consistent. On a single consumer machine (one RTX 4090, 32 GiB of host memory, one NVMe SSD), long sessions with such memory hit two walls. The first is capacity: the KV of Matrix-Game 2.0 exhausts host memory after 45 seconds of video in bf16 and after 2.8 minutes in int4. The second is the model’s positional horizon of 4.3 minutes. We show that this memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and that its access set is known before compute, because the camera pose is an input. An analytical model built on these observations predicts spill points to within one chunk and classifies zero versus non-zero stalls correctly on held-out configurations. Guided by it, WorldPager stores int4 KV in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk’s memory from the extrapolated pose, never waits on a miss, and writes back in the background; to our knowledge, it is the first to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With training-free position handling, it generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously with zero stalls and constant host memory, at about 9.5 frames per second. On a sealed test set, int4 storage shows no measurable quality loss; on long-gap revisits it lowers image quality by about one MUSIQ point.

I Introduction

Interactive world models generate video chunk by chunk in response to a user’s keyboard and mouse actions [1, 2, 3]. For such a world to stay consistent, a place the user returns to must look as it did before, and recent systems achieve this with retrieval memory: they keep the keys and values (KV) of past chunks and let a new chunk attend to the ones whose camera pose matches [4, 5]. These systems are evaluated on data-center GPUs. We study the same workload under tight resources: one consumer GPU (an RTX 4090 with 24 GB), a 32 GiB host-memory budget, and one NVMe SSD. The question is how long such a machine can keep generating a consistent world.

Two walls stop it, and Fig. 1 shows both for Matrix-Game 2.0 (MG2) [1]. The first wall is capacity. The KV of one chunk, 0.75 s of video, occupies 486.6 MB in bf16, and retrieval memory keeps all of it. Kept on the GPU, memory runs out at chunk 21 (16 s of video); kept in host memory, at chunk 60 (45 s); quantized to int4 and kept in host memory, at chunk 226 (2.8 minutes). The second wall is the positional horizon: the model’s rotary position table covers 1024 latent frames, and generation fails at chunk 341 (4.3 minutes) whatever the memory system.

Existing approaches do not remove these walls on a single consumer machine. LLM offloading systems move KV between GPU, host memory, and disk [6, 7, 8], but they are built on the premise that decoding is limited by the bandwidth of that movement, and those that load only a subset of entries must compute or speculate the access set at run time [7]. World-model memory systems keep KV on the GPU [4] or in host memory [5, 9, 10], which only moves the first wall from chunk 21 to chunk 60; WorldKV notes that transfer latency limits its CPU-offloaded variant [4]. WorldPlay [3] keeps frames and recomputes their KV for every chunk, which costs 3.07× a denoising step per retrieved chunk on our GPU. KV quantization [11, 12, 13] reduces bytes per chunk by a constant factor, which delays the first wall but does not remove it.

Our starting point is a characterization of this workload. World-model memory is capacity-bound, not bandwidth-bound: a chunk takes about 1.2 s to compute, while the KV it must read fits in that window many times over, even from NVMe. Its access set is also known before compute: the retrieval key is the camera pose, which follows from the control input. An operating system cannot prefetch reliably because the future page-reference string is unknown; here the control input makes that string known one chunk ahead. From these two properties we derive a first-order analytical model that predicts where each budget spills, how much bandwidth prefetching needs, and how long an on-demand design stalls, and we test it on configurations held out from its construction.

Guided by the model, we build WorldPager, a memory runtime that sits below the retrieval policy. It stores int4 KV in a GPU / pinned-DRAM / NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk’s retrieval set from the extrapolated pose while the previous chunk is denoised, falls back to the previous set on a miss instead of waiting, and writes spilled blocks back in the background. To cross the second wall it handles positions at inference time, without training: the position table is extended, which leaves the native horizon bit-identical, and retrieved memory is re-placed near the current frame beyond it, following established practice [14, 15, 16, 3].

We make three contributions.

  • •

    Two walls, characterized and modeled. We show that memory-augmented world models on a consumer machine hit a capacity wall long before a bandwidth limit, and a positional wall at the model’s native horizon. Our analytical model predicts the spill point, the bandwidth at which prefetching fails, and the stall of on-demand swap-in. On held-out configurations its eight spill-point and first-read predictions fall within one chunk, all 15 zero/non-zero stall predictions are correct, and 22 of 24 registered criteria on MG2 and int8 are met (Sec. II).

  • •

    Crossing the first wall. We store int4 KV instead of recomputing it and, to our knowledge, WorldPager is the first system to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With all retrieved KV read from NVMe, prefetching removes the 60 ms per-chunk stall of on-demand swap-in and keeps the median stall at zero down to 0.25 GB/s (Sec. III, Sec. IV-C).

  • •

    Crossing the second wall, end to end. With training-free position handling, one consumer machine generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously, instead of 45 seconds before host memory runs out (2.8 minutes with int4 alone), with zero stalls and constant host memory. Long-gap memory is read back from NVMe without stalls; int4 storage leaves revisit consistency unharmed and lowers long-gap image quality by about one MUSIQ point; on a sealed test set, int4 shows no measurable quality loss (Sec. IV-E, Sec. IV-F).

    • WorldPager does not make generation real-time: the 37.5 minutes of video take 63 minutes to generate (about 9.5 fps). Sec. V reports what did not work and why, and Sec. VII lists the limits of our evidence.

    II Two Walls: Characterization and an Analytical Model

    This section characterizes memory-augmented generation on our platform, identifies the two walls that bound a session, and turns the characterization into an analytical model whose predictions we test on configurations that were not used to build it.

    II-ASetting

    A chunk-wise interactive world model generates video one chunk at a time, conditioned on the user’s keyboard and mouse actions. MG2 [1] has 1.8B parameters including its action modules; a chunk is three latent frames, or 12 video frames (0.75 s at 16 fps), and is denoised in four steps. Attention covers an attention sink, a short local window, and, with retrieval memory, k=3 earlier chunks selected by camera pose [4, 5]. Retrieval memory therefore keeps the KV of every generated chunk, and that KV grows linearly with session length: one chunk occupies B_c=486.6 MB in bf16 across the 30 layers. Our platform is one RTX 4090 (24 GB), a 32 GiB host-memory budget, and one NVMe SSD (5.82 GB/s sequential read with O_DIRECT; 24–25 GB/s host-to-device copies from pinned memory).

    II-BThe first wall: capacity, not bandwidth

    Memory runs out long before moving it becomes a problem. Keeping retrieved KV on the GPU exhausts the 24 GB at chunk 21 (16 s of video). Counting allocated bytes alone gives an upper bound of 28 chunks; adding the allocator slack and non-PyTorch memory measured in the same run gives 21, which is a calibration rather than an independent prediction. Moving it to host memory in bf16 lasts until chunk 60 (45 s), and int4 storage until chunk 226 (2.8 min); all three points come before the model’s native limit of 341 chunks.

    Bandwidth, by contrast, is not the constraint. A chunk takes about 1.2 s to compute, and reading 1.46 GB (the KV of three bf16 chunks) from NVMe into pinned memory and on to the GPU takes 276 ms when the two stages are pipelined. With one chunk of double buffering, the read is hidden completely: in a microbenchmark with the real MG2 computation and synthetic transfer payloads, the stall is 0.0 ms for 0.37 GB and 1.46 GB payloads from DRAM and from NVMe, against 15.8 to 289.1 ms when the same payloads are copied synchronously. The working set per chunk is small compared with the compute window, while the total state grows without bound.

    This is the opposite of the premise of LLM offloading. Systems such as FlexGen [6] and InfiniGen [7] offload KV because decoding is limited by the bandwidth of moving it: a decoding step is short, so a transfer cannot hide behind it. Table I summarizes the contrast. We use this observation as the basis of the design; we do not claim the general observation that video diffusion is compute-heavy, which is well known.

    II-CThe access set is known before compute

    In LLM decoding with selective KV retrieval, the entries a step needs depend on its query, which exists only after the preceding computation; systems either select them on the critical path or speculate, as InfiniGen does by rehearsing the next layer’s attention [7]. (Coarser look-ahead exists, for example a fixed layer order [6] or a queue of waiting requests [8].) In an interactive world model, the retrieval key is the camera pose, which follows from the user’s actions. An operating system cannot prefetch reliably because the future page-reference string is unknown; here the control input makes the reference string known one chunk ahead. In practice the next action may not be known yet, so WorldPager extrapolates the pose, and the prediction can miss. On synthetic trajectories of four motion classes, constant-velocity extrapolation finds the retrieval set of the next chunk with a hit rate of 0.66–0.94, against 0.03–0.52 when the current pose is reused (CPU simulation, 50 trajectories of 800 chunks per class, assuming a 90° field of view). In the end-to-end runs, the fraction of retrieved blocks that the prefetch missed is 0.010 on a_yaw and 0.020 on b1_ws, and the stale-set fallback covers these cases.

    II-DThe second wall: the positional horizon

    MG2 encodes time with a rotary position table of 1024 latent frames, so with the original table generation fails at chunk 341 (about 4.3 minutes of video). This wall is independent of memory. Removing it by recomputing memory at new positions, as WorldPlay does [3], costs 3.07× a denoising step per retrieved chunk on our GPU (Sec. III-A); Sec. III-E handles it at inference time instead.

    II-EAn analytical model

    We turn the characterization into five first-order relations. Let B_c be the bytes stored per chunk, T_c the compute time of a chunk (the window available to hide a transfer), P the host-memory pool (the budget minus the process baseline and a 2 GiB margin), r_new the bytes a chunk must read from NVMe because they are not yet staged, and BW_R, BW_W the NVMe read and write bandwidths.

    N_fit=1+⌊P/B_c⌋(1)
    stall_prefetch≈\max (0, r_new/BW_R-T_c)(2)
    stall_on-demand≈r_new/BW_R+o(3)
    BW_W≥B_c/T_c(4)
    NVMe use≥(N-N_fit)·B_c(5)

    Eq. (1) gives the spill point, the chunk at which a DRAM-only design runs out of host memory and a tiered design starts writing to NVMe (the 1 is the attention sink). Eq. (2) gives the stall of prefetching and, by setting it to zero, the bandwidth below which prefetching fails, r_new/T_c. Eq. (3) gives the stall of on-demand swap-in, which cannot overlap with compute; o is a fixed per-chunk overhead of submitting 30 per-layer reads and copies, which we fit (about 34 ms) rather than measure.
