PowerInfer [23] serves LLMs on a consumer-grade GPU. Quest [24] shows that which KV entries matter depends on the query. The LLM setting differs from ours in two ways that change the design: a decoding step is short, so moving KV is bandwidth-bound, and a selective access set is known only after the query is computed. In a world model a chunk computes for about a second and its access set follows from the camera pose, which makes zero-stall prefetching from NVMe possible on a consumer machine.

    Long video beyond the native horizon. StreamingLLM [14] keeps attention-sink tokens and assigns positions within the cache. Rolling Forcing [15] re-applies RoPE to cached keys at effective indices so that they keep a fixed relative position to the frames being denoised, and Deep Forcing [16] shifts the temporal RoPE phase of sink tokens to the current timeline. WorldPlay applies a related reframing to retrieved memory in an interactive world model. WorldPager’s position handling follows this practice; we apply it to pose-retrieved long-term memory that may be read back from NVMe and enable it only beyond the native horizon, so that the first 341 chunks stay bit-identical.

    VII Limitations and Conclusion

    Limitations. Our evidence has the following scope.

  • •

    One machine, one drive. All timing comes from one RTX 4090 with one NVMe SSD; slower drives are emulated with a software token bucket, including the SATA-class case.

  • •

    One scene and one seed for timing. System measurements use one starting image and one seed per configuration (with up to five rollouts), so we do not report confidence intervals for them.

  • •

    Quality on one model. Image-quality and consistency results are for MG2 only; on LingBot-World retrieval did not improve consistency, so we report system metrics only for it.

  • •

    Long-gap image quality. int4 tiered storage lowers MUSIQ on long-gap revisits by about one point (-1.28 [-2.25, -0.36]), within the registered tolerance; scene 0000 keeps only two seeds after drifting runs are excluded.

  • •

    Long-range texture drift. Memory-conditioned generation develops a repeated texture after about 100 chunks, independently of KV precision (Sec. V).

  • •

    Model accuracy. Three held-out predictions miss (near the failure bandwidth, LingBot at 0.075 GB/s, and LingBot read-back volume), and int8 was emulated by byte accounting only.

  • •

    Speed. At about 9.5 frames per second, WorldPager generates video continuously but not in real time.

    • Conclusion. On a single consumer machine, long sessions of a memory-augmented world model stop at two walls: host memory runs out after 45 seconds of video, and the model’s positions run out after 4.3 minutes. The memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound, and its access set is known before compute, so an analytical model can predict where each budget spills and what bandwidth prefetching needs. WorldPager follows that model: it stores int4 KV in a GPU, DRAM, and NVMe hierarchy, prefetches from the extrapolated pose without ever waiting, writes back in the background, and handles positions at inference time. One RTX 4090 with 32 GiB of host memory and one NVMe drive then generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously, with zero stalls and constant host memory.

    Use of AI

    Large language models (Anthropic’s Claude) were used to draft and revise the text of this paper, to write the figure-generation scripts, and to write and run parts of the experiment code under the authors’ direction. All experimental designs were registered before the runs, every number in the paper was traced to a result file, and the authors reviewed the full text and take responsibility for its content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Per-scene and per-seed results for int4 versus bf16 long-gap recall

    Table IX lists, for each scene and seed, the paired differences (int4 minus bf16) averaged over the 13 revisit events of each gap tier, and the drift flag. A run is flagged when the two arms differ by more than two MUSIQ points on the outbound leg (chunks 3–299) or on the first-visit frames, that is, before any revisit.

item.title: agent 从建游戏到看数据全包：Summer 4.0 把整个引擎收成一个 API，Claude Code / Codex / Cursor 都能直接驱动 ｜ Summer 4.0, the Game Engine for AI Agents
item.description:
一句话：从写游戏、出美术音效、发布到读数据，全链路给 agent；发布/删除这类动作要先问人。

要点：

  • 任意 agent（Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Claude、ChatGPT）都能驱动：做完一款完整多人游戏、生成美术与音效、发布到 Summer Games、再回读表现数据
  • 此前的问题是引擎核心能被 agent 驱动，但 Summer 的其余部分只能以「一长串工具」的形式暴露；4.0 把它收成一条链、一个账号覆盖全部应用

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Blog·Summer Engine（English）

原文发布：2026-10-16

本期推送：2026-10-28

Your AI agent can now reach every part of Summer. Summer 4.0 is the game engine for AI agents. Any agent, from Claude Code, Codex and Cursor to Claude and ChatGPT, can use it. Your coding agent builds a full multiplayer game in Summer Engine, makes its art and sound, publishes it on Summer Games and then reads how it does. One link connects Summer's cloud. One Summer account covers every app. Publishing a game, live changes, deleting for good and contacting people ask you first.

Summer was always the game engine built for AI. Agents drove the engine well, but the rest of Summer reached them as a long list of tools that grew one feature at a time. 4.0 replaces that list with one catalog of operations. An agent finds the right action, knows what it will use from your credits, and knows when to ask you.

What is new in Summer 4.0?

  • One catalog for everything. Assets, publishing, analytics, plans, Summer Apps, the Studio and the engine are operations with plain names, such as 
    assets.generate_3d
    , 
    store.publish
    and 
    analytics.summary
    . The operations reference lists every one.
  • One link and one Summer account for every agent app.
  • A short list of everyday tools, including search and call for everything else.
  • The same commands in your terminal, as 
    summer
    .
  • Agent permissions. Building and generating run on their own. Publishing a game, live changes, deletes and invites ask you first.
  • Approval cards in your Studio tab when your agent needs you.
  • Agent activity with Undo, so you see what your agent changed and undo the changes that support it.
  • Auto top-up, so agents keep going when credits run low.
  • Versions for the ChatGPT and Claude app directories.

    • What does a game engine for AI agents need?

    An agent that makes games does more than edit scenes. It makes art, uploads a build, fills in a store page, checks the numbers and changes what players see. Each step touches a different service and carries a different risk. A wrong scene edit is undone with one key. A wrong store page reaches every player.

    So every operation in 4.0 follows the same rules:

  • Names in plain words. Each operation is 
    area.action
    , like 
    assets.search
    or 
    jobs.wait
    . The area is a word you would use yourself.
  • Typed input and one answer shape. One flat input, and the same kind of answer every time, so the agent never guesses.
  • A dry run for every change. The agent can ask what would happen before anything changes. For asset generation, the dry run shows the most credits it will use.
  • Jobs for long work. A 3D model or a video answers at once with a job, and the agent waits on it with 
    jobs.wait
    . Nothing in the cloud blocks for minutes.
  • One error shape. Out of credits or signed out, the answer has a stable code, a plain message and the next step to take. How Summer answers lists the codes.
  • A clear risk level. Each operation is marked by the strongest thing it can do: read, change your own drafts, spend credits, publish, change what players see, or delete for good. Your agent permissions decide which of those run without asking.

    • How do you connect any agent with one link?

    The Summer address works in every agent app that can add an MCP server by its address:

    https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp

    In Claude Code, run this in your terminal, then type 

    /mcp
    and sign in:

    claude mcp add --transport http summer https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp

    In Codex, run 

    codex mcp add summer --url https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp
    , then 
    codex mcp login summer
    . Cursor and VS Code take the address in their MCP config. Claude and ChatGPT take it as a custom connector. The Summer MCP page has the exact line for every app. The connect your agent guide covers Claude and ChatGPT step by step.

    The first time, a Summer sign-in page opens in your browser. Every app you connect after that uses the same Summer account and the same agent permissions.

    The link reaches everything that runs in Summer's cloud. To let your agent build and play the game in Summer Engine on your computer, add the local server too:

    npx -y summer-engine@latest setup claude-code --yes

    Replace 

    claude-code
    with your agent, or just tell your agent "Install Summer Engine and let's make a game." Already use Summer? Run 
    npx -y summer-engine@latest login
    once after you update.

    How does your agent find the right operation?

    The Summer link starts your agent with 20 tools for the everyday jobs: your account, Summer's docs, your games and projects, searching and generating assets, the store page and publishing, a game's numbers, and waiting on jobs. A short list keeps the agent fast and its context small.

    Everything else is two tools away. 

    summer_search
    takes plain words, like "set a new trailer on my store page", and returns the matching operation with its exact input. 
    summer_call
    runs it by name. The rules hold either way. Dry runs, permissions and approvals are checked on Summer's side, not in the prompt.

    Can you run the same commands in the terminal?

    Yes. Every operation is also a command, 

    summer
    , with its input as flags:

    summer whoami
summer ops search set a new trailer
summer assets generate-image --prompt "a cozy pixel-art tavern at night" --dry-run
summer analytics summary --game-id g_123 --days 7

    Without a global install, run them as 

    npx -y summer-engine
    . Add 
    --dry-run
    to see what would happen, 
    --wait
    to follow a job until it ends, and 
    --json
    to print the exact answer an agent gets. An agent with a terminal can script a hundred calls this way instead of making them one by one. The CLI reference has every flag.

    What can your agent do without asking?

    In Studio, Settings > Agent permissions shows six switches and their defaults. Publish and Prices and live changes show On, but today Summer Games still asks you first for those:

    PermissionWhat it coversToday
    Make and buildEdit drafts, plans and uploads, and start buildsRuns on its own
    Spend creditsGenerate assets and run paid builds, within your credits and auto top-up limitRuns on its own
    PublishPublish store pages, versions and releases. The game goes live as soon as Summer's automatic checks passAsks you once, as the game's owner
    Prices and live changesChange prices and sales, start or stop A/B tests, change member rolesAsks you
    Delete for goodDelete or remove things for goodAsks you
    Contact peopleSend invites and other emails to real peopleAsks you

    Reading never asks. Changing these switches yourself is coming soon, and only you will be able to turn one on. The permissions guide explains each group. A few things always ask: changing these permissions or auto top-up, entering a game jam (it agrees to the jam's rules) and changing your event limit.

    What happens when your agent needs your approval?

    When something needs you, the agent does not fail. It asks. If Summer Studio is open in your browser, a card appears in that tab. It starts with "Your agent wants to", says exactly what would change, before and after, and which agent asked. Owner requests show Approve and Decline. Other requests show the action's own word, such as Invite or Remove, and Cancel. With no Studio tab open, the agent gives you the link instead.

    Nothing changes until you press it. If what the request would change has changed since, it stops instead of overwriting.

    Publishing to Summer Games asks you once today. Your agent uploads the build, fills in the store page and sends you one link to publish. You approve once, then the game goes live as soon as Summer's automatic checks pass, with no review. Our guide to store art from your agent covers the store page itself, and the publishing docs cover the checks.

    How do you see and undo what your agent did?

    Under the switches, Agent activity lists what your agents changed or asked for through the Summer link, newest first, each marked Done, Waiting for you, Started or Undone. Changes to prices, sales, member roles, team names and the event limit have an Undo button. Only you can press it, and it runs once. For prices, roles and the event limit, it refuses if the value changed again since.

    How do agents keep going when credits run low?

    Generation and paid builds use your Summer credits. Before an asset generation runs, the agent can see the most credits it will use. When you run out, the answer says so and gives one link to add more.

    Auto top-up can keep your agents going. Turn it on in Studio on the Billing page or in the Add credits step. You set when credits fall below an amount, how much to add, and a monthly limit. Summer charges your saved card only by that rule, emails a receipt for every charge, and turns the rule off if a charge fails. Your agent never buys credits on its own.

    Is Summer in ChatGPT and Claude?

    Summer has versions made for the ChatGPT and Claude app directories. Each follows its store's rules. Every action is its own tool, with no search-and-run tool, and the ChatGPT version never shows checkout or billing links. Until the listings are live, add the Summer address as a custom connector in either app. The ChatGPT and Claude guide shows how.

    What does a full session look like?

    Each line is one ask to your agent.

  • "Make a two-player co-op game about frogs racing on lily pads." The agent builds it in Summer Engine and tests it with two players on your computer. Read how to add multiplayer to your game for that step.
  • "Make the frog model and a jump sound." The model runs as a job, and the sound comes back at once. Our post on game audio with your AI agent goes deeper.
  • "Publish it on Summer Games." The agent fills in the store page and sends you the publish link.
  • "How did it do this week?" The agent reads page views, launches, sessions and play time, with one reading of what to fix. It is the same data you see in Grow in Summer Studio.
  • "Invite sam@example.com to the team." Contacting people asks you first, so a card appears, and the invite goes out when you press Invite.

    • What are the limits today?

  • The engine runs on your computer. The hosted link cannot edit scenes. Add the local server for that. Scene edits show in the editor, where undo works, not in Agent activity.
  • Publishing asks you once, then the game goes live as soon as Summer's automatic checks pass.
  • Game numbers come from Summer Games. Games launched in other stores are not counted. The analytics guide explains what is tracked.
  • Some Grow tools are still rolling out, such as store page A/B tests.

    • What should you do next?

    Connect one agent with the link above and ask it what it can do for your game. Then let it make something.

    Tell your agent "Install Summer Engine and let's make a game."

    Frequently asked questions

    What is a game engine for AI agents?

    It is a game engine where an AI agent can do every step of making and running a game, not only edit code. In Summer 4.0, assets, publishing, analytics, plans and the Studio are one catalog of operations with plain names, typed inputs, dry runs and one error format, so any agent can find the right action and use it safely.

    Which AI agents work with Summer 4.0?

    Any agent app that can add an MCP server by its address, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Claude and ChatGPT. Agents with a terminal can also run the same operations as summer commands.

    What can my agent do without asking me?

    It can make and build, and spend credits within your credits and auto top-up limit. Today it asks you first before it publishes a game, makes a live change such as a price or an A/B test, changes a member, deletes anything for good or contacts a real person. Agent permissions in Studio settings shows the switches; changing them is coming soon.

    Can I undo what my agent did?

    Agent activity in Studio settings lists the changes and requests your agents made through the Summer link, newest first. Changes to prices, sales, member roles, team names and the event limit have an Undo button that only you can press.

    What happens when my agent runs out of credits?

    It stops, says it needs more credits, and gives one link to add more. If you turn on auto top-up, Summer adds credits from your saved card when your balance runs low, up to the monthly limit you set, so your agents keep running.

    Do the old Summer tool names still work?

    Yes. summer_call runs any earlier Summer tool name, within your agent permissions. While your installed Summer skills are older than 4.0, the local server also lists the earlier names again. Engine tools keep their names.

    All posts
  • MCP·Oct 16, 2026·6min read

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI. Add one link to your AI agent, or let it run Summer as commands in its terminal. Here is how both work.

  • MCP·Oct 16, 2026·9min read

    Designing an MCP Server for AI Agents

    How we went about designing an MCP server for AI agents in Summer MCP and CLI 4.0. One catalog, plain names, dry runs, retry keys and a 168-run eval.

  • MCP·Jun 7, 2026·5min read

    Summer Engine MCP Prompt Templates for AI Game Development

    Copyable prompts for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Devin Desktop, and other MCP agents using Summer Engine's MCP bridge.

要点：

  • 起点是承认 3.x 的失败：工具是一个一个长出来的，最终变成 agent 难以发现与组合的长清单——于是 4.0 重做成「每个能力一个带类型的操作」
  • 设计目标是让 agent 用平白的语言就能找到操作，并在真正执行前用 dry run 预检——把「猜工具」变成「查契约」
  • 作者用 168 次运行的评测来说明取舍，并明确写了哪里还不行（不是只讲成功）

为什么值得看：MCP 现在被当成万能胶，但「工具列表」和「可供 agent 推理的 API 契约」是两件事。这篇是目前少见的、带评测数字与失败清单的接口设计复盘，任何要把编辑器/引擎暴露给 agent 的团队都该先读。

中文摘要：Summer 团队把引擎重做成「一个 API」时，顺手写下这份给 agent 设计 MCP Server 的复盘：为什么推倒重来、选了什么、168 次运行的评测说明了什么、以及哪里还不行。核心判断是 3.x 的增长方式会失败——工具一个一个长出来，最后成为 agent 既难发现也难组合的长清单；4.0 改为「每个能力一个带类型的操作」，让 agent 用自然语言就能找到，并在执行前用 dry run 做预检，把「猜工具」换成「查契约」。发布同时包含 4.0 导览与 MCP/CLI 的安装方式，CLI、本地 MCP 与 skills 都放在一个开源包 summer-engine 里。对做引擎接口的人来说，这类带评测与失败清单的复盘，比功能列表有用得多。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Blog·Summer Engine（English）

原文发布：2026-10-16

本期推送：2026-10-28

Summer MCP and CLI 4.0 are out (npm 

summer-engine
4.2.0). Summer Engine is a game engine that AI agents drive, with a store, Summer Games, where the games go live. Every part of it is now one typed operation that your agent finds in plain words and checks with a dry run. This post is about designing an MCP server for AI agents: what we chose, why, what a 168-run eval showed, and where it falls short.

The tour of 4.0 is in Summer 4.0, the game engine for AI agents, and the setup lines are in Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI.

Why did we start over with one API?

Summer 3.x grew one tool at a time. Signed in, the last 3.x build listed 217 tools. Some tools mixed a read with a change. Asked to change a price on 3.x, one agent re-submitted the whole store page in 5 of 6 runs, because that tool happened to take a price too.

So 4.0 starts from one catalog. Each operation is declared once: a permanent name, a summary, one effect (read, write, spend, publish, change what players see, or delete), an input and output schema, and at least one example that a test checks against the input. The hosted MCP, the npm MCP, the CLI and the approval cards in Summer Studio are views of that catalog. A view adds no behavior, so a fix to an operation is a fix everywhere.

The catalog holds 320 operations: 229 run on Summer's servers and 91 on your computer, most of them in the Summer Engine editor. Each lives next to the code that runs it, and all pass one public contract schema. We share the contract, not the code, because the contract changes rarely and the operations change daily. The operations reference is generated from the same catalog.

How did we choose the names?

We asked the models first. Two fresh model runs got four tasks, such as a weekend sale, with only a one-line description of Summer, and were asked how they would most want to reach it.

Both asked for an MCP server with typed tools, plus a CLI that mirrors it. One wrote names like 

games.list
, 
analytics.summary
, 
store.publish
and 
jobs.wait
; the other wrote 
store_publish
. Both asked for dry runs, retry keys, job ids, structured errors, scoped permissions and an audit log.

So every name is 

area.action
; only 
whoami
stands alone. The area is a word a person uses, such as 
pricing
, and the action is usually a verb. A read and a change are never one operation. A name is permanent, so a new meaning gets a new name.

On MCP, 

store.get_listing
is the tool 
summer_store_get_listing
, because some clients reject dots in tool names. In a terminal it is 
summer store get-listing
. Two exceptions: engine tools kept their 3.x names, such as 
summer_add_node
, and makers kept 
summer_tool_
. 78% of the 3,141 tool mentions in our skills library name engine and file tools, so a rename would churn most skills for no gain.

Why search and call instead of 320 tools?

The hosted MCP lists 20 tools: 18 everyday operations, plus 

summer_search
and 
summer_call
. 
summer_search
takes the job in plain words and returns the matching operations with their exact input schema, so the next call needs no second lookup. 
summer_call
runs any operation by name, with the same input checks, dry runs and approvals as its own tool. Its MCP hints state the worst case, so clients ask before it runs.

Input tokens on the first model call, measured once per client (with no Summer server, about 2,700, or 13,161 in Codex CLI):

Client3.x4.0Change
npm server, client loads every tool147,36664,74756% less
Hosted server, client loads every tool43,06212,91570% less
npm server, Claude Code7,5015,93821% less
npm server, Codex CLI13,16113,161none

Claude Code and Codex already defer MCP tools, so they gain little or nothing. The 4.0 npm list still has 106 tools, because most of them are engine tools. Against 3.x with short descriptions and the engine toolset picked by hand, 4.0 saved 8%, and a hand-picked cloud-only 3.x toolset was smaller than 4.0. The gain over tuned 3.x is never picking toolsets by hand.

This only works if search is good, and in 4.0.0 it was not. "Publish my game" missed 

store.publish
. Agents in our eval searched with keywords, so they still found the right operation 50 of 55 times, but people type sentences. A test holds 35 real phrases, such as "lower my price", and all pass. It is live on the hosted server and in 4.2.0.

What does every answer look like?

Every operation answers one shape, on every surface:

{ "ok": true, "status": "done", "result": { "items": [] } }
{ "ok": true, "status": "running", "job": { "id": "gen:", "state": "running" } }
{ "ok": true, "status": "needs_approval",
  "approval": { "id": "apr_", "url": "https://www.summerengine.com/studio/approvals/apr_" },
  "job": { "id": "apr:", "state": "awaiting_approval" } }
{ "ok": false, "error": { "code": "no_credits", "message": "Not enough credits for this call.",
  "next": { "url": "https://www.summerengine.com/studio/credits", "label": "Add credits" }, "retry": "no" } }
  • Waiting for a person is a status, not an error.
    needs_approval
    tells the agent to hand you a link and wait, not to retry.
  • Slow cloud work never blocks. Anything that can take more than about 20 seconds answers 
    running
    with a job id, and 
    jobs.wait
    waits up to 50 seconds at a time. An engine export still blocks, by default up to 15 minutes.
  • Errors come from a closed list of 18 codes. Each has a plain message, at most one 
    next
    step (an operation, a link, or a sentence to tell you) and a 
    retry
    hint: 
    no
    , 
    safe
    , 
    same_key
    , or 
    after
    a wait. One step, not a list, so the agent does not have to choose. 
    invalid_input
    names the failed field in 
    details.path
    .

    • A last fix before 4.0.0 split the cloud failure that always said "sign in" into 

    not_signed_in
    , 
    forbidden
    , 
    unavailable
    and 
    outcome_unknown
    . The last means a change may have run: retry only with the same key, or check first. How Summer answers lists every code.

    How do dry runs and retry keys work?

    Every operation that changes something takes 

    dryRun: true
    . Summer checks the call and describes it, and nothing changes, is spent or is sent. The preview gives the approval a call needs, the estimated credits for generation, and before and after for publishing, live changes and deletes. The types enforce it: a spend operation cannot be defined without a cost estimate, and one that publishes, changes what players see or deletes cannot be defined without a preview.

    Every change on Summer's servers also takes an 

    idempotencyKey
    . The same key with the same input within 24 hours returns the first answer, marked 
    replayed
    , and never does the work twice. The same key with different input is an 
    idempotency_conflict
    . Publishing, releasing and the five price and sale changes require a key. Generation keeps it optional, because "the same prompt again" is often what you want. Engine edits on your computer have no retry key.

    What may an agent do without asking?

    Both blind-test runs asked for scoped permissions. Most operations that change something belong to one of six switches in Summer Studio under Settings > Agent permissions:

    SwitchDefaultOperations
    Make and buildOn120
    Spend creditsOn51
    PublishOn, but Summer Games still asks the owner today8
    Prices and live changesOn, but Summer Games still asks you today9
    Delete for goodOff, asks you18
    Contact peopleOff, asks you5

    The 104 reads never ask. Five operations always ask, such as auto top-up settings, and an agent can never turn a switch on by itself. The defaults trust the agent, and the approval card is the fallback.

    When something asks, the answer is 

    needs_approval
    with a link, and an open Studio tab shows a card too. The request is bound to its exact input. If the value changed since the agent asked, it ends 
    stale
    instead of overwriting. Agent activity lists what your agents did, with Undo for prices, sales, member roles, team names and the analytics event limit.

    What is live today: the switches show their defaults, and changing them is not available yet. Summer Games runs its own check on agent changes, and that check does not yet follow saved permissions. Until it does, an agent's publish always asks the game's owner, and price, A/B test and member changes always ask you. The agent permissions guide has the details.

    The approval lives on Summer's side, not in the prompt or the client, and 

    summer_call
    passes the same checks as a direct tool. For terminal agents, 
    npx -y summer-engine@latest setup claude-code --cli --allow-rules --yes
    adds allow rules for read commands and for dry runs of spend commands. Everything else still asks.

    How did we test 4.0 against 3.x?

    Right after 4.0.0 shipped, we ran 168 agent sessions: two clients (Claude Code and Codex CLI), four setups, seven tasks, three runs each. The setups were 3.x in full, 3.x tuned with short descriptions and toolsets picked per task, 4.0, and 4.0 with the old names too. The tasks were real asks, from "How did my game do this week?" (the numbers in Grow) to a price change, a publish and fixing an error on play. The npm server was real; the hosted server was a stand-in with the real catalog and search. Account and engine answers were fixtures with the real shapes.

  • Success was the same. 4.0 passed 21 of 21 in both clients. So did tuned 3.x.
  • No false claims. In all 168 runs, no agent said a change was live while it waited for approval. On 4.0, price, invite and publish gave the approval link 18 of 18 times.
  • The right operation. On 4.0, every price change used 
    pricing.set_base
    and every invite made an approval card. Our 3.x setup could not invite.
  • More first-try mistakes. 4.0 had 4 bad calls where tuned 3.x had none, such as 
    name
    instead of 
    op
    and a 
    limit
    over the maximum. Each was fixed on the next call, and 4.2.0 also accepts 
    name
    .
  • Upgrades hid the gain. While installed skills were older than 4.0, the old names stayed listed. That gave back about half the token saving, and Claude Code picked the old tools. 4.2.0 refreshes the skills on first start.

    • Three of our five pass rules held. The 50% token rule held only for clients that load every tool, and "no more bad calls than tuned 3.x" failed narrowly. The tasks were too easy to tell setups apart on success, three runs per cell is a small sample, and no editor client such as Cursor ran; the "loads every tool" rows count what such a client would load.

    What did we learn designing an MCP server for AI agents?

  • Ask a model with little context first. It named the operations the way agents look for them.
  • Test search with the sentences people type, not keywords.
  • Ship the switch with the gate. We showed the switches before Summer Games could follow them.

    • What comes next?

  • A harder eval with real accounts and a running engine.
  • An HTTP API and a typed SDK from the same catalog, for agents that script hundreds of calls. Specified, not built.
  • A tool list that follows use: once there is enough 4.0 data, the 18 direct operations are re-picked each month by how many people call each one. Telemetry records the operation name, never its arguments or results.

    • To try it, follow the MCP setup guide.

    Tell your agent "Install Summer Engine and let's make a game."

    Frequently asked questions

    What is Summer MCP and CLI 4.0?

    It is how AI agents use Summer Engine. Every part of Summer is one operation with a plain name such as store.publish or assets.generate_3d. Agents reach the operations through the hosted MCP at https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp, the local npm MCP, or the summer CLI in a terminal. The current npm release is summer-engine 4.2.0.

    Why not list every operation as its own MCP tool?

    A client that loads every tool pays for all of them before the agent reads a word. The hosted MCP lists 20 tools for everyday jobs, and summer_search finds any other operation on Summer's servers from plain words and returns its exact input. In our tests this cut the first model call by 70% on the hosted server for clients that load every tool. Clients that already defer tools, such as Claude Code and Codex, gained little.

    What do dry runs and idempotency keys do?

    A dry run checks a change and describes it, often with before and after and the credits it would use, and changes nothing. An idempotency key makes a retry of a change on Summer's servers safe. The same key with the same input within 24 hours returns the first answer again and never does the work twice. Publishing and price changes require a key.

    Can my agent publish or change prices without asking me?

    Not today. Agent permissions in Summer Studio show their defaults, and changing them comes soon. Until Summer Games follows saved permissions, an agent's publish asks the game's owner, and price, A/B test and member changes ask you. Your agent gives you an approval link, and nothing changes until you approve.

    How did you test Summer 4.0 against 3.x?

    We ran 168 agent sessions in Claude Code and Codex CLI, across four setups, seven real tasks and three runs each. 4.0 matched a tuned 3.x setup on success, and no run claimed a change was live while it waited for approval. Account and engine answers were fixtures, so the test did not touch a real account or a running engine.

    Do the old 3.x tool names still work?

    Yes, for all of 4.x. summer_call accepts any 3.x tool name and runs the operation that replaced it. Engine tools keep their 3.x names. To get the full 3.x tool list back, run the local server with --surface v3.

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI. Add one link to your AI agent, or let it run Summer as commands in its terminal. Here is how both work.

  • Summer Engine·Oct 16, 2026·8min read

    Summer 4.0, the Game Engine for AI Agents

    Summer 4.0 is the game engine for AI agents. Any agent can build your game, make its assets and publish it once you approve.

  • MCP·Jun 7, 2026·5min read

    Summer Engine MCP Prompt Templates for AI Game Development

    Copyable prompts for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Devin Desktop, and other MCP agents using Summer Engine's MCP bridge.

    adds allow rules for read commands and for dry runs of spend commands. Everything else still asks.

    How did we test 4.0 against 3.x?

    Right after 4.0.0 shipped, we ran 168 agent sessions: two clients (Claude Code and Codex CLI), four setups, seven tasks, three runs each. The setups were 3.x in full, 3.x tuned with short descriptions and toolsets picked per task, 4.0, and 4.0 with the old names too. The tasks were real asks, from "How did my game do this week?" (the numbers in Grow) to a price change, a publish and fixing an error on play. The npm server was real; the hosted server was a stand-in with the real catalog and search. Account and engine answers were fixtures with the real shapes.

  • Success was the same. 4.0 passed 21 of 21 in both clients. So did tuned 3.x.
  • No false claims. In all 168 runs, no agent said a change was live while it waited for approval. On 4.0, price, invite and publish gave the approval link 18 of 18 times.
  • The right operation. On 4.0, every price change used 
    pricing.set_base
    and every invite made an approval card. Our 3.x setup could not invite.
  • More first-try mistakes. 4.0 had 4 bad calls where tuned 3.x had none, such as 
    name
    instead of 
    op
    and a 
    limit
    over the maximum. Each was fixed on the next call, and 4.2.0 also accepts 
    name
    .
  • Upgrades hid the gain. While installed skills were older than 4.0, the old names stayed listed. That gave back about half the token saving, and Claude Code picked the old tools. 4.2.0 refreshes the skills on first start.

    • Three of our five pass rules held. The 50% token rule held only for clients that load every tool, and "no more bad calls than tuned 3.x" failed narrowly. The tasks were too easy to tell setups apart on success, three runs per cell is a small sample, and no editor client such as Cursor ran; the "loads every tool" rows count what such a client would load.

    What did we learn designing an MCP server for AI agents?

  • Ask a model with little context first. It named the operations the way agents look for them.
  • Test search with the sentences people type, not keywords.
  • Ship the switch with the gate. We showed the switches before Summer Games could follow them.

    • What comes next?

  • A harder eval with real accounts and a running engine.
  • An HTTP API and a typed SDK from the same catalog, for agents that script hundreds of calls. Specified, not built.
  • A tool list that follows use: once there is enough 4.0 data, the 18 direct operations are re-picked each month by how many people call each one. Telemetry records the operation name, never its arguments or results.

    • To try it, follow the MCP setup guide.

    Tell your agent "Install Summer Engine and let's make a game."

    Frequently asked questions

    What is Summer MCP and CLI 4.0?

    It is how AI agents use Summer Engine. Every part of Summer is one operation with a plain name such as store.publish or assets.generate_3d. Agents reach the operations through the hosted MCP at https://mcp.summerengine.com/mcp, the local npm MCP, or the summer CLI in a terminal. The current npm release is summer-engine 4.2.0.

    Why not list every operation as its own MCP tool?

    A client that loads every tool pays for all of them before the agent reads a word. The hosted MCP lists 20 tools for everyday jobs, and summer_search finds any other operation on Summer's servers from plain words and returns its exact input. In our tests this cut the first model call by 70% on the hosted server for clients that load every tool. Clients that already defer tools, such as Claude Code and Codex, gained little.

    What do dry runs and idempotency keys do?

    A dry run checks a change and describes it, often with before and after and the credits it would use, and changes nothing. An idempotency key makes a retry of a change on Summer's servers safe. The same key with the same input within 24 hours returns the first answer again and never does the work twice. Publishing and price changes require a key.

    Can my agent publish or change prices without asking me?

    Not today. Agent permissions in Summer Studio show their defaults, and changing them comes soon. Until Summer Games follows saved permissions, an agent's publish asks the game's owner, and price, A/B test and member changes ask you. Your agent gives you an approval link, and nothing changes until you approve.

    How did you test Summer 4.0 against 3.x?

    We ran 168 agent sessions in Claude Code and Codex CLI, across four setups, seven real tasks and three runs each. 4.0 matched a tuned 3.x setup on success, and no run claimed a change was live while it waited for approval. Account and engine answers were fixtures, so the test did not touch a real account or a running engine.

    Do the old 3.x tool names still work?

    Yes, for all of 4.x. summer_call accepts any 3.x tool name and runs the operation that replaced it. Engine tools keep their 3.x names. To get the full 3.x tool list back, run the local server with --surface v3.

    All posts
  • MCP·Oct 16, 2026·6min read

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI

    Summer Engine now comes as an MCP and a CLI. Add one link to your AI agent, or let it run Summer as commands in its terminal. Here is how both work.

  • Summer Engine·Oct 16, 2026·8min read

    Summer 4.0, the Game Engine for AI Agents

    Summer 4.0 is the game engine for AI agents. Any agent can build your game, make its assets and publish it once you approve.

  • MCP·Jun 7, 2026·5min read

    Summer Engine MCP Prompt Templates for AI Game Development

    Copyable prompts for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Devin Desktop, and other MCP agents using Summer Engine's MCP bridge.

item.title: Unity Spark：不装引擎、在浏览器里把游戏做出来，而且直连 Asset Store 的真人资产 ｜ Why we built Unity Spark
item.description:
一句话：和 Google 合作、浏览器内做游戏；官方明确反对「一句话吐一个完整游戏」那条路。

要点：

  • Unity 与 Google 合作推出 Unity Spark：在浏览器里制作与分享游戏，不需要 Unity 经验
  • 官方立场很直白地反对「one-shotting」——让 AI 复述一个已经存在的游戏并不能让人变成小岛秀夫，Spark 要的是能做、能打磨、能分享的真实交互体验
  • 差异点在资产：Spark 直连 Unity Asset Store，用的是社区里真人美术做的高质量资产，而不是让模型凭空生成全部美术

为什么值得看：大多数「AI 做游戏」产品把模型放在中心；Unity 这条把「资产来源」放在中心——直连商店意味着可商用、风格可控、且能继续打磨。对引擎团队，这更像一个提示：AI 化的入口可能不是生成，而是把已有资产的可达性做到极致。

中文摘要：Unity 与 Google 合作发布 Unity Spark：在浏览器里制作并分享游戏，不要求任何 Unity 或游戏开发经验。官方在文中花了不少笔墨划清立场——这不是「一句话出一个完整游戏」那类 one-shotting：让 AI 复述一个已经存在的游戏，不会让人变成小岛秀夫。Spark 的目标是让人做出真实的、独特的交互体验，并且值得继续打磨与分享。文章认为这一切从游戏美术开始，因此 Spark 直接连到 Unity Asset Store，用的是社区里真人美术创作的高质量资产（数千个），而不是让模型凭空生成全部美术。这条路线与「端到端生成」形成有意思的对照：它把 AI 放在降低门槛与加速迭代上，把资产质量交给生态。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Unity Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-07

本期推送：2026-10-28

Today, together with our partners at Google, we announced Unity Spark - a new way for people to come together to make and share games right in their browser, no prior Unity or game development experience required.

This isn’t about “one-shotting”. Asking AI to regurgitate an already invented game does not make you the next Hideo Kojima, any more than re-typing the first paragraph of War and Peace in your word processor makes you Tolstoy.

Unity Spark is about being able to create real, unique interactive experiences. To build something worth working on, polishing, and sharing. It’s about using the new technology to enable more people to express themselves. And it all begins with the game art. Unity Spark connects directly to the Unity Asset Store, so you can build with thousands of high-quality, artist-created assets made by our community.

We made Unity Spark for the gamers who have spent a thousand hours inside a genre and know exactly what’s missing. The graphic artist who wants to bring their vision to life but doesn’t know how to code. Modders who now want to create something entirely new. That's the opportunity we see: Folks with real creative conviction who can now fulfill their full potential.

Will some graduate to become professionals in our industry? Will some current professionals use Unity Spark as well to explore new ideas? We certainly hope both are true. We’ll see. One thing is certain: Trying to build a real game for yourself will only deepen the respect you have for the people who apply the art and craft of gamemaking at the highest level.

Making even rudimentary interactive entertainment is very hard, demanding expertise in many crafts - narrative, design, art, sound, UI, level design, front-and-back end development, systems design, scripting, just to name a few. Producing a polished experience of your own has long been beyond the capabilities of most people.

As a consequence, although about 3 billion people play a game made with Unity each month, almost none of them have ever made one. Electronic games are the last major form of entertainment that nearly everyone consumes but almost nobody creates. That’s something we’d like to help change.

We don't know exactly who will walk through this door, or what they'll make. That's the whole point. Democratizing game creation is Unity's founding mission. Unity Spark was incubated in that spirit. We can't wait to see what you build together.
