item.title: agent 做的游戏像灰盒？AnyGameRenderer 用 33B 视频模型把它渲染成成品画面，实体一个不多一个不少 ｜ AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark
item.description:
一句话：输入只要一段普通视频，输出换成成品美术，版面/相机/每个实体的位置与时序都不动。

要点：

  • 定位很具体：coding agent 几分钟就能做出可玩的小游戏，但画面是灰盒、彩色几何体和语义色块（programmer art）；这一层交给视频到视频的生成式渲染器来补
  • 输入门槛极低——普通视频即可，不需要引擎 G-buffer、逐物体类别标签或低模代理，灰盒/几何体/语义图/线框都能吃；输出必须保住实体对应关系：分组数量对、实体在该出现的帧出现
  • 实现是 LoRA 微调 MiniMax-H3 ref2va（33B 参考视频条件生成）；训练用约 1 万对视频，来自 38 个 agent 做的游戏、Unreal 程序化控制的群组数据、以及用 3D 盒检测重建配对真实游戏录像；自建 59 例 753 实体的实体级基准，时间匹配 50.9%→62.9%、漏掉的实体数量变化 34.7%→21.3%

为什么值得看：这是「AI 造的游戏怎么不像玩具」的正面回答：不重做引擎、不要求 agent 输出结构化 G-buffer，只在最后加一层视频级渲染器，并用实体级指标约束「别多画也别少画」。对做生成式内容的团队，这套「输入只要视频 + 实体对应关系可测」的组合最值得抄。

中文摘要：AI coding agent 现在几分钟就能造出可玩的小游戏，但成品通常是一副「程序员美术」：灰盒子、彩色几何体、扁平的语义色块。AnyGameRenderer 就是补这一层的视频到视频生成式渲染器：把这类画面换成带角色、动作细节与特效的高质量视觉，同时严格保持布局、相机与每个实体的位置与时序不变。它对输入的要求很低——普通视频即可，不需要引擎 G-buffer、逐物体类别标签或低模代理，灰盒、几何体、语义图、线框都能用；难点在于实体对应：分组数量要正确，实体要在该出现的帧出现。实现上是对 33B 的参考视频条件生成模型 MiniMax-H3 ref2va 做 LoRA 微调，训练数据约 1 万对，来自 38 个 agent 造的游戏、Unreal 程序化控制的群组渲染，以及用 3D 盒检测重建配对的真实录像；作者另建了 59 例、753 个实体的实体级基准，时间匹配率从 50.9% 提到 62.9%。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·生成式渲染（English）

原文发布：2026-10-25

本期推送：2026-10-28

AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark

October 25, 2026

Abstract

AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity’s position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses ∼10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.

1 Introduction

Coding agents and game-creation tools can now turn a one-paragraph prompt into a playable game in minutes, complete with game logic, physics, camera, win conditions, and working HUD [6]. What they cannot produce is good art. The output usually contains gray boxes, colored cylinders, and cones on flat-shaded ground. Human studios spend months replacing this kind of “programmer art” through modeling, texturing, and lighting. Splitting a game into an engine that manages state and a generative model that renders pixels has quickly become a common idea. Concurrent systems such as CWM [7], PWM [14], Matrix-Game 4.0 [31], StreamRender-H3 [28], Marionette [25], and SolarRenderer [32] all adopt it in some form. We do not argue for this setting. Instead, we build a rendering layer that is more general in what it accepts and more faithful in what it keeps.

As shown in Figure1, AnyGameRenderer takes a crude gameplay recording and a text prompt (optionally with a style anchor image), and outputs the same gameplay re-rendered in the prompted style, frame-aligned with the input. It adds characters, motion detail, and effects, while keeping the layout, camera, and every entity’s position and timing. This brings two practical benefits. A game can easily switch to a new visual style by changing only the prompt. It also makes vibe gaming faster, since a game only needs code and a blockout, without modeling, texturing or animation.

There are three properties that set AnyGameRenderer apart. (1) It generalizes across genres. Prior and concurrent works are demonstrated mainly on third-person, first-person, or driving footage, with limited coverage of the genres that agents actually produce. As illustrated in Figure1, AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres, including tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, crowd runners, arena survival, co-op games, and shooters. In addition, it accepts diverse input types, including gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, wireframes, and coarse mockup.

(2) It keeps entity correspondence. The hard part of game rendering is bookkeeping: twelve enemies become nine when three die; a reinforcement wave walks in at t=4.2 s; a tiny far-away mob must not dissolve into fog. AnyGameRenderer substantially improves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, entities appear and disappear on the right frame, and fewer small entities are lost. The zero-shot base model often fails here: entities never appear, colored blocks stay unrendered, and characters appear even when they are not in the input.

(3) Its input is plain video. Many concurrent systems rely on costly or complex representations, such as per-object class labels (StreamRender-H3, CWM), state-augmented 3D boxes (PWM), or low-poly engine proxies (Matrix-Game 4.0). AnyGameRenderer instead accepts whatever a crude game looks like, including gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic-colored maps, wireframes, and coarse clay figures, at different granularities and with one checkpoint.

To achieve these properties, we build paired (crude video, styled video) data from three sources. (i) Multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games helps the model generalize across genres and input types. (ii) Two-stream rendering in Unreal Engine uses scenes scripted with same-color groups that change count mid-clip, entity sizes from 20 to 600 px, and frame-aligned appearance and disappearance, teaching the model to keep entity correspondence. (iii) Real gameplay recordings, converted into crude inputs by 3D-box detection, help the model render realistic scenes. Together they yield 10,330 training clips.

Existing renderers are evaluated at the frame level, with edge agreement, point tracks, or pairwise judges, which cannot tell whether each entity is rendered correctly. We therefore design an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, each annotated with ground-truth boxes, and evaluate it with four metrics. Temporal match measures whether each entity appears and disappears on time; position match measures whether it stays at the right place; unrendered rate measures how often crude input blocks are left unrendered; and hallucination rate measures how often the output contains entities that do not exist in the input. Compared with the zero-shot base, AnyGameRenderer raises temporal match from 50.9% to 62.9% and position match from 57.1% to 61.9%, and lowers the unrendered rate from 4.1% to 2.9% and the hallucination rate from 52.1% to 46.0%.

Contributions.

  • •

    We propose a video-to-video generative renderer for games. A single checkpoint handles a wide range of genres and input types, renders them in diverse prompted styles, and preserves entity correspondence with the input.

  • •

    We build a paired dataset with three sources: multi-stream rendering data from agent-made games, two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine with scenarios designed for correspondence, and detection-based reconstruction from real gameplay recordings. Together they yield 10,330 training clips.

  • •

    We propose an entity-level benchmark and metrics for entity correspondence. The metrics measure whether each entity appears on time, stays in place, and is neither unrendered nor hallucinated. On this benchmark, AnyGameRenderer improves temporal match from 50.9% to 62.9% and reduces missed count changes from 34.7% to 21.3% over the zero-shot base.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 AI-driven game creation

    Early work uses large language models to generate game content such as levels and rules. MarioGPT [33] generates Super Mario Bros. levels from text, Word2World [27] turns stories into playable 2D tile worlds, and LLMGG [12] generates game rules and levels in the Video Game Description Language. Multi-agent frameworks such as GameGPT [5] split game development into roles that collaborate on a full project. More recently, coding agents build complete games end-to-end. Recursive Game Creator [6] iterates designer, builder, player and reviewer roles over HTML and Godot projects; OpenGame [16] is an open-source agentic framework for web games across genres such as action and tower defense. While these systems produce working game logic, their visuals are usually limited to simple shapes and placeholder assets, far from the art quality of commercial games.

    2.2 Interactive world models

    Another line of work replaces the game engine altogether: an autoregressive video model, conditioned on player actions, generates the next frames. Examples include Genie [3, 29, 1], GameNGen [35], Oasis [8], MineWorld [10], GameGen-X [4], GameFactory [40], Hunyuan-GameCraft [17, 34], the Matrix-Game line [11, 36, 9], and Yume [24, 23]. These models are strong simulators but hard to control in the ways a game needs: exact entity counts, scripted events, and rules that hold for minutes. Long-horizon memory [38, 39, 37, 21] reduces drift but does not make the world programmable.

    2.3 Generative rendering for games

    A growing body of work keeps the engine in charge of game state and uses a generative model only to render pixels. Neural forward rendering from G-buffers [18, 2, 41, 22] and earlier generative world renderers [15, 19] follow this split, but require engine-exact inputs. Several concurrent systems extend it to crude inputs that a game or an agent can produce cheaply. CWM [7] lets a coding agent maintain world state and renders a 12-class proxy video with a MiniMax-H3 LoRA. PWM [14] converts real AAA recordings into state-augmented 3D oriented boxes and renders them with a structured spatial ControlNet on a frozen backbone. Matrix-Game 4.0 [31] renders low-poly engine proxies in real time with a distilled causal DiT. StreamRender-H3 [28] streams a 13-class semantic map into video. SolarRenderer [32] trains a control LoRA on a frozen MiniMax-H3 with six types of structural video, passes them without type labels, and generalizes to structure types unseen in training; it also renders in four steps and supports streaming.

    AnyGameRenderer differs from these systems in three ways. First, they are demonstrated mainly on realistic third-person, driving, or a few self-built 3D scenes; our method generalizes across a wide range of genres, including tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, crowd runners, arena survival, co-op games, and shooters. Second, many of them rely on a fixed intermediate representation, while we take plain video. Third, none of them measures entity-level correspondence. Frame-level metrics barely change when a small entity is missing or a group arrives late, and edge agreement even rewards leaving crude blocks unrendered. We make correspondence, including the count, timing and position of every entity, the main target of both training data and evaluation.

    3 Method

    AnyGameRenderer treats game rendering as reference-conditioned video editing: given a crude gameplay recording (a plain reference video) and a caption saying what each crude entity stands for, it generates the same gameplay in a target style (Figure2). We design a caption schema to enforce entity correspondence (Section3.2).

    3.1 Task setting

    Task.

    Let Vᵢₙ∈ℝ^T×H×W×3 be a crude gameplay clip and c be a text prompt describing the target style and what each crude entity represents. AnyGameRenderer produces Vₒᵤₜ of the same length and resolution such that (i) camera, layout, and timing match Vᵢₙ frame by frame; (ii) every crude entity becomes its finished counterpart at the same position, apparent size, and heading, appearing and disappearing on the same frames; and (iii) appearance, including materials, lighting, character design, and environment, follows c and an optional anchor image Iₐ.

    Base model.

    We build on the ref2va mode of MiniMax-H3 [26], which edits a reference video according to a text prompt. We pass the crude clip as

    Conditioning.

    Each sample has three conditions: 1) the crude clip as reference video

    Trainable parameters.

    We train a LoRA [13] of rank 128 on all transformer blocks with the standard flow-matching objective [20], keeping the base weights frozen. All reported results use 20-step Euler sampling on base+LoRA.

    3.2 Caption schema: the correspondence contract

    We keep the base model’s six-segment format (subject_definitions, summary, retention_analysis, detailed_description, overall_soundscape, non_diegetic_music) and follow four rules, which we call the correspondence contract.

    Subjects are entities; crude shapes are their representation.

    Each subject is defined as the real entity, and the crude input is named as its representation, e.g., “every blue ellipsoid in

    Retention analysis fixes what follows the input.

    This segment declares position, apparent size, timing, and head count as preserved exactly, and leaves appearance to the prompt. It also describes empty space positively: “areas empty in

    Positive assertions only.

    The base model has no negative prompt, and negative phrasing tends to produce what it names (“no HUD” reliably produces a HUD). All captions are therefore written as positive statements.

    Programmatic captions with deliberate noise.

    Captions are generated automatically from engine metadata and detection results, not written by hand. Each caption lists every character that may appear in the game, even if some never show up in the clip. We keep this noise on purpose: it teaches the model to decide what exists from the video, not from the text. As a result, the model rarely adds characters that are named in the caption but missing from the input.

    3.3 Training recipe

    Unified format.

    All sources are resampled to 124-frame clips at 24 fps (5.17 s) and 1344×768, with the target’s first frame as the anchor and a silent 32 kHz audio track. Latents and text embeddings are cached once per source.

    Optimization.

    We train a rank-128 LoRA on all blocks with a global batch size of 16. The learning rate warms up over 100 steps and then follows a cosine decay, with a peak between 2×10⁻⁵ and 2.8×10⁻⁵; weight decay is 0.01. We use bf16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and block swapping, while FlashAttention-3 [30] speeds up each step by about 30%. Training runs on 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs (141 GB). Each step takes about 129 s, and three epochs over all 10,330 training clips take about 48 hours.

    Deployment.

    We use a LoRA multiplier of 1.0 for in-domain inputs and styles. For out-of-domain text-only styles (no anchor image, and a style unseen in training), a multiplier of 0.7 recovers the zero-shot visual quality while keeping the correspondence gains. We recommend it as the default for open-ended styling.

    4 Data

    We build (crude video, styled video) pairs from three sources: multi-stream rendering data from agent-made games covers different genres and input types; two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine targets entity correspondence; and real gameplay recordings add realistic layouts, cameras, and motion. In every pair, the crude and styled videos share the same camera and layout and are frame-aligned by construction.

    4.1 Agent-made games

    Our multi-stream rendering data comprises 38 agent-made games, covering shooters, survivors, tower defense, kart racing, arena, and co-op designs. This source contributes 3,221 clips. Each clip has five aligned passes: the target render; a primitive pass, where the scene is a gray blockout and characters are simple geometric shapes; a coarse pass, with a more detailed blockout and low-poly clay figures; a 12-class semantic map; and depth. Each clip also comes with an anchor image, a caption, and 3D boxes. We train on the pair of primitive and target.

    4.2 Unreal Engine

    Each Unreal Engine scene uses two-stream rendering: it is rendered from the same simulation and camera as a gray blockout with colored blocks for characters and as a full render. The protagonist is always blue, and other characters use a six-color set.

    Rather than collecting generic gameplay, we script scenes around the zero-shot failures (see examples in Figure3) to ensure entity correspondence:

  • •

    Count changes in same-color groups. Groups of 2 to 20 characters walk in, spawn, walk out, or despawn during the clip, in dense clusters, columns, or scattered formations. This targets crowds left as unrendered blocks and entities that appear late or never.

  • •

    Characters of different colors entering and leaving. This targets wrong entry and exit timing when several character types share a scene.

  • •

    Entity sizes from 20 to 600 pixels, including boss-sized characters and characters moving toward or away from the camera. This targets small, distant entities that dissolve into the background.

  • •

    Mixed camera views: 35% follow, 30% top-down, 20% isometric, and 15% side. This keeps the model from relying on a single viewpoint.

    • We keep clips where the protagonist is visible in at least 95% of frames. Each clip carries metadata on the scene, characters, colors, and events, from which its caption is generated. This source contributes 3,910 clips.

    4.3 Real gameplay recordings

    Following the reconstruction approach in PWM [14], we convert real gameplay recordings of combat, driving, and pedestrian scenes into crude inputs. We detect 3D bounding boxes in each frame and render them over a checkerboard ground as proxies of varied shapes: solid boxes, wireframe boxes, cylinders, and upright ellipsoids, with about 800 clips per shape. The original recording is the target, and captions come from the detection labels plus one sentence describing the environment. This source adds real-world scenes, with realistic camera work and vehicle and pedestrian motion. It contributes 3,199 clips.

    The three sources are mixed at roughly equal weight (Table1), giving 10,330 clips of 124 frames, about 14.8 hours of paired video.

    5 Experiments

    We first describe the evaluation protocol (Section5.1), then evaluate entity correspondence (Section5.2) and generalization across genres (Section5.3).

    5.1 Evaluation protocol

    Benchmark.

    The benchmark contains 59 cases with 753 annotated entities: 11 held-out two-stream rendering cases from Unreal Engine (gray blockouts), 14 real recordings with detected solid boxes, and 34 multi-stream rendering cases from six held-out agent-made games. Each case uses a source clip excluded from training, rendered in a style or with characters not seen in training. All models are run with the same seed, 20 sampling steps, and the same captions.

    Entity-sync metrics.

    Input entities are the ground-truth 2D boxes shipped with each crude video; entities that exist for fewer than 12 frames are ignored. In the generated video, we locate characters with SAM3 open-vocabulary segmentation, prompted with the caption’s subject phrases plus generic person and vehicle terms. We remove shadow and reflection detections and link the remaining detections into tracks. In each frame, input boxes and detections are matched with the Hungarian method, and a pair is accepted only if IoU≥0.3 or the centroid offset is within half the input box size. We report four main metrics, averaged over entities:

  • •

    Temporal match: the IoU between the frames in which an entity exists in the input and the frames in which its track is in place. Late or missing appearance, lingering after despawn, and identity swaps all lower it.

  • •

    Position match: 1-d/(0.5 s) on matched frames, where d is the centroid offset and s is the input box size.

  • •

    Unrendered rate: the fraction of entity-frames in which the input block is still visible as a flat color patch.

  • •

    Hallucination rate: the fraction of detected entity-frames that belong to tracks matching no input entity.

    • We also report three secondary statistics:

  • •

    On-time appearance: an entity is recognized at the first frame t where it is matched in both t and t+1, giving an onset delay Δₒₙ=t-tᵢₙ, where tᵢₙ is its first frame in the input. An entity is on time if |Δₒₙ|≤4 frames (≈0.17 s).

  • •

    Never appears: the fraction of entities that are never recognized.

  • •

    Missed count changes: a count change is a rise of at least two entities in the input within six frames, nᵢₙ[t+3]-nᵢₙ[t-3]≥2, with target count nᵢₙ[t+8]. It is reproduced if, within the next 60 frames, the detected count stays at or above the target minus one for three consecutive frames. We report the fraction of the 75 count changes in the benchmark that are missed.

    • The GT floor in Table2 runs the ground-truth RGB video through the same pipeline and marks the best score the pipeline can measure.

    5.2 Entity correspondence

    Quantitative results.

    Table2 reports results on all 59 cases and on each source. Over all cases, our method improves all four main metrics: temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, position match from 57.1% to 61.9%, the unrendered rate falls from 4.1% to 2.9%, and the hallucination rate falls from 52.1% to 46.0%. The secondary statistics show the same trend. On-time appearance rises from 55.9% to 67.6%, entities that never appear fall from 26.0% to 20.2%, and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%.

    Gains differ by source. On the multi-stream rendering cases from agent-made games, temporal match rises by 13 points and missed count changes nearly halve. On Unreal Engine’s two-stream rendering cases, temporal match reaches 96.6%, close to the GT floor of 98.5%, and no entity is missed. Real recordings improve the least: temporal match rises from 46.5% to 51.1%, the unrendered rate is similar, and missed count changes stay at 20.0%.

    Qualitative comparison.

    Figure4 shows seven held-out cases. The zero-shot model works well on sparse scenes with clean captions, but on game footage it fails in three ways. First, it leaves crude shapes in the output: blue cubes in an orchard, cyan cylinders in an arena, and a blue cylinder in the grass where an elk should be. Second, it drops the input viewpoint when the style is far from typical game footage, turning a top-down blockout into a frontal anime group shot or a first-person Minecraft-like scene. Third, it adds characters named in the caption that have no block in the input. AnyGameRenderer fixes all three in these cases while keeping the prompted style.

    5.3 Generalization across genres

    A single checkpoint handles all five genres in our benchmark: first-person shooters, top-down, third-person, crowd, and vehicle games (Figure5). AnyGameRenderer improves temporal match over the zero-shot model in every genre, with the largest gains on crowd and third-person games. It also lowers the unrendered rate in every genre except crowd games, where both models are already near zero, and improves position match most on vehicle games. The hallucination rate falls on crowd games but rises slightly on top-down and third-person games. Top-down games remain the hardest, with low temporal match for both models.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns the programmer art of agent-made games into high-quality visuals. We train a single LoRA on MiniMax-H3, using paired data from agent-made games, Unreal Engine’s two-stream rendering, and real gameplay recordings. The resulting checkpoint handles a wide range of genres. It takes plain video as input, from gray blockouts and colored primitives to semantic maps and wireframes. It also keeps entities in sync with the input. On a held-out benchmark, temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%. As coding agents build more and more games, we believe a general renderer that keeps every entity in place will help these games look as good as they play.

    7 Acknowledgments

    We thank Zheng-Hui Huang for providing the real gameplay recordings and the detection method used to process it. We also thank Xiaojie Xu and Zhengyuan Lin for providing the Unreal Engine rendering repository.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：输入只要一段普通视频，输出换成成品美术，版面/相机/每个实体的位置与时序都不动。

要点：

  • 定位很具体：coding agent 几分钟就能做出可玩的小游戏，但画面是灰盒、彩色几何体和语义色块（programmer art）；这一层交给视频到视频的生成式渲染器来补
  • 输入门槛极低——普通视频即可，不需要引擎 G-buffer、逐物体类别标签或低模代理，灰盒/几何体/语义图/线框都能吃；输出必须保住实体对应关系：分组数量对、实体在该出现的帧出现
  • 实现是 LoRA 微调 MiniMax-H3 ref2va（33B 参考视频条件生成）；训练用约 1 万对视频，来自 38 个 agent 做的游戏、Unreal 程序化控制的群组数据、以及用 3D 盒检测重建配对真实游戏录像；自建 59 例 753 实体的实体级基准，时间匹配 50.9%→62.9%、漏掉的实体数量变化 34.7%→21.3%

为什么值得看：这是「AI 造的游戏怎么不像玩具」的正面回答：不重做引擎、不要求 agent 输出结构化 G-buffer，只在最后加一层视频级渲染器，并用实体级指标约束「别多画也别少画」。对做生成式内容的团队，这套「输入只要视频 + 实体对应关系可测」的组合最值得抄。

中文摘要：AI coding agent 现在几分钟就能造出可玩的小游戏，但成品通常是一副「程序员美术」：灰盒子、彩色几何体、扁平的语义色块。AnyGameRenderer 就是补这一层的视频到视频生成式渲染器：把这类画面换成带角色、动作细节与特效的高质量视觉，同时严格保持布局、相机与每个实体的位置与时序不变。它对输入的要求很低——普通视频即可，不需要引擎 G-buffer、逐物体类别标签或低模代理，灰盒、几何体、语义图、线框都能用；难点在于实体对应：分组数量要正确，实体要在该出现的帧出现。实现上是对 33B 的参考视频条件生成模型 MiniMax-H3 ref2va 做 LoRA 微调，训练数据约 1 万对，来自 38 个 agent 造的游戏、Unreal 程序化控制的群组渲染，以及用 3D 盒检测重建配对的真实录像；作者另建了 59 例、753 个实体的实体级基准，时间匹配率从 50.9% 提到 62.9%。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·生成式渲染（English）

原文发布：2026-10-25

本期推送：2026-10-28

AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark

October 25, 2026

Abstract

AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity’s position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses ∼10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.

1 Introduction

Coding agents and game-creation tools can now turn a one-paragraph prompt into a playable game in minutes, complete with game logic, physics, camera, win conditions, and working HUD [6]. What they cannot produce is good art. The output usually contains gray boxes, colored cylinders, and cones on flat-shaded ground. Human studios spend months replacing this kind of “programmer art” through modeling, texturing, and lighting. Splitting a game into an engine that manages state and a generative model that renders pixels has quickly become a common idea. Concurrent systems such as CWM [7], PWM [14], Matrix-Game 4.0 [31], StreamRender-H3 [28], Marionette [25], and SolarRenderer [32] all adopt it in some form. We do not argue for this setting. Instead, we build a rendering layer that is more general in what it accepts and more faithful in what it keeps.

As shown in Figure1, AnyGameRenderer takes a crude gameplay recording and a text prompt (optionally with a style anchor image), and outputs the same gameplay re-rendered in the prompted style, frame-aligned with the input. It adds characters, motion detail, and effects, while keeping the layout, camera, and every entity’s position and timing. This brings two practical benefits. A game can easily switch to a new visual style by changing only the prompt. It also makes vibe gaming faster, since a game only needs code and a blockout, without modeling, texturing or animation.

There are three properties that set AnyGameRenderer apart. (1) It generalizes across genres. Prior and concurrent works are demonstrated mainly on third-person, first-person, or driving footage, with limited coverage of the genres that agents actually produce. As illustrated in Figure1, AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres, including tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, crowd runners, arena survival, co-op games, and shooters. In addition, it accepts diverse input types, including gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, wireframes, and coarse mockup.

(2) It keeps entity correspondence. The hard part of game rendering is bookkeeping: twelve enemies become nine when three die; a reinforcement wave walks in at t=4.2 s; a tiny far-away mob must not dissolve into fog. AnyGameRenderer substantially improves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, entities appear and disappear on the right frame, and fewer small entities are lost. The zero-shot base model often fails here: entities never appear, colored blocks stay unrendered, and characters appear even when they are not in the input.

(3) Its input is plain video. Many concurrent systems rely on costly or complex representations, such as per-object class labels (StreamRender-H3, CWM), state-augmented 3D boxes (PWM), or low-poly engine proxies (Matrix-Game 4.0). AnyGameRenderer instead accepts whatever a crude game looks like, including gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic-colored maps, wireframes, and coarse clay figures, at different granularities and with one checkpoint.

To achieve these properties, we build paired (crude video, styled video) data from three sources. (i) Multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games helps the model generalize across genres and input types. (ii) Two-stream rendering in Unreal Engine uses scenes scripted with same-color groups that change count mid-clip, entity sizes from 20 to 600 px, and frame-aligned appearance and disappearance, teaching the model to keep entity correspondence. (iii) Real gameplay recordings, converted into crude inputs by 3D-box detection, help the model render realistic scenes. Together they yield 10,330 training clips.

Existing renderers are evaluated at the frame level, with edge agreement, point tracks, or pairwise judges, which cannot tell whether each entity is rendered correctly. We therefore design an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, each annotated with ground-truth boxes, and evaluate it with four metrics. Temporal match measures whether each entity appears and disappears on time; position match measures whether it stays at the right place; unrendered rate measures how often crude input blocks are left unrendered; and hallucination rate measures how often the output contains entities that do not exist in the input. Compared with the zero-shot base, AnyGameRenderer raises temporal match from 50.9% to 62.9% and position match from 57.1% to 61.9%, and lowers the unrendered rate from 4.1% to 2.9% and the hallucination rate from 52.1% to 46.0%.

Contributions.

  • •

    We propose a video-to-video generative renderer for games. A single checkpoint handles a wide range of genres and input types, renders them in diverse prompted styles, and preserves entity correspondence with the input.

  • •

    We build a paired dataset with three sources: multi-stream rendering data from agent-made games, two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine with scenarios designed for correspondence, and detection-based reconstruction from real gameplay recordings. Together they yield 10,330 training clips.

  • •

    We propose an entity-level benchmark and metrics for entity correspondence. The metrics measure whether each entity appears on time, stays in place, and is neither unrendered nor hallucinated. On this benchmark, AnyGameRenderer improves temporal match from 50.9% to 62.9% and reduces missed count changes from 34.7% to 21.3% over the zero-shot base.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 AI-driven game creation

    Early work uses large language models to generate game content such as levels and rules. MarioGPT [33] generates Super Mario Bros. levels from text, Word2World [27] turns stories into playable 2D tile worlds, and LLMGG [12] generates game rules and levels in the Video Game Description Language. Multi-agent frameworks such as GameGPT [5] split game development into roles that collaborate on a full project. More recently, coding agents build complete games end-to-end. Recursive Game Creator [6] iterates designer, builder, player and reviewer roles over HTML and Godot projects; OpenGame [16] is an open-source agentic framework for web games across genres such as action and tower defense. While these systems produce working game logic, their visuals are usually limited to simple shapes and placeholder assets, far from the art quality of commercial games.

    2.2 Interactive world models

    Another line of work replaces the game engine altogether: an autoregressive video model, conditioned on player actions, generates the next frames. Examples include Genie [3, 29, 1], GameNGen [35], Oasis [8], MineWorld [10], GameGen-X [4], GameFactory [40], Hunyuan-GameCraft [17, 34], the Matrix-Game line [11, 36, 9], and Yume [24, 23]. These models are strong simulators but hard to control in the ways a game needs: exact entity counts, scripted events, and rules that hold for minutes. Long-horizon memory [38, 39, 37, 21] reduces drift but does not make the world programmable.

    2.3 Generative rendering for games

    A growing body of work keeps the engine in charge of game state and uses a generative model only to render pixels. Neural forward rendering from G-buffers [18, 2, 41, 22] and earlier generative world renderers [15, 19] follow this split, but require engine-exact inputs. Several concurrent systems extend it to crude inputs that a game or an agent can produce cheaply. CWM [7] lets a coding agent maintain world state and renders a 12-class proxy video with a MiniMax-H3 LoRA. PWM [14] converts real AAA recordings into state-augmented 3D oriented boxes and renders them with a structured spatial ControlNet on a frozen backbone. Matrix-Game 4.0 [31] renders low-poly engine proxies in real time with a distilled causal DiT. StreamRender-H3 [28] streams a 13-class semantic map into video. SolarRenderer [32] trains a control LoRA on a frozen MiniMax-H3 with six types of structural video, passes them without type labels, and generalizes to structure types unseen in training; it also renders in four steps and supports streaming.

    AnyGameRenderer differs from these systems in three ways. First, they are demonstrated mainly on realistic third-person, driving, or a few self-built 3D scenes; our method generalizes across a wide range of genres, including tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, crowd runners, arena survival, co-op games, and shooters. Second, many of them rely on a fixed intermediate representation, while we take plain video. Third, none of them measures entity-level correspondence. Frame-level metrics barely change when a small entity is missing or a group arrives late, and edge agreement even rewards leaving crude blocks unrendered. We make correspondence, including the count, timing and position of every entity, the main target of both training data and evaluation.

    3 Method

    Rather than collecting generic gameplay, we script scenes around the zero-shot failures (see examples in Figure3) to ensure entity correspondence:

  • •

    Count changes in same-color groups. Groups of 2 to 20 characters walk in, spawn, walk out, or despawn during the clip, in dense clusters, columns, or scattered formations. This targets crowds left as unrendered blocks and entities that appear late or never.

  • •

    Characters of different colors entering and leaving. This targets wrong entry and exit timing when several character types share a scene.

  • •

    Entity sizes from 20 to 600 pixels, including boss-sized characters and characters moving toward or away from the camera. This targets small, distant entities that dissolve into the background.

  • •

    Mixed camera views: 35% follow, 30% top-down, 20% isometric, and 15% side. This keeps the model from relying on a single viewpoint.

    • We keep clips where the protagonist is visible in at least 95% of frames. Each clip carries metadata on the scene, characters, colors, and events, from which its caption is generated. This source contributes 3,910 clips.

    4.3 Real gameplay recordings

    Following the reconstruction approach in PWM [14], we convert real gameplay recordings of combat, driving, and pedestrian scenes into crude inputs. We detect 3D bounding boxes in each frame and render them over a checkerboard ground as proxies of varied shapes: solid boxes, wireframe boxes, cylinders, and upright ellipsoids, with about 800 clips per shape. The original recording is the target, and captions come from the detection labels plus one sentence describing the environment. This source adds real-world scenes, with realistic camera work and vehicle and pedestrian motion. It contributes 3,199 clips.

    The three sources are mixed at roughly equal weight (Table1), giving 10,330 clips of 124 frames, about 14.8 hours of paired video.

    5 Experiments

    We first describe the evaluation protocol (Section5.1), then evaluate entity correspondence (Section5.2) and generalization across genres (Section5.3).

    5.1 Evaluation protocol

    Benchmark.

    The benchmark contains 59 cases with 753 annotated entities: 11 held-out two-stream rendering cases from Unreal Engine (gray blockouts), 14 real recordings with detected solid boxes, and 34 multi-stream rendering cases from six held-out agent-made games. Each case uses a source clip excluded from training, rendered in a style or with characters not seen in training. All models are run with the same seed, 20 sampling steps, and the same captions.

    Entity-sync metrics.

    Input entities are the ground-truth 2D boxes shipped with each crude video; entities that exist for fewer than 12 frames are ignored. In the generated video, we locate characters with SAM3 open-vocabulary segmentation, prompted with the caption’s subject phrases plus generic person and vehicle terms. We remove shadow and reflection detections and link the remaining detections into tracks. In each frame, input boxes and detections are matched with the Hungarian method, and a pair is accepted only if IoU≥0.3 or the centroid offset is within half the input box size. We report four main metrics, averaged over entities:

  • •

    Temporal match: the IoU between the frames in which an entity exists in the input and the frames in which its track is in place. Late or missing appearance, lingering after despawn, and identity swaps all lower it.

  • •

    Position match: 1-d/(0.5 s) on matched frames, where d is the centroid offset and s is the input box size.

  • •

    Unrendered rate: the fraction of entity-frames in which the input block is still visible as a flat color patch.

  • •

    Hallucination rate: the fraction of detected entity-frames that belong to tracks matching no input entity.

    • We also report three secondary statistics:

  • •

    On-time appearance: an entity is recognized at the first frame t where it is matched in both t and t+1, giving an onset delay Δₒₙ=t-tᵢₙ, where tᵢₙ is its first frame in the input. An entity is on time if |Δₒₙ|≤4 frames (≈0.17 s).

  • •

    Never appears: the fraction of entities that are never recognized.

  • •

    Missed count changes: a count change is a rise of at least two entities in the input within six frames, nᵢₙ[t+3]-nᵢₙ[t-3]≥2, with target count nᵢₙ[t+8]. It is reproduced if, within the next 60 frames, the detected count stays at or above the target minus one for three consecutive frames. We report the fraction of the 75 count changes in the benchmark that are missed.

    • The GT floor in Table2 runs the ground-truth RGB video through the same pipeline and marks the best score the pipeline can measure.

    5.2 Entity correspondence

    Quantitative results.

    Table2 reports results on all 59 cases and on each source. Over all cases, our method improves all four main metrics: temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, position match from 57.1% to 61.9%, the unrendered rate falls from 4.1% to 2.9%, and the hallucination rate falls from 52.1% to 46.0%. The secondary statistics show the same trend. On-time appearance rises from 55.9% to 67.6%, entities that never appear fall from 26.0% to 20.2%, and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%.

    Gains differ by source. On the multi-stream rendering cases from agent-made games, temporal match rises by 13 points and missed count changes nearly halve. On Unreal Engine’s two-stream rendering cases, temporal match reaches 96.6%, close to the GT floor of 98.5%, and no entity is missed. Real recordings improve the least: temporal match rises from 46.5% to 51.1%, the unrendered rate is similar, and missed count changes stay at 20.0%.

    Qualitative comparison.

    Figure4 shows seven held-out cases. The zero-shot model works well on sparse scenes with clean captions, but on game footage it fails in three ways. First, it leaves crude shapes in the output: blue cubes in an orchard, cyan cylinders in an arena, and a blue cylinder in the grass where an elk should be. Second, it drops the input viewpoint when the style is far from typical game footage, turning a top-down blockout into a frontal anime group shot or a first-person Minecraft-like scene. Third, it adds characters named in the caption that have no block in the input. AnyGameRenderer fixes all three in these cases while keeping the prompted style.

    5.3 Generalization across genres

    A single checkpoint handles all five genres in our benchmark: first-person shooters, top-down, third-person, crowd, and vehicle games (Figure5). AnyGameRenderer improves temporal match over the zero-shot model in every genre, with the largest gains on crowd and third-person games. It also lowers the unrendered rate in every genre except crowd games, where both models are already near zero, and improves position match most on vehicle games. The hallucination rate falls on crowd games but rises slightly on top-down and third-person games. Top-down games remain the hardest, with low temporal match for both models.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns the programmer art of agent-made games into high-quality visuals. We train a single LoRA on MiniMax-H3, using paired data from agent-made games, Unreal Engine’s two-stream rendering, and real gameplay recordings. The resulting checkpoint handles a wide range of genres. It takes plain video as input, from gray blockouts and colored primitives to semantic maps and wireframes. It also keeps entities in sync with the input. On a held-out benchmark, temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%. As coding agents build more and more games, we believe a general renderer that keeps every entity in place will help these games look as good as they play.

    7 Acknowledgments

    We thank Zheng-Hui Huang for providing the real gameplay recordings and the detection method used to process it. We also thank Xiaojie Xu and Zhengyuan Lin for providing the Unreal Engine rendering repository.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: DLSS 5 上 RTX Spark：10 月模型比 9 月快 2 倍，4K 下显存再省 20%、GPU 开销减半 ｜ NVIDIA RTX Spark Powers Neural Rendering and AI Characters in Games
item.description:
一句话：128 GB 统一内存的新 PC 平台，DLSS 5 与 ACE 一起上；模型一个月内又提速一倍。

要点：

  • RTX Spark 是面向 AI 开发、创作与游戏的 Windows PC 平台，最高 128 GB 统一内存，带完整 CUDA 栈与光追/DLSS 5
  • DLSS 5（3D 引导神经渲染）在 RTX Spark 上跑起来，首发作品是 NBA 2K27；10 月模型比 9 月版快 2 倍，GPU 开销减半，4K 下显存占用再降 20%
  • 同批还有 ACE 的端侧 AI 角色、Nemotron 3.5 系列与 RTX Kit 的多项更新

为什么值得看：两个数字值得记：神经渲染模型在上线后一个月还能再快一倍，说明这条路的成本曲线还在快速下降；而「4K 省 20% 显存」直接决定了能不能和传统管线共存。做渲染预算的人应当把这类月度更新当成变量，而不是一次性选型。

中文摘要：NVIDIA 把 RTX Spark 定位成面向 AI 开发、创作与游戏的 Windows PC 平台：最高 128 GB 统一内存，配完整 CUDA 栈，并包含光追与 DLSS 5。DLSS 5 的 3D 引导神经渲染已在 RTX Spark 上运行，首发作品是 NBA 2K27；更值得注意的是迭代速度——10 月版本的模型比 9 月快 2 倍，GPU 开销减半，4K 下显存占用再降 20%。同批更新还包括 ACE 的端侧 AI 角色能力、Nemotron 3.5 系列以及 RTX Kit 的多项改进。对做渲染预算的团队，这意味着神经渲染不再是一个「选定就不动」的模块：它的性能与显存画像每个月都在变，规划时得把它当变量。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：NVIDIA Developer（English）

原文发布：2026-10-27

本期推送：2026-10-28

Content Creation / Rendering

NVIDIA RTX Spark Powers Neural Rendering and AI Characters in Games

Oct 27, 2026 By Phillip Singh
  • L
  • T
  • F
  • R
  • E
  • NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new Windows PC platform for AI development, creation, and gaming in slim laptops and compact desktops, combining up to 128 GB of unified memory with the full NVIDIA CUDA stack and RTX technologies including ray tracing and DLSS 5.
  • DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering runs on RTX Spark, starting with NBA 2K27, and an October model update runs 2x faster than the September version while halving GPU overhead and reducing VRAM use at 4K by 20%.
  • Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB offers ~40% higher average quality against the prior model on relevant benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens versus peers, enabling responsive local AI character interactions on GeForce RTX and RTX Spark.
  • NVIDIA RTX Kit brings eight neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark, including RTX Neural Texture Compression, RTX Mega Geometry, and RTX Character Rendering for strand-based hair and skin with path tracing.
  • NVIDIA Nsight tools support graphics developer workflows across native Arm64, emulated x64, and Arm64EC applications on RTX Spark from day one, with Nsight Graphics 2026.3 introducing a Windows on Arm installer and Nsight Systems 2026.5 providing a single installer for all Windows versions.
  • The NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 provides an updated foundation for advanced ray tracing and neural graphics in UE 5.8 projects, while MotionBricks adds new SOMA human-motion models, downloadable checkpoints, ONNX exports, and an interactive reference implementation built with Newton.

    • Next Steps

  • Download the In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK to access Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB for on-device AI characters.
  • Download Nsight Graphics for RTX Spark to capture, inspect, and profile frames for native Arm64 and emulated applications.
  • Explore the RTX Neural Texture Compression repository to integrate AI-powered texture compression into game projects.
    • Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more

    NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new Windows PC platform for AI development, creation, and gaming in slim laptops and compact desktops. Powered by an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and NVIDIA Grace CPU, it combines up to 128 GB of unified memory with the full NVIDIA CUDA stack and RTX technologies including ray tracing and DLSS 5.

    This post covers the following technologies for game developers building on RTX Spark:

  • DLSS suite of technologies that boost FPS and improve image quality
  • NVIDIA ACE updates for responsive, on-device AI characters
  • RTX Kit SDKs for neural rendering, geometry, and character rendering
  • NVIDIA Nsight tools for optimizing and debugging native Arm64 and x64 applications
  • NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 for integrating RTX technologies into your Unreal Engine projects
  • MotionBricks update for human-character motion

    • DLSS on RTX Spark

    RTX Spark benefits from the full suite of DLSS technologies in supported games, including Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, and 3D-Guided Neural Rendering.

    DLSS Super Resolution reconstructs frames from a lower resolution input to improve performance. DLSS Ray Reconstruction generates additional pixels to enhance ray-traced scenes. DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation can generate up to 5 additional frames per rendered frame, automatically adjusting the multiplier to maximize smoothness.

    The latest NVIDIA app beta also brings a faster Performance Mode (Preset C) for Frame Generation, with minor trade-offs in image quality.

    DLSS 5 brings 3D-Guided Neural Rendering to RTX Spark

    DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering is supported on NVIDIA RTX Spark, starting with NBA 2K27.

    An October model update runs 2x faster than the September version and halves GPU overhead while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. It also reduces VRAM use at 4K by 20%. The model will ship by default in future DLSS 5 games.

    For developers, DLSS 5 adds a final stage to the graphics pipeline that enhances lighting and material detail. The engine-rendered frame, including artist-designed geometry, textures, and lighting buffers, remains the foundation, while developer controls determine what can change. Avalanche Software has taken advantage of DLSS 5’s SDK controls to tune the integration to maintain the artistic intent and style of the game.

    Read the full DLSS 5 update here.

    DLSS 4.5 Unreal Engine plugin

    The updatedNVIDIA DLSS 4.5 plugin for Unreal Engine gives developers powerful tools for delivering sharper images and smoother gameplay. Its second-generation transformer model for Super Resolution improves image stability, anti-aliasing, and visual clarity, while Ray Reconstruction enhances ray-traced image quality.

    On supported GeForce RTX 50 Series and RTX PRO Blackwell GPUs, Dynamic Multi Frame Generation adapts the frame-generation multiplier as workloads change, with 6x Multi Frame Generation producing up to five additional frames per rendered frame.

    A key addition in plugin version 8.9.0 is official Windows on Arm (WoA) support for Unreal Engine 5.8. Native ARM64 binaries and support for building and packaging UE 5.8 applications give developers a supported path to bring DLSS-enabled projects to RTX Spark systems. Alongside updated Streamline and NGX components and fixes for UE 5.8 Frame Generation issues, this release expands the plugin’s platform reach and helps developers prepare their applications for RTX Spark.

    NVIDIA ACE introduces Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for on-device AI characters

    NVIDIA ACE is our technology suite for creating in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences, and we’ve shared two exciting showcases this year:

  • PUBG rolled out AI teammates in a public beta powered by our first-generation Nemotron small language model (SLM). It helped new players land their first chicken dinners and generated viral clips across social media.
  • Aniimo debuted our more efficient second-generation Nemotron SLM, turning standard in-game pets into responsive AI companions that react to your voice. Players can check in on their pets’ feelings or teach them new tricks, which will bring a new level of immersion when it releases in early 2027.

    • More intelligence, less memory

    Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is now available. This model offers ~40% higher average quality against our prior model on relevant benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens vs peers.

    It is purpose-built to power richer, faster in-game character interactions, with strong conversational capability, autonomous multi-turn tool use, instruction adherence, and grounding to game state, all running locally on GeForce RTX and RTX Spark.

    Engineered for maximum intelligence and speed per GB of memory, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB enables responsive local experiences while preserving headroom for graphics rendering and local speech models. Key features include:

  • Multi-turn tool use: Call application APIs to carry out tasks across a conversation, with integration guidance for asynchronous tool calls
  • Conversational mode: Toggle to encourage concise, speech-ready responses for natural back-and-forth interactions.
  • Configurable reasoning: Enable reasoning for complex requests or disable it for faster responses, with integration options to cap thinking to meet latency targets.
  • 64k context: Accommodate conversation history, instructions, tool definitions, retrieved information and game state.
  • Multilingual capability: Support for 35 languages, building on a base model pre-trained on more than 140 languages.

    • Get started with NVIDIA ACE

    Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is available to developers via the In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK.

    To test it in a game, check out SkyrimNET, an AI NPC modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character with personal memory, voice, and autonomy, enabling dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly. The platform supports both cloud and local inference across multiple language models.

  • Download the SkyrimNET Plugin:GitHub Repository
  • Download the ARM-Supported Loader:Mod Organizer Release

    • NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark

    NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering, complex geometry, and realistic character rendering to game development. Eight RTX Kit technologies are published with support for RTX Spark:

  • RTX Neural Texture Compression (NTC): Uses AI to shrink texture storage while maintaining visual fidelity comparable to traditional block compression.
  • RTX Texture Filtering: Uses stochastic texture sampling after shading to reduce artifacts and improve image quality, including for difficult volumes.
  • RTX Neural Shaders: Lets developers train neural networks and run them within shaders for new asset compression and approximation techniques.
  • RTX Mega Geometry: Speeds up bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) construction for cluster-based geometry, helping developers ray trace more triangles and improve performance in complex scenes.
  • NVIDIA Real-Time Denoisers (NRD): Provides denoisers for diffuse and specular lighting and shadows, producing cleaner images from low ray-per-pixel inputs.
  • RTX Character Rendering: Provides tools for rendering strand-based hair and skin with path tracing, including subsurface scattering and Blackwell-accelerated hair primitives.
  • RTX Global Illumination (RTXGI): Provides several techniques for efficient indirect lighting for ray traced and path traced applications.
  • Opacity Micro-Maps (OMM): Used to accelerate ray tracing of high detail geometry by efficiently encoding the opacity states of micro-triangles and micro meshes.

    • Optimizing and debugging RTX Spark applications

    NVIDIA Nsight tools are ready for RTX Spark from day one, supporting graphics developer workflows across native Arm64, emulated x64, and Arm64EC applications.

    Nsight Graphics lets developers capture, inspect, and profile individual frames, examining every draw call, shader, and resource to diagnose rendering bugs and tune GPU performance. Nsight Graphics release 2026.3 introduces a new Windows on Arm installer for RTX Spark systems, supporting native Arm64 target applications as well as emulated x64 and Arm64EC targets.

    Nsight Systems delivers a system-wide view of application performance, correlating CPU threads, GPU workloads, API calls, and memory activity on a single timeline so developers can pinpoint bottlenecks and balance work across the platform. Starting with Nsight Systems 2026.5, a single installer for all versions of Windows supports both native Arm64 and emulated applications.

    Nsight Aftermath helps teams resolve GPU crashes and hangs by generating detailed crash dumps that show what the GPU was doing at the moment of failure, both during development and in the field. Nsight Aftermath SDK 2026.3 includes a Windows on Arm version for integrating into native Arm64 applications. Crash dumps from emulated x64 applications will continue to function as expected with the x64 version of the SDK.

  • Download Nsight Graphics for RTX Spark here
  • Download Nsight Systems for RTX Spark here
  • Download Nsight Aftermath SDK for RTX Spark here

    • NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8

    The release ofNVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 (NvRTX 5.8) gives developers an updated foundation for bringing advanced ray tracing and neural graphics to UE 5.8 projects. This update focuses on codebase refactoring, stabilization, and compatibility improvements. Developers can access the branch source through GitHub to integrate and customize NVIDIA RTX technologies for their games and applications.

    Simplify runtime character animation with MotionBricks

    MotionBricks is open-source research for generating character motion in real time. Rather than hand-authoring every transition and wiring it into an increasingly complex animation graph, developers guide motion through target poses. MotionBricks generates the connecting movement at runtime and adapts as player input or game event changes.PaperGitHub

    The model supports control over speed, direction, and movement style, along with pose-guided interactions such as sitting and picking up objects. These capabilities let developers build varied character behaviors through a common pose-based interface. The original research demonstration shows these behaviors working together in Unreal Engine. Research demonstrations

    The update builds on this work with:

  • New SOMA human-motion models, alongside the existing G1 robot model.
  • Downloadable checkpoints, ONNX exports, and export tools for developers building their own integrations.
  • An interactive reference implementation built with Newton, demonstrating pose-guided human and robot motion.

    • MotionBricks is provided as research code and models. The Unreal Engine integration shown in the research demonstration is not included in this release.

    Resources for game developers

    Check out the full list of game developer resources and stay up to date with the latest NVIDIA game development news:

  • Subscribe to our newsletter (select gaming as your industry)
  • Follow us on social: X, LinkedIn, Facebook, and YouTube
  • Join our Discord community

    • Tags

    Content Creation / Rendering | Gaming | DLSS | Nsight Tools - Graphics | RTX Kit | Intermediate Technical | News | ACE | DGX Spark | Unreal Engine

    About the Authors

    About Phillip Singh
    Phillip Singh is a senior developer marketing manager at NVIDIA, specializing in games and consumer AI. He is dedicated to empowering the next generation of game developers through neural rendering and AI graphics technology. Phillip earned his master's in business administration from the Santa Clara University Leavey School of Business. View all posts by Phillip Singh
