Alongside updated Streamline and NGX components and fixes for UE 5.8 Frame Generation issues, this release expands the plugin’s platform reach and helps developers prepare their applications for RTX Spark.

    NVIDIA ACE introduces Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for on-device AI characters

    NVIDIA ACE is our technology suite for creating in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences, and we’ve shared two exciting showcases this year:

  • PUBG rolled out AI teammates in a public beta powered by our first-generation Nemotron small language model (SLM). It helped new players land their first chicken dinners and generated viral clips across social media.
  • Aniimo debuted our more efficient second-generation Nemotron SLM, turning standard in-game pets into responsive AI companions that react to your voice. Players can check in on their pets’ feelings or teach them new tricks, which will bring a new level of immersion when it releases in early 2027.

    • More intelligence, less memory

    Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is now available. This model offers ~40% higher average quality against our prior model on relevant benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens vs peers.

    It is purpose-built to power richer, faster in-game character interactions, with strong conversational capability, autonomous multi-turn tool use, instruction adherence, and grounding to game state, all running locally on GeForce RTX and RTX Spark.

    Engineered for maximum intelligence and speed per GB of memory, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB enables responsive local experiences while preserving headroom for graphics rendering and local speech models. Key features include:

  • Multi-turn tool use: Call application APIs to carry out tasks across a conversation, with integration guidance for asynchronous tool calls
  • Conversational mode: Toggle to encourage concise, speech-ready responses for natural back-and-forth interactions.
  • Configurable reasoning: Enable reasoning for complex requests or disable it for faster responses, with integration options to cap thinking to meet latency targets.
  • 64k context: Accommodate conversation history, instructions, tool definitions, retrieved information and game state.
  • Multilingual capability: Support for 35 languages, building on a base model pre-trained on more than 140 languages.

    • Get started with NVIDIA ACE

    Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is available to developers via the In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK.

    To test it in a game, check out SkyrimNET, an AI NPC modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character with personal memory, voice, and autonomy, enabling dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly. The platform supports both cloud and local inference across multiple language models.

  • Download the SkyrimNET Plugin:GitHub Repository
  • Download the ARM-Supported Loader:Mod Organizer Release

    • NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark

    NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering, complex geometry, and realistic character rendering to game development. Eight RTX Kit technologies are published with support for RTX Spark:

  • RTX Neural Texture Compression (NTC): Uses AI to shrink texture storage while maintaining visual fidelity comparable to traditional block compression.
  • RTX Texture Filtering: Uses stochastic texture sampling after shading to reduce artifacts and improve image quality, including for difficult volumes.
  • RTX Neural Shaders: Lets developers train neural networks and run them within shaders for new asset compression and approximation techniques.
  • RTX Mega Geometry: Speeds up bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) construction for cluster-based geometry, helping developers ray trace more triangles and improve performance in complex scenes.
  • NVIDIA Real-Time Denoisers (NRD): Provides denoisers for diffuse and specular lighting and shadows, producing cleaner images from low ray-per-pixel inputs.
  • RTX Character Rendering: Provides tools for rendering strand-based hair and skin with path tracing, including subsurface scattering and Blackwell-accelerated hair primitives.
  • RTX Global Illumination (RTXGI): Provides several techniques for efficient indirect lighting for ray traced and path traced applications.
  • Opacity Micro-Maps (OMM): Used to accelerate ray tracing of high detail geometry by efficiently encoding the opacity states of micro-triangles and micro meshes.

    • Optimizing and debugging RTX Spark applications

    NVIDIA Nsight tools are ready for RTX Spark from day one, supporting graphics developer workflows across native Arm64, emulated x64, and Arm64EC applications.

    Nsight Graphics lets developers capture, inspect, and profile individual frames, examining every draw call, shader, and resource to diagnose rendering bugs and tune GPU performance. Nsight Graphics release 2026.3 introduces a new Windows on Arm installer for RTX Spark systems, supporting native Arm64 target applications as well as emulated x64 and Arm64EC targets.

    Nsight Systems delivers a system-wide view of application performance, correlating CPU threads, GPU workloads, API calls, and memory activity on a single timeline so developers can pinpoint bottlenecks and balance work across the platform. Starting with Nsight Systems 2026.5, a single installer for all versions of Windows supports both native Arm64 and emulated applications.

    Nsight Aftermath helps teams resolve GPU crashes and hangs by generating detailed crash dumps that show what the GPU was doing at the moment of failure, both during development and in the field. Nsight Aftermath SDK 2026.3 includes a Windows on Arm version for integrating into native Arm64 applications. Crash dumps from emulated x64 applications will continue to function as expected with the x64 version of the SDK.

  • Download Nsight Graphics for RTX Spark here
  • Download Nsight Systems for RTX Spark here
  • Download Nsight Aftermath SDK for RTX Spark here

    • NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8

    The release ofNVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 (NvRTX 5.8) gives developers an updated foundation for bringing advanced ray tracing and neural graphics to UE 5.8 projects. This update focuses on codebase refactoring, stabilization, and compatibility improvements. Developers can access the branch source through GitHub to integrate and customize NVIDIA RTX technologies for their games and applications.

    Simplify runtime character animation with MotionBricks

    MotionBricks is open-source research for generating character motion in real time. Rather than hand-authoring every transition and wiring it into an increasingly complex animation graph, developers guide motion through target poses. MotionBricks generates the connecting movement at runtime and adapts as player input or game event changes.PaperGitHub

    The model supports control over speed, direction, and movement style, along with pose-guided interactions such as sitting and picking up objects. These capabilities let developers build varied character behaviors through a common pose-based interface. The original research demonstration shows these behaviors working together in Unreal Engine. Research demonstrations

    The update builds on this work with:

  • New SOMA human-motion models, alongside the existing G1 robot model.
  • Downloadable checkpoints, ONNX exports, and export tools for developers building their own integrations.
  • An interactive reference implementation built with Newton, demonstrating pose-guided human and robot motion.

    • MotionBricks is provided as research code and models. The Unreal Engine integration shown in the research demonstration is not included in this release.

    Resources for game developers

    Check out the full list of game developer resources and stay up to date with the latest NVIDIA game development news:

  • Subscribe to our newsletter (select gaming as your industry)
  • Follow us on social: X, LinkedIn, Facebook, and YouTube
  • Join our Discord community

    • Tags

    Content Creation / Rendering | Gaming | DLSS | Nsight Tools - Graphics | RTX Kit | Intermediate Technical | News | ACE | DGX Spark | Unreal Engine

    About the Authors

    About Phillip Singh
    Phillip Singh is a senior developer marketing manager at NVIDIA, specializing in games and consumer AI. He is dedicated to empowering the next generation of game developers through neural rendering and AI graphics technology. Phillip earned his master's in business administration from the Santa Clara University Leavey School of Business. View all posts by Phillip Singh

item.title: NPC 对话的首 token 要 7.8 倍快、输入价 48% 更低：Inworld 自建推理层，90% 提示走缓存 ｜ Introducing Inworld Inference
item.description:
一句话：同硬件多服务 1.8 倍请求、90% 提示命中缓存且最多省 99%，99.999% 请求无错。

要点：

  • 首 token 比 OpenRouter 中位供应商快至 7.8 倍；输入价格比中位低至 48%，且在不拿用户数据训练的服务里最低
  • 同样硬件上多服务 1.8 倍请求，同时首 token 中位时延下降；单条提示最多 90% 走缓存，缓存部分最多省 99%
  • 99.999% 请求无错误完成——这组数字针对的正是游戏里 NPC 对话最怕的「说不出来/说一半断」

为什么值得看：NPC 对话的工程瓶颈从来不是模型质量，而是首 token 延迟、单位成本与稳定性。Inworld 把这三项一起公布，等于给「AI NPC 能不能上线」提供了一组可对标的基准线。

中文摘要：Inworld 推出自建推理层 Inworld Inference，并给出四组可对标的数据：首 token 比 OpenRouter 中位供应商快至 7.8 倍；输入价格比中位供应商低至 48%，且是不拿用户数据训练的服务里最低的；同样硬件上可多服务 1.8 倍请求，同时首 token 中位时延还下降；单条提示最多 90% 走缓存，缓存部分最多省 99%；99.999% 的请求无错误完成。这组指标恰好对应 AI NPC 上线时最痛的三件事——延迟、成本与稳定性，而不是模型跑分。作者同时在文中说明了这批能力面向的是「给个人用的 AI」这一波应用，游戏内角色对话是其直接场景。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：Inworld AI（English）

原文发布：2026-10-14

本期推送：2026-10-28

Key resultsup to 7.8×faster first token than the median provider on OpenRouterup to 48%lower input price than the median provider, and the lowest of any that doesn't train on your data1.8×more requests served on the same hardware, while median time to first token improvesup to 90%of each prompt served from cache, at up to 99% off99.999%of requests completed without an error

AI's first wave was built for companies. Developers have felt it, and so have finance teams, but most people haven't yet seen AI change their lives. The bigger wave is built for people: a tutor on the commute, a coach mid-run, a language partner who waits for you to finish your sentence, someone to talk to after a hard day. Today only 2% of US households, and 3% of US consumers, spend anything on AI.[7] Consumer AI is where the internet was in 1995.

Building for people is a different engineering problem. In consumer AI, latency is revenue: when a reply is slow, people go back to tapping buttons. Every turn resends the whole history, so prompts run 13 to 36 times longer than replies. One interaction fans out into many model calls, from moderation and memory to ranking and the reply itself. People pay $5 to $20 a month, or nothing, so each of those calls has to cost almost nothing. And when a consumer app goes down for ten minutes, its users leave for another one, while an enterprise workflow just waits.

The big labs and most inference providers have doubled down on enterprise and coding. Consumer AI needs the opposite on every count. So we built Inworld Inference, the first inference service designed for consumer AI, and today it is open to every developer.

Rather than list thousands of models, we go deep on the open models consumer apps choose. Each one, from Gemma 4 to GLM, DeepSeek and MiMo, gets its own serving build: new attention kernels, realtime decoding where a small draft writes ahead and the full model checks it in one pass, lower-precision weights wherever the evals hold, and a router that sends every turn back to the server that already holds its context.

The same research gives lower latency, lower cost and higher reliability. On Gemma 4 26B, first tokens arrive up to 7.8 times faster than from the median provider on OpenRouter, and the same hardware serves 1.8 times the requests it did in September, with a faster median first token. Input prices are the lowest of any provider that doesn't train on your data, on three of the five models we feature. Up to 90% of each prompt is served from cache, and cached input costs up to 99% less. On GLM 5.3 Flash, 99.999% of more than 20 million requests in 30 days completed without an error. Every build ships only if it matches the eval scores of the build it replaces.

Consumer AI is all we do, so being good at this is existential for us. Almost every token we serve comes from an app people use in their own lives, tens of trillions of tokens a month, 25 times what we served in March. Use the hosted models with no rate limits and a service tier per request, route across them with automatic failover, or bring your own model for a dedicated deployment.

01Consumer vs. enterprise inference

For an enterprise task that replaces expensive manual work, a single result can justify a lot of compute, and the result can wait. A consumer app has to deliver interaction after interaction inside one subscription or one free session, while a person waits for each reply. So the number to optimize is the cost of one completed interaction, at the quality and response time the product needs.

Our goal is to get this down to a few cents per user per day, and that's something that you can only do with true experts and an ML team that really understands the trade-offs and techniques for accomplishing that.

FaiStatus by Wishroll

The table below sets the two workloads side by side, with what we built for each.

The tightest constraint is time. In conversation, people leave 0 to 300 ms between turns.[7] The model's first token is only part of that window, because the network and, in a voice app, speech synthesis use the rest. So the first token has to arrive well inside 300 ms, at production load. On Gemma 4 26B, the median first token now lands in 117 ms, which leaves most of the window for the voice.

The second difference is the size of each request. A consumer turn sends the whole conversation as the prompt and gets one short reply back. Across the apps we served in the 28 days to 23 September, median prompts were 13 to 36 times the length of replies. Enterprise work leans the other way, toward long outputs such as code and documents.

That workload already runs on Inworld at scale. On the most-used Gemma 4 models, we process up to 1.8 times the daily tokens that OpenRouter publicly reports across every provider on its platform combined.

We also serve those models faster. OpenRouter publishes first-token latency for every provider of a model. Against those measurements:[6]

  • Gemma 4 26B: the lowest median (0.17 s) and p95 (0.31 s) first token of the providers compared. That is 3.6 times faster at the median and 7.8 times faster at p95 than the median provider, at an input price nearly 40% below the median provider's.
  • MiMo 2.6 Pro: the lowest input price of the providers on OpenRouter, with the lowest median (0.39 s) and p95 (0.91 s) first token. That is 2.6 times faster at the median and 4.6 times faster at p95 than the next-fastest provider.

    • The sections below cover the calls a consumer app makes, then each technique and what it changes for the app.

    02Consumer inference tasks, and how we serve each

    A consumer app doesn't make one kind of model call. A single turn can check the message for safety, classify what the person wants, read their memory, write the reply, call a tool and update the memory afterwards. Each of those calls has a different size, a different deadline and a different budget, and a provider built around one of them leaves the rest slow or expensive.

    TaskWhat it needsHow we serve itWhat you get
    Conversation repliescompanions, tutors, assistantsFast first token responses, even as the conversation gets longerRealtime decoding speeds up generation, and KV-aware routing reuses the conversation history already processedup to 7.8× faster first token than the median OpenRouter provider; up to 90% of the prompt from cache
    Voice turnsthe reasoning inside speech to speechText fast enough for speech to start, and a fallback when a model is slowThe same serving path inside speech to speech, with a first-token timeout that moves to the next modelfirst audio as fast as 204 ms after the turn ends
    Intent, safety and moderation checksrun before every replyFast checks on every message, before the reply startsSpecialized decision models such as Clef on an optimized serving path, along with lightweight Flash models for quicker checks11.5× the throughput of Clef's reference code for high-volume checks
    Ranking and next-action decisionswhat to show or say nextStructured output, cheap at high volumeStructured outputs, with Flex for lower-cost background work or Priority for faster decisions while users waitfrom $0.07 per million input tokens
    Memory and summariesupdating what the app remembersLong input that can wait a few seconds, at the lowest priceThe Flex tier for background work, with the cached conversation reusedcached input at up to 99% less
    Stories and long repliesbedtime stories, interactive fictionA long answer that streams faster than people readDraft-and-verify decoding and fused mixture-of-experts kernelsup to 3× faster first token and 1.6× faster streaming on large MoE models
    Model failoveroutages, timeouts, failed requestsKeep the app responsive when the primary model fails, without building separate recovery logicConfigure a primary model and compatible fallback models once. The router automatically tries the next model when a request meets the failure conditions you setautomatic recovery through one API, with each attempt reported in the response
    Many model calls per turnrules, state and story in one turnSeveral model calls within one turn's latency and cost budgetOne API for every call, with a service tier per request and routing matched to each taskLatitude: tens of millions of calls in six weeks, about 20 per turn
    Your own modela fine-tune for your appBetter quality for your app's agents, at lower cost and lower latencyPost-training with app-specific evals, served on a dedicated deployment with lower-precision weights and a draft trained on your trafficbetter efficiency at your quality targets, with quality measured against your existing model; +35% throughput on one customer's fine-tune

    The same work sits underneath every row: kernels and decoding built for each model, a router that keeps each conversation's cache warm, precision checked against the evals, and a service tier per request so each call gets the speed or price it needs.

    03The serving challenge: long context in, short reply out

    Consumer apps have a distinctive traffic pattern. They send very long context to get a short reply, so processing and reusing the input matters as much as generation speed. And the calls one user action triggers each have their own size and deadline, as the timeline below shows.

    A dialogue turn with 3,500 tokens of history and a 200-token reply puts most of the work on the prompt. Long conversations pull the average far above the median: on GLM 5.3 Flash, the average request is 13,433 tokens in for 309 out.

    A story with a longer answer shifts the weight to decoding. The two phases hit different limits. Prefill, the work of processing the input, is bound by compute and gains from cache reuse and batching. Decode, the work of generating the output, is bound by memory bandwidth and gets faster when each step is cheaper or produces more than one token.

    So we work on both sides of the turn. On the prompt side, we avoid recomputing context the model has already seen, and chunked prefill processes a long prompt in pieces so it never holds up the replies streaming to other users. On the output side, we make every decode step cheaper and let each step produce several tokens. And because a background summary can wait while a reply cannot, every request carries a service tier. The next two sections cover the prompt side first, then the output side.

    04KV-aware routing for long conversations at scale

    Each turn resends the conversation so far. Prefix caching keeps the attention keys and values (the KV cache) for context the model has already processed, so the engine computes only the new part of the prompt. Every reply is still generated fresh.[2]

    At fleet scale, the hard part is placement. A conversation's cache lives on the replica that served its last turn, while another replica may have more free capacity. Our router is KV-aware. It hashes each block of the prompt, tracks which replica holds which blocks, and scores every replica on two things: how much of this request's prefix it already holds, and how busy it is. Sending every turn to the warmest cache would overload it, so the score trades reuse against load, tuned on representative traffic. KV that doesn't fit in accelerator memory spills to host memory instead of being evicted and recomputed.

    Built into each engine, model by model

    Cache-hit rate is one of the numbers we watch most closely, because it sets both how soon a reply starts and what the turn costs. Getting it high on real traffic takes more than turning prefix caching on. Different models and engines represent cached context differently: draft modes for realtime decoding, hybrid attention layouts, recurrent state and data-parallel ranks each change how prompt tokens become cache blocks, and the router finds a match only when its view agrees with the engine's.

    So we integrate the router with every model's serving path and measure the hit rate on production traffic. That work roughly doubled cache hits on GLM 5.3 Flash, from 25% to 47% on a replay of 5,000 production requests, and tripled them on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Our stack holds high hit rates on mixed traffic from many apps at once, and on one customer's dedicated deployment, cache hits reach 80% in production.[1]

    For your app. MiMo 2.6 Pro lists cached input at $0.0036 per million tokens and uncached input at $0.43, so every cached token costs 99% less. When 90% of a prompt comes from cache, the input cost of that turn falls by about 89%, and only a tenth of the prompt has to be processed before the reply can start.

    Under the hood. Each cached block skips its share of prefill. With more of every prompt coming from cache, each replica can carry more conversations at once, and time to first token grows far more slowly as a conversation gets longer.

    05Faster replies through model-specific decoding and precision

    People experience latency twice: while waiting for a response to begin, and while waiting for it to finish. Time to first token (TTFT) measures the first wait. Inter-token latency (ITL) sets the pace of the stream. A serving configuration has to handle both at the app's production concurrency.

    Draft-and-verify, tuned for each model

    Realtime decoding is our draft-and-verify serving approach, based on speculative decoding. A lightweight draft model proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies them together in one forward pass, accepting consecutive tokens until the first rejection. With exact acceptance and correction, generation can advance by multiple tokens per target-model step while preserving the target model's output distribution, with the same quality.[3]

    We optimize the drafts and the verify step for each model. Gemma 4 uses the draft models Google publishes for it, and GLM and DeepSeek use their own multi-token prediction layers. On a dedicated deployment, with the customer's approval, we train the draft on a sample of that app's traffic. A draft that predicts that app's outputs more accurately gets more tokens accepted per verification step, and we measure the gain at production load, because draft overhead, acceptance rate and concurrency all affect it.

    Verify attention on split-KV: up to 7.5× faster

    On Gemma 4 26B, a mixture-of-experts model, the verify step turned out to be the bottleneck. Verifying a 7-token draft sends 8 query tokens per sequence through attention, and the stock kernel only uses its faster split-KV path for single-token decoding. Verify fell back to a 2D kernel that split the work into about 60 blocks and left most of the chip's compute units idle.

    We changed the kernel so verify batches of up to 16 query tokens take the split-KV path. On the model's global (full-context) attention layers, verify attention ran 3.4 to 7.5 times faster, and attention fell from 27.5% to 16.5% of each decode step. The full build, which also runs the whole verify step as one captured graph and sets the draft length to 7 tokens, took ITL p50 from 6.4 to 5.2 ms and TTFT p50 from 154 to 117 ms on replayed production traffic, with the same math and reasoning scores.[1]

    For your app. ITL sets how fast a reply streams: at 5.2 ms per token, a 200-token reply finishes in about a second after it starts. Faster decode steps also let each accelerator serve more requests, which is what keeps prices low.

    Under the hood. Decode is bound by memory bandwidth: every step reads all of the weights to produce one token per sequence. A draft lets one read of the weights produce several tokens, so the speed of the verify step sets the gain. When attention dropped from 27.5% to 16.5% of the step, every request in the batch got faster.

    Same eval scores, fewer bytes per token

    A cheaper build ships only if it scores the same. Every build has to match the production build it replaces on our evals, including MATH, MMLU-Pro and GSM8K. Within that gate, each layer runs at the lowest precision its evals allow. On Gemma 4 31B, the MLP, which holds most of the weights, runs in 4-bit floating point (NVFP4), while attention and the KV cache stay at FP8.

    The gate catches regressions before they ship. It found a scaling bug in FP8 attention, and the fix brought MATH back from 87.4 to 89.6. It also blocked a build that was 80% cheaper to serve, because that build lost 5 points on MATH.

    For your app. Fewer bytes per weight keeps inference affordable as your app grows, at the same latency and quality. That is part of how Gemma 4 26B lists at $0.07 per million input tokens and $0.34 output.

    06Continuous optimization, model by model

    Our work doesn't stop when a model goes live. We continually profile production traffic to improve response times, serving efficiency and reliability, from new attention kernels that accelerate generation to resolving memory leaks that require periodic restarts. Each change is evaluated against our quality benchmarks before release. The table below shows a selection of these improvements and their measured results.

    Measured serving improvements

    ModelWhat changedResultBasis
    Gemma 4 26BRealtime-decoding verify moved onto split-KV attentionup to 7.5× faster verify attentionmicrobenchmark and replay, Oct
    MiMo 2.6 ProFused expert kernels and a custom collective3× faster first token (1.93 → 0.63 s)replay, pre-release build
    DeepSeek V3.2Turned on the model's own multi-token prediction1.6× faster token generation (62.4 → 39.9 ms/token)replay, Jul
    DeepSeek V4 FlashBlock draft-and-verify decoding, fused verify kernels+20% throughputreplay, Jul
    ClefFP8 serving path for a decision model11.5× throughput vs the reference implementationEqual benchmark accuracy, Oct
    A customer's 31B fine-tuneConverted to 4-bit weights in-house+35% throughputsaturation benchmark, Apr
    Gemma 4 31BFixed the scaling in FP8 attentionMATH 87.4 → 89.6eval harness, Sep
    DeepSeek V3.2Fixed a deadlock in TensorRT-LLM10-min stalls → 0fault injection, 20,500 requests
    GLM 5.3 FlashGraph-captured prefill and a tuned scheduler8× faster p90 first token (~10 → ~1.2 s)A/B, production prompts
    Gemma 4min_p was ignored on the draft path; now applieddraft acceptance +5 ptsproduction, Aug
    GLM 5.3 Flash

The big labs and most inference providers have doubled down on enterprise and coding. Consumer AI needs the opposite on every count. So we built Inworld Inference, the first inference service designed for consumer AI, and today it is open to every developer.

Rather than list thousands of models, we go deep on the open models consumer apps choose. Each one, from Gemma 4 to GLM, DeepSeek and MiMo, gets its own serving build: new attention kernels, realtime decoding where a small draft writes ahead and the full model checks it in one pass, lower-precision weights wherever the evals hold, and a router that sends every turn back to the server that already holds its context.

The same research gives lower latency, lower cost and higher reliability. On Gemma 4 26B, first tokens arrive up to 7.8 times faster than from the median provider on OpenRouter, and the same hardware serves 1.8 times the requests it did in September, with a faster median first token. Input prices are the lowest of any provider that doesn't train on your data, on three of the five models we feature. Up to 90% of each prompt is served from cache, and cached input costs up to 99% less. On GLM 5.3 Flash, 99.999% of more than 20 million requests in 30 days completed without an error. Every build ships only if it matches the eval scores of the build it replaces.

Consumer AI is all we do, so being good at this is existential for us. Almost every token we serve comes from an app people use in their own lives, tens of trillions of tokens a month, 25 times what we served in March. Use the hosted models with no rate limits and a service tier per request, route across them with automatic failover, or bring your own model for a dedicated deployment.

01Consumer vs. enterprise inference

For an enterprise task that replaces expensive manual work, a single result can justify a lot of compute, and the result can wait. A consumer app has to deliver interaction after interaction inside one subscription or one free session, while a person waits for each reply. So the number to optimize is the cost of one completed interaction, at the quality and response time the product needs.

Our goal is to get this down to a few cents per user per day, and that's something that you can only do with true experts and an ML team that really understands the trade-offs and techniques for accomplishing that.

FaiStatus by Wishroll

The table below sets the two workloads side by side, with what we built for each.

The tightest constraint is time. In conversation, people leave 0 to 300 ms between turns.[7] The model's first token is only part of that window, because the network and, in a voice app, speech synthesis use the rest. So the first token has to arrive well inside 300 ms, at production load. On Gemma 4 26B, the median first token now lands in 117 ms, which leaves most of the window for the voice.

The second difference is the size of each request. A consumer turn sends the whole conversation as the prompt and gets one short reply back. Across the apps we served in the 28 days to 23 September, median prompts were 13 to 36 times the length of replies. Enterprise work leans the other way, toward long outputs such as code and documents.

That workload already runs on Inworld at scale. On the most-used Gemma 4 models, we process up to 1.8 times the daily tokens that OpenRouter publicly reports across every provider on its platform combined.

We also serve those models faster. OpenRouter publishes first-token latency for every provider of a model. Against those measurements:[6]

  • Gemma 4 26B: the lowest median (0.17 s) and p95 (0.31 s) first token of the providers compared. That is 3.6 times faster at the median and 7.8 times faster at p95 than the median provider, at an input price nearly 40% below the median provider's.
  • MiMo 2.6 Pro: the lowest input price of the providers on OpenRouter, with the lowest median (0.39 s) and p95 (0.91 s) first token. That is 2.6 times faster at the median and 4.6 times faster at p95 than the next-fastest provider.

    • The sections below cover the calls a consumer app makes, then each technique and what it changes for the app.

    02Consumer inference tasks, and how we serve each

    A consumer app doesn't make one kind of model call. A single turn can check the message for safety, classify what the person wants, read their memory, write the reply, call a tool and update the memory afterwards. Each of those calls has a different size, a different deadline and a different budget, and a provider built around one of them leaves the rest slow or expensive.

    TaskWhat it needsHow we serve itWhat you get
    Conversation repliescompanions, tutors, assistantsFast first token responses, even as the conversation gets longerRealtime decoding speeds up generation, and KV-aware routing reuses the conversation history already processedup to 7.8× faster first token than the median OpenRouter provider; up to 90% of the prompt from cache
    Voice turnsthe reasoning inside speech to speechText fast enough for speech to start, and a fallback when a model is slowThe same serving path inside speech to speech, with a first-token timeout that moves to the next modelfirst audio as fast as 204 ms after the turn ends
    Intent, safety and moderation checksrun before every replyFast checks on every message, before the reply startsSpecialized decision models such as Clef on an optimized serving path, along with lightweight Flash models for quicker checks11.5× the throughput of Clef's reference code for high-volume checks
    Ranking and next-action decisionswhat to show or say nextStructured output, cheap at high volumeStructured outputs, with Flex for lower-cost background work or Priority for faster decisions while users waitfrom $0.07 per million input tokens
    Memory and summariesupdating what the app remembersLong input that can wait a few seconds, at the lowest priceThe Flex tier for background work, with the cached conversation reusedcached input at up to 99% less
    Stories and long repliesbedtime stories, interactive fictionA long answer that streams faster than people readDraft-and-verify decoding and fused mixture-of-experts kernelsup to 3× faster first token and 1.6× faster streaming on large MoE models
    Model failoveroutages, timeouts, failed requestsKeep the app responsive when the primary model fails, without building separate recovery logicConfigure a primary model and compatible fallback models once. The router automatically tries the next model when a request meets the failure conditions you setautomatic recovery through one API, with each attempt reported in the response
    Many model calls per turnrules, state and story in one turnSeveral model calls within one turn's latency and cost budgetOne API for every call, with a service tier per request and routing matched to each taskLatitude: tens of millions of calls in six weeks, about 20 per turn
    Your own modela fine-tune for your appBetter quality for your app's agents, at lower cost and lower latencyPost-training with app-specific evals, served on a dedicated deployment with lower-precision weights and a draft trained on your trafficbetter efficiency at your quality targets, with quality measured against your existing model; +35% throughput on one customer's fine-tune

    The same work sits underneath every row: kernels and decoding built for each model, a router that keeps each conversation's cache warm, precision checked against the evals, and a service tier per request so each call gets the speed or price it needs.

    03The serving challenge: long context in, short reply out

    Consumer apps have a distinctive traffic pattern. They send very long context to get a short reply, so processing and reusing the input matters as much as generation speed. And the calls one user action triggers each have their own size and deadline, as the timeline below shows.

    A dialogue turn with 3,500 tokens of history and a 200-token reply puts most of the work on the prompt. Long conversations pull the average far above the median: on GLM 5.3 Flash, the average request is 13,433 tokens in for 309 out.

    A story with a longer answer shifts the weight to decoding. The two phases hit different limits. Prefill, the work of processing the input, is bound by compute and gains from cache reuse and batching. Decode, the work of generating the output, is bound by memory bandwidth and gets faster when each step is cheaper or produces more than one token.

    So we work on both sides of the turn. On the prompt side, we avoid recomputing context the model has already seen, and chunked prefill processes a long prompt in pieces so it never holds up the replies streaming to other users. On the output side, we make every decode step cheaper and let each step produce several tokens. And because a background summary can wait while a reply cannot, every request carries a service tier. The next two sections cover the prompt side first, then the output side.

    04KV-aware routing for long conversations at scale

    Each turn resends the conversation so far. Prefix caching keeps the attention keys and values (the KV cache) for context the model has already processed, so the engine computes only the new part of the prompt. Every reply is still generated fresh.[2]

    At fleet scale, the hard part is placement. A conversation's cache lives on the replica that served its last turn, while another replica may have more free capacity. Our router is KV-aware. It hashes each block of the prompt, tracks which replica holds which blocks, and scores every replica on two things: how much of this request's prefix it already holds, and how busy it is. Sending every turn to the warmest cache would overload it, so the score trades reuse against load, tuned on representative traffic. KV that doesn't fit in accelerator memory spills to host memory instead of being evicted and recomputed.

    Built into each engine, model by model

    Cache-hit rate is one of the numbers we watch most closely, because it sets both how soon a reply starts and what the turn costs. Getting it high on real traffic takes more than turning prefix caching on. Different models and engines represent cached context differently: draft modes for realtime decoding, hybrid attention layouts, recurrent state and data-parallel ranks each change how prompt tokens become cache blocks, and the router finds a match only when its view agrees with the engine's.

    So we integrate the router with every model's serving path and measure the hit rate on production traffic. That work roughly doubled cache hits on GLM 5.3 Flash, from 25% to 47% on a replay of 5,000 production requests, and tripled them on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Our stack holds high hit rates on mixed traffic from many apps at once, and on one customer's dedicated deployment, cache hits reach 80% in production.[1]

    For your app. MiMo 2.6 Pro lists cached input at $0.0036 per million tokens and uncached input at $0.43, so every cached token costs 99% less. When 90% of a prompt comes from cache, the input cost of that turn falls by about 89%, and only a tenth of the prompt has to be processed before the reply can start.

    Under the hood. Each cached block skips its share of prefill. With more of every prompt coming from cache, each replica can carry more conversations at once, and time to first token grows far more slowly as a conversation gets longer.

    05Faster replies through model-specific decoding and precision

    People experience latency twice: while waiting for a response to begin, and while waiting for it to finish. Time to first token (TTFT) measures the first wait. Inter-token latency (ITL) sets the pace of the stream. A serving configuration has to handle both at the app's production concurrency.

    Draft-and-verify, tuned for each model

    Realtime decoding is our draft-and-verify serving approach, based on speculative decoding. A lightweight draft model proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies them together in one forward pass, accepting consecutive tokens until the first rejection. With exact acceptance and correction, generation can advance by multiple tokens per target-model step while preserving the target model's output distribution, with the same quality.[3]

    We optimize the drafts and the verify step for each model. Gemma 4 uses the draft models Google publishes for it, and GLM and DeepSeek use their own multi-token prediction layers. On a dedicated deployment, with the customer's approval, we train the draft on a sample of that app's traffic. A draft that predicts that app's outputs more accurately gets more tokens accepted per verification step, and we measure the gain at production load, because draft overhead, acceptance rate and concurrency all affect it.

    Verify attention on split-KV: up to 7.5× faster

    On Gemma 4 26B, a mixture-of-experts model, the verify step turned out to be the bottleneck. Verifying a 7-token draft sends 8 query tokens per sequence through attention, and the stock kernel only uses its faster split-KV path for single-token decoding. Verify fell back to a 2D kernel that split the work into about 60 blocks and left most of the chip's compute units idle.

    We changed the kernel so verify batches of up to 16 query tokens take the split-KV path. On the model's global (full-context) attention layers, verify attention ran 3.4 to 7.5 times faster, and attention fell from 27.5% to 16.5% of each decode step. The full build, which also runs the whole verify step as one captured graph and sets the draft length to 7 tokens, took ITL p50 from 6.4 to 5.2 ms and TTFT p50 from 154 to 117 ms on replayed production traffic, with the same math and reasoning scores.[1]

    For your app. ITL sets how fast a reply streams: at 5.2 ms per token, a 200-token reply finishes in about a second after it starts. Faster decode steps also let each accelerator serve more requests, which is what keeps prices low.

    Under the hood. Decode is bound by memory bandwidth: every step reads all of the weights to produce one token per sequence. A draft lets one read of the weights produce several tokens, so the speed of the verify step sets the gain. When attention dropped from 27.5% to 16.5% of the step, every request in the batch got faster.

    Same eval scores, fewer bytes per token

    A cheaper build ships only if it scores the same. Every build has to match the production build it replaces on our evals, including MATH, MMLU-Pro and GSM8K. Within that gate, each layer runs at the lowest precision its evals allow. On Gemma 4 31B, the MLP, which holds most of the weights, runs in 4-bit floating point (NVFP4), while attention and the KV cache stay at FP8.

    The gate catches regressions before they ship. It found a scaling bug in FP8 attention, and the fix brought MATH back from 87.4 to 89.6. It also blocked a build that was 80% cheaper to serve, because that build lost 5 points on MATH.

    For your app. Fewer bytes per weight keeps inference affordable as your app grows, at the same latency and quality. That is part of how Gemma 4 26B lists at $0.07 per million input tokens and $0.34 output.

    06Continuous optimization, model by model

    Our work doesn't stop when a model goes live. We continually profile production traffic to improve response times, serving efficiency and reliability, from new attention kernels that accelerate generation to resolving memory leaks that require periodic restarts. Each change is evaluated against our quality benchmarks before release. The table below shows a selection of these improvements and their measured results.

    Measured serving improvements

    ModelWhat changedResultBasis
    Gemma 4 26BRealtime-decoding verify moved onto split-KV attentionup to 7.5× faster verify attentionmicrobenchmark and replay, Oct
    MiMo 2.6 ProFused expert kernels and a custom collective3× faster first token (1.93 → 0.63 s)replay, pre-release build
    DeepSeek V3.2Turned on the model's own multi-token prediction1.6× faster token generation (62.4 → 39.9 ms/token)replay, Jul
    DeepSeek V4 FlashBlock draft-and-verify decoding, fused verify kernels+20% throughputreplay, Jul
    ClefFP8 serving path for a decision model11.5× throughput vs the reference implementationEqual benchmark accuracy, Oct

    DeepSeek V3.2Fixed a deadlock in TensorRT-LLM10-min stalls → 0fault injection, 20,500 requests

item.description:
一句话：AI 负责梳理问题簇、算影响面、比版本差异；符号表解析与单局现场仍归工程师。

要点：

  • 分工划得很清楚：小Q（接 MCP）用日常语言提问就能梳理问题簇、统计受影响设备规模、横向对比版本差异，输出排查顺序与优先级
  • 深度定位仍交给工程师：堆栈详情、单局会话现场、符号表解析不让 AI 代劳
  • 线上排障绕三条主线轮转并复用同一套真机数据：发版窗口期（新增崩溃簇、崩溃与 ANR 是否抬升）、卡顿与内存、机型适配；样本量少时给出保守判断

为什么值得看：这是「AI 进工程流程」里最少被讨论但最实用的一环：不是让模型修 bug，而是先把「海量真机数据里该看哪里」这一步自动化。三条主线的划分可以直接搬成团队的上线检查表。

中文摘要：文章从客户端工程师最熟悉的那种折磨讲起：本地一切正常，上线后冒出大量偶现崩溃与卡顿，后台一堆崩溃簇、会话与机型报表，却不知道第一下点哪里。UWA 的做法是让 GPM 2.0（采集真机崩溃、ANR、卡顿、内存、温度并按版本/场景/机型聚合）接上 MCP，把「小Q」变成团队里的分诊同事：用日常语言提问，它先梳理问题簇、统计受影响设备规模、横向比较版本差异，给出排查顺序与优先级。分工也被明确划开——堆栈详情、单局会话现场与符号表解析仍旧由工程师往下深挖。线上排查围绕发版窗口期、卡顿与内存、机型适配三条主线轮转，复用同一套真机数据，样本量不足时给保守判断而不是草率结论。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：UWA 博客（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-28

客户端程序怎么用 GPM 2.0：线上问题本地复现不了，该从哪下手？｜GPM 小Q MCP 实战

  • 作者：admin
  • /
  • 时间：5天前
  • /
  • 浏览：286 次
  • /
  • 分类：万象更新

    • 做游戏客户端工程师，有一类折磨几乎人人都经历过：本地跑一切正常，版本上线后冒出一堆偶现崩溃、诡异卡顿。客服和运营不停过来追问：玩家大量报错，到底是什么问题？影响多少人？什么时候能修好？打开性能后台，大量的崩溃簇、会话、机型报表。你明明手握海量数据，却不知道第一下该点哪里。

    GPM 2.0采集玩家真机真实的崩溃、ANR、卡顿、内存、温度数据，按版本、场景、机型完成聚合。接入MCP的小Q，更像是团队里一位专职做线上问题分诊的同事。你用日常工作语言直接提问，它帮你先梳理问题簇、统计受影响设备规模、横向对比版本差异，输出排查顺序与优先级；堆栈详情、单局会话现场、符号表解析这些深度定位工作，仍然交给工程师自己往下深挖。

    ▍线上排障三条主线：发版、卡顿和内存、机型适配

    线上排查可以围绕三条主线轮转，复用同一套真机数据，避免团队内部各看各的数据，班车迭代各自为战。

    ▍发版窗口期：分清新增崩溃簇，拒绝凭感觉评估版本好坏
    新版本灰度刚上线，不要被主观感受“感觉这版更稳”误导。
    重点确认：有没有冒出新增崩溃簇？对比上一主力版本，崩溃、ANR是否抬升？波及多少活跃设备？当上报样本量还比较少的时候，小Q会给出保守判断：优先持续观察，紧盯新增问题，而不是草率得出版本优化成功的结论。

    ◆ 口语化提问示例：“刚灰度的这个版本，对比上一个主力版，崩溃、ANR新增了哪几类？哪些问题需要优先处理？”

    ◆ 实际收益：不用手动聚合多份崩溃报表，快速区分是老问题延续还是版本回归，减少被运营反复追问的沟通成本。

    ▍卡顿 & 内存：别被全服均值欺骗，问题要落到具体场景

    大盘平均帧率好看，不代表高负载玩法没有灾难。很多时候只是大量正常玩家，把一部分场景的严重卡顿给平均抹平。排查需要下钻真实会话：卡顿发生在加载、战斗还是结算？根源偏向逻辑、资源还是渲染？结合卡顿帧与无损截帧，区分是瞬时尖峰，还是持续的高负载。修复完成之后，再做版本对照，校验同类问题事件数量是否真实下降，而不是只看大盘数字变好看。

    ◆ 口语化提问示例：“当前哪个场景内存、卡顿问题最突出？异常集中在哪些会话？”

    ◆ 实际收益：跳过人工多维度筛选，快速定位受害场景，避免对着虚假的大盘均值做无效优化。

    ▍机型维度：区分是全局问题还是尾部机型问题，拒绝一刀切优化

    同一个玩法，部分设备仅预警，少数机型已经严重卡顿、高温降频。需要先判断：问题是全机型普遍现象，还是集中在特定SoC、某一档画质配置。简单粗暴全局降低画质，往往只能把大盘指标压下去，真正受害的尾部机型体验并没有改善。

    ◆ 口语化提问示例：“这个场景的卡顿和高温，是不是集中在少数机型、特定画质档位？”

    ◆ 实际收益：规避一刀切优化，判断是否需要机型特化，避免做投入大但收效甚微的修改。

    ▍实战案例：项目一周线上排障复盘

    拿示例项目「云澜纪」某一周线上数据举例，样本覆盖七千多台设备，线上聚合出二十余类崩溃问题。头部问题包含原生段错误、视频播放模块空指针、播放器非法状态；ANR整体数量不高，但存在输入超时、主线程被网络阻塞卡住的现象。

    经过小Q分诊，可以直接输出排期参考：优先处理原生崩溃与视频播放模块问题，ANR作为次优先级跟进。


    这周崩溃头部分哪几类？今晚先查哪条？

    版本对比可以快速识别版本取舍。新版2.4.112相对上一主力版本，内存从1974MB下降至1636MB，卡顿指标也得到改善，但崩溃率由0.23%上升至1.62%，新版样本量仅有一千出头。内存优化拿到成效，但新增崩溃风险不容忽视，灰度阶段不能只看内存变好就盲目加码放量。


    新版崩溃率是不是抬上去了？内存改善能不能盖过它？

    进一步下钻到具体玩法，「云舸商路」场景平均内存约2880MB。均值看上去尚可，但部分机型出现上千次每十分钟卡顿、内存冲到4GB、温度突破70℃。

    真正需要修复的，是“该场景 + 这批尾部机型”的组合问题，验收标准也要对齐：修复包上线，回看该场景内存严重设备数、卡顿次数是否下降，而不是只看全服平均帧率。


    这个场景的卡顿和内存，是不是集中在少数机型？

    ▍小Q MCP：缩短线上排障的第一步

    接入MCP之后，小Q适合放在你点开GPM详细分析页面之前。

  • 发版后：查询新版崩溃簇、版本指标差异，拿到优先排查清单；
  • 卡顿专项：定位高风险场景，判断问题是否绑定特定机型；
  • Hotfix上线后：校验同类故障事件、受影响设备数量，验证修复效果。

    • ► 重要边界：小Q不能替代符号表解析，也替代不了你对引擎、业务代码的深度判断。完整调用栈、卡顿帧画面、单条玩家会话原始现场，仍然需要进入GPM详情页手动查看。

    它帮你省掉的，是面对海量数据时“不知道从哪一个看板开始”的迷茫。

    对于客户端工程师，GPM把亿万玩家设备上的线上现象，转化成可供分析的线索；小Q MCP把海量线索整理成可直接开工的修复顺序。本地调试跑通只完成一半；另一半，是确认真实玩家设备上同类问题真的变少。

    如果你想要体验这套分析逻辑，可以访问GPM 2.0 Demo，感受从大盘到专项分析的完整链路。

    立即访问GPM 2.0 Demo（由于功能模块较多，建议在电脑端浏览）：
    https://gpm-console.uwa4d.com/?tab=demo_app

    看完Demo，想要了解正式环境、SaaS/私有云部署方案，可以通过以下方式预约您的UWA顾问！
    技术支持：gpm-support@uwa4d.com
    微信：18683824

item.content:encoded:
一句话：AI 负责梳理问题簇、算影响面、比版本差异；符号表解析与单局现场仍归工程师。

要点：

  • 分工划得很清楚：小Q（接 MCP）用日常语言提问就能梳理问题簇、统计受影响设备规模、横向对比版本差异，输出排查顺序与优先级
  • 深度定位仍交给工程师：堆栈详情、单局会话现场、符号表解析不让 AI 代劳
  • 线上排障绕三条主线轮转并复用同一套真机数据：发版窗口期（新增崩溃簇、崩溃与 ANR 是否抬升）、卡顿与内存、机型适配；样本量少时给出保守判断

为什么值得看：这是「AI 进工程流程」里最少被讨论但最实用的一环：不是让模型修 bug，而是先把「海量真机数据里该看哪里」这一步自动化。三条主线的划分可以直接搬成团队的上线检查表。

中文摘要：文章从客户端工程师最熟悉的那种折磨讲起：本地一切正常，上线后冒出大量偶现崩溃与卡顿，后台一堆崩溃簇、会话与机型报表，却不知道第一下点哪里。UWA 的做法是让 GPM 2.0（采集真机崩溃、ANR、卡顿、内存、温度并按版本/场景/机型聚合）接上 MCP，把「小Q」变成团队里的分诊同事：用日常语言提问，它先梳理问题簇、统计受影响设备规模、横向比较版本差异，给出排查顺序与优先级。分工也被明确划开——堆栈详情、单局会话现场与符号表解析仍旧由工程师往下深挖。线上排查围绕发版窗口期、卡顿与内存、机型适配三条主线轮转，复用同一套真机数据，样本量不足时给保守判断而不是草率结论。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：UWA 博客（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-28

客户端程序怎么用 GPM 2.0：线上问题本地复现不了，该从哪下手？｜GPM 小Q MCP 实战

  • 作者：admin
  • /
  • 时间：5天前
  • /
  • 浏览：286 次
  • /
  • 分类：万象更新

    • 做游戏客户端工程师，有一类折磨几乎人人都经历过：本地跑一切正常，版本上线后冒出一堆偶现崩溃、诡异卡顿。客服和运营不停过来追问：玩家大量报错，到底是什么问题？影响多少人？什么时候能修好？打开性能后台，大量的崩溃簇、会话、机型报表。你明明手握海量数据，却不知道第一下该点哪里。

    GPM 2.0采集玩家真机真实的崩溃、ANR、卡顿、内存、温度数据，按版本、场景、机型完成聚合。接入MCP的小Q，更像是团队里一位专职做线上问题分诊的同事。你用日常工作语言直接提问，它帮你先梳理问题簇、统计受影响设备规模、横向对比版本差异，输出排查顺序与优先级；堆栈详情、单局会话现场、符号表解析这些深度定位工作，仍然交给工程师自己往下深挖。

    ▍线上排障三条主线：发版、卡顿和内存、机型适配

    线上排查可以围绕三条主线轮转，复用同一套真机数据，避免团队内部各看各的数据，班车迭代各自为战。

    ▍发版窗口期：分清新增崩溃簇，拒绝凭感觉评估版本好坏
    新版本灰度刚上线，不要被主观感受“感觉这版更稳”误导。
    重点确认：有没有冒出新增崩溃簇？对比上一主力版本，崩溃、ANR是否抬升？波及多少活跃设备？当上报样本量还比较少的时候，小Q会给出保守判断：优先持续观察，紧盯新增问题，而不是草率得出版本优化成功的结论。

    ◆ 口语化提问示例：“刚灰度的这个版本，对比上一个主力版，崩溃、ANR新增了哪几类？哪些问题需要优先处理？”

    ◆ 实际收益：不用手动聚合多份崩溃报表，快速区分是老问题延续还是版本回归，减少被运营反复追问的沟通成本。

    ▍卡顿 & 内存：别被全服均值欺骗，问题要落到具体场景

    大盘平均帧率好看，不代表高负载玩法没有灾难。很多时候只是大量正常玩家，把一部分场景的严重卡顿给平均抹平。排查需要下钻真实会话：卡顿发生在加载、战斗还是结算？根源偏向逻辑、资源还是渲染？结合卡顿帧与无损截帧，区分是瞬时尖峰，还是持续的高负载。修复完成之后，再做版本对照，校验同类问题事件数量是否真实下降，而不是只看大盘数字变好看。

    ◆ 口语化提问示例：“当前哪个场景内存、卡顿问题最突出？异常集中在哪些会话？”

    ◆ 实际收益：跳过人工多维度筛选，快速定位受害场景，避免对着虚假的大盘均值做无效优化。

    ▍机型维度：区分是全局问题还是尾部机型问题，拒绝一刀切优化

    同一个玩法，部分设备仅预警，少数机型已经严重卡顿、高温降频。需要先判断：问题是全机型普遍现象，还是集中在特定SoC、某一档画质配置。简单粗暴全局降低画质，往往只能把大盘指标压下去，真正受害的尾部机型体验并没有改善。

    ◆ 口语化提问示例：“这个场景的卡顿和高温，是不是集中在少数机型、特定画质档位？”

    ◆ 实际收益：规避一刀切优化，判断是否需要机型特化，避免做投入大但收效甚微的修改。

    ▍实战案例：项目一周线上排障复盘

    拿示例项目「云澜纪」某一周线上数据举例，样本覆盖七千多台设备，线上聚合出二十余类崩溃问题。头部问题包含原生段错误、视频播放模块空指针、播放器非法状态；ANR整体数量不高，但存在输入超时、主线程被网络阻塞卡住的现象。

    经过小Q分诊，可以直接输出排期参考：优先处理原生崩溃与视频播放模块问题，ANR作为次优先级跟进。


    这周崩溃头部分哪几类？今晚先查哪条？

    版本对比可以快速识别版本取舍。新版2.4.112相对上一主力版本，内存从1974MB下降至1636MB，卡顿指标也得到改善，但崩溃率由0.23%上升至1.62%，新版样本量仅有一千出头。内存优化拿到成效，但新增崩溃风险不容忽视，灰度阶段不能只看内存变好就盲目加码放量。


    新版崩溃率是不是抬上去了？内存改善能不能盖过它？

    进一步下钻到具体玩法，「云舸商路」场景平均内存约2880MB。均值看上去尚可，但部分机型出现上千次每十分钟卡顿、内存冲到4GB、温度突破70℃。

    真正需要修复的，是“该场景 + 这批尾部机型”的组合问题，验收标准也要对齐：修复包上线，回看该场景内存严重设备数、卡顿次数是否下降，而不是只看全服平均帧率。


    这个场景的卡顿和内存，是不是集中在少数机型？

    ▍小Q MCP：缩短线上排障的第一步

    接入MCP之后，小Q适合放在你点开GPM详细分析页面之前。

  • 发版后：查询新版崩溃簇、版本指标差异，拿到优先排查清单；
  • 卡顿专项：定位高风险场景，判断问题是否绑定特定机型；
  • Hotfix上线后：校验同类故障事件、受影响设备数量，验证修复效果。

    • ► 重要边界：小Q不能替代符号表解析，也替代不了你对引擎、业务代码的深度判断。完整调用栈、卡顿帧画面、单条玩家会话原始现场，仍然需要进入GPM详情页手动查看。

    它帮你省掉的，是面对海量数据时“不知道从哪一个看板开始”的迷茫。

    对于客户端工程师，GPM把亿万玩家设备上的线上现象，转化成可供分析的线索；小Q MCP把海量线索整理成可直接开工的修复顺序。本地调试跑通只完成一半；另一半，是确认真实玩家设备上同类问题真的变少。

    如果你想要体验这套分析逻辑，可以访问GPM 2.0 Demo，感受从大盘到专项分析的完整链路。

    立即访问GPM 2.0 Demo（由于功能模块较多，建议在电脑端浏览）：
    https://gpm-console.uwa4d.com/?tab=demo_app

    看完Demo，想要了解正式环境、SaaS/私有云部署方案，可以通过以下方式预约您的UWA顾问！
    技术支持：gpm-support@uwa4d.com
    微信：18683824
