It is also supported in part by the National Science and Technology Council, Taiwan, under Grant NSTC-115-2634-F-A49-011, Grant NSTC-114-2218-E-A49-024, Grant NSTC-115-2425-H-A49-001, Grant NSTC-114-2622-E-A49-027, Grant NSTC-115-2221-E-A49-124-MY3, Grant NSTC-115-2218-E-A49-017 and in part by the Higher Education Sprout Project of the National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University and the Ministry of Education (MOE), Taiwan. It is also partly supported by MediaTek Inc., Hon Hai Research Institute, E.SUN Bank, and Industrial Technology Research Institute. (Corresponding author: Ching-Chun Huang.) During this research, Thanh-Nguyen Truong was kindly supported by the TaiwanICDFHigher Education Scholarship Program.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 多人世界模型别做全连接：Multics 用玩家/小组/全局三层通信，把注意力从平方级压回可扩展 ｜ Multics: Generative Multi-Player World Model with Hierarchical Communication
item.description:
一句话：全连接随人数平方涨、全局表示又互相干扰；分层通信把无关事件隔在小组内。

要点：

  • 现有做法两难：全连接通信（如 Solaris）随玩家数带来平方级注意力开销；集中式（如 γ-World）让不相关事件在共享全局表示里互相干扰
  • Multics 在玩家、小组、全局三层组织信息交换：组 token 作为中间表示聚合局部相关玩家信息，再与全局 token 通信，拓扑天然限制了无关局部事件之间的直接混合
  • 组 token 参数在组槽间共享，因此同一套通信模块能吃不同玩家数而不引入新参数；作者另提了 budget-conscious 的预算分配

为什么值得看：多人交互是目前世界模型最没解的一块：两人还行，八人就崩。分层通信是分布式系统里的老办法（分区 + 聚合 + 全局同步），搬到世界模型上同样成立，对做多人游戏/协同仿真的团队是可借的结构。

中文摘要：多人交互世界模型要从多个玩家视角生成同一个共享环境，但随着玩家数增加，生成质量与可扩展性都难以维持。现有两条路各有硬伤：全连接通信（如 Solaris）随玩家数带来平方级注意力成本；集中式方案（如 γ-World）把所有事件塞进一个共享全局表示，导致不相关事件互相干扰。Multics 提出分层通信，把信息交换组织成玩家、小组、全局三层：组 token 作为中间表示聚合局部相关的玩家信息，再与全局 token 通信，这个拓扑限制了无关局部事件之间的直接混合；组 token 的参数在各组槽位间共享，因此同一套通信模块能适应不同玩家数而不新增组专属参数。作者还提出预算感知的容量分配，并在实验中验证了可扩展性。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-12

本期推送：2026-10-28

Multics: Generative Multi-Player World Model with Hierarchical Communication

Abstract

Multi-player interactive world models aim to simulate shared environments from multiple players’ perspectives, but achieving robust generation while scaling to more players remains challenging. Existing approaches that rely on fully-connected communication (e.g., Solaris) incur quadratic attention costs as the number of players grows, while centralized approaches (e.g., γ-World) suffer from interference between unrelated events in a shared global representation. To address these challenges, we present Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures information exchange across player, group, and global levels. This hierarchy introduces group tokens into self-attention as intermediate group-level representations that aggregate locally relevant player information. These tokens connect to global tokens for cross-group communication, while the hierarchical topology limits direct mixing between unrelated local events. Group-token parameters are shared across group slots, allowing the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. We further propose budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories, which adaptively groups relevant players while limiting unnecessary communication. Experiments demonstrate that Multics achieves state-of-the-art performance in 4- and 6-player settings, with improved cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness. Moreover, Multics generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining, while reducing self-attention computation compared with fully-connected communication.

††footnotemark: ††footnotetext: † Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Multi-player interactive video world models aim to simulate shared environments from multiple players’ perspectives. They have broad applications in game entertainment [(Bruce et al., 2024)] and interactive simulation [(Ren et al., 2025; Fung et al., 2025)]. However, most video world models focus on single-player simulation [(Wang et al., 2026; HunyuanWorld, 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026)] and generate observations conditioned on a single player’s action, camera trajectory, and text prompt. Moving from single-player to multi-player simulation introduces two challenges: robust multi-player generation and scalability to more players (Figure1). Robust multi-player generation requires generated observations to maintain cross-player consistency across overlapping views, faithfully follow player-specific action and camera controls, and remain robust to interference from unrelated concurrent events. Scalability to more players requires the model to generalize to larger player counts without retraining and scale efficiently as the number of players increases.

Existing multi-player video generation methods adopt different communication mechanisms for inter-player information exchange, but remain limited in jointly supporting robust generation and scalability. Fully-connected communication methods [(Savva et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026a)] such as Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] enable unrestricted information exchange across players but incur quadratic computational cost as the player count grows. In contrast, centralized communication methods such as γ-World [(Liu et al., 2026a)] improve computational scalability through a shared global representation. However, routing heterogeneous interactions through the same communication pathway can mix information from unrelated events, increasing cross-event interference. This can further degrade cross-player consistency and player-specific controllability as concurrent interactions become more numerous and diverse. These limitations motivate structured local and global communication under a limited communication budget.

To address these challenges, we present Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures information exchange across the player, group, and global levels. Our key insight is that players vary in their relevance to one another, motivating a hierarchy that combines group-level aggregation of locally relevant information with global communication across groups. As shown in Figure2, the hierarchy incorporates group tokens into self-attention as intermediate group-level representations that aggregate locally relevant player information and connect to global tokens for cross-group communication. This topology limits direct mixing between unrelated local events. Group-token parameters are shared across group slots, allowing the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. To determine which players should share group-level representations, we propose budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories. This strategy adapts group assignments to player relevance while limiting unnecessary communication.

Experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in 4- and 6-player settings, with strong cross-player consistency, controllability, and interference robustness. Models trained with 4 players further generalize to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining. Efficiency comparisons show substantially reduced self-attention computation relative to fully-connected communication. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of our key designs. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures inter-player information exchange across player, group, and global levels. Group tokens provide intermediate group-level representations for local aggregation while preserving global communication for cross-group exchange.

  • •

    We propose shared group-token parameters across group slots, enabling the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. We further introduce budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories to organize relevant players while limiting unnecessary communication.

  • •

    Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in multi-player generation, with strong cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness.  Multics further demonstrates generalization to larger player counts without retraining and maintains computational efficiency.

    • 2 Related Work

    Video Generation and Video World Models. Recent advances in video generation span Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) [(Peebles & Xie, 2023; OpenAI, 2024)], next-token and masked-token prediction [(Villegas et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2023; Kondratyuk et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023a; Yu et al., 2023b; Chang et al., 2022)], and hybrid methods [(Chen et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025)], enabling high-quality video synthesis [(DeepMind, 2024; Kling, 2025; Kong et al., 2024; Runway AI, 2025; Wang et al., 2025)]. Conditioning on camera trajectories [(Bai et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b)], actions [(Yu et al., 2025b; Valevski et al., 2025)], and multimodal references [(MiniMax, 2026)] further enables controllable generation. Building on the world-model paradigm of predicting future states from past states and actions [(Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018)], video world models serve as visual simulators by generating future observations [(Bar et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023b)]. These models have been explored in robotics [(Li et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2023a; Ye et al., 2026a)], video games [(Fan et al., 2022; Alonso et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026; Valevski et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026)], autonomous driving [(Ren et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023)], and physical simulation [(Yuan et al., 2026)], demonstrating their potential as general-purpose visual simulators.

    Multi-Player World Models. Recent multi-player world models use different communication mechanisms to maintain cross-player consistency. Dense joint-generation methods [(Sun et al., 2026; Odyssey, 2026; Hu et al., 2026b)], including Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] and MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026a)], couple player streams through shared or cross-agent attention, enabling fine-grained interactions with increasing computational cost as player counts grow. Centralized methods, including γ-World [(Liu et al., 2026a)] and MultiWorld [(Wu et al., 2026)], improve scalability by aggregating information through sparse hubs or compact global visual representations [(Mo et al., 2026)]. Another line of work uses persistent or structured shared world states to decouple world-state evolution from per-player rendering [(Po et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a; Mo et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026b)]. These shared-state methods primarily address population scalability through state-rendering decomposition. Our work explores an orthogonal design dimension: scalable communication within learned visual representations, using a hierarchical player-group-global topology to structure information exchange across representation levels.

    Communication Topologies. Multi-agent communication includes dense exchange in CommNet [(Sukhbaatar et al., 2016)], selective or targeted communication in ATOC [(Jiang & Lu, 2018)] and TarMAC [(Das et al., 2019)], and hierarchical exchange across agent groups [(Zhao et al., 2026b)]. While these methods primarily support multi-agent decision making, we study communication within high-dimensional video representations for multi-player world modeling.

    3 Method

    Given N players in an environment, each player i has an initial image Iᵢ∈ℝ^c×h×w, a text prompt Pᵢ, an action sequence Aᵢ∈ℝ^(f-1)×dₐ, and a camera trajectory Cᵢ∈ℝ^f×3×4, where f,c,h,w,dₐ denote the frame count, number of channels, height, width, and action dimension, respectively. Our goal is to jointly generate videos V={Vᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, Vᵢ∈ℝ^f×c×h×w, conditioned on {Iᵢ,Pᵢ,Aᵢ,Cᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N. The videos should maintain cross-player consistency when players observe overlapping views of the same scene or one another, and follow player-specific action and camera controls. Thus, we introduce hierarchical communication across the player, group, and global levels, as shown in Figure2.

    3.1 Multi-Player Video Generation with Conditioning

    For each player i, the initial image Iᵢ serves as a clean anchor, while the action sequence Aᵢ, camera trajectory Cᵢ, and prompt Pᵢ condition the transformer blocks as detailed below. All players’ visual tokens are concatenated along the sequence dimension for inter-player communication (Section3.2).

    Action Conditioning. We decompose Aᵢ=(Dᵢ,Uᵢ) into discrete controls Dᵢ∈ℝ^(f-1)×23 and relative yaw/pitch changes Uᵢ∈ℝ^(f-1)×2[(Savva et al., 2026)]. Following GameFactory [(Yu et al., 2025b)], we condition each latent frame on rw_c action steps collected from a causal window spanning w_c latent intervals. Here, r is the video VAE’s temporal compression ratio and f_z=(f-1)/r+1 is the latent frame count. Discrete controls are projected to the transformer hidden dimension d, forming tokens in ℝ^f_z×rw_c×d that are injected into the visual tokens via cross-attention. Mouse controls are flattened into ℝ^f_z×2rw_c features and fused with visual tokens through a lightweight temporal module.

    Camera and Prompt Conditioning. Following ReCamMaster [(Bai et al., 2025)], we express all players’ camera rotations and translations in a shared coordinate system anchored at the first player’s initial frame, forming C∈ℝ^N×f×3×4. Learnable camera adapters project C to the transformer hidden dimension and inject the resulting features into the corresponding player tokens’ query and key features. For the group and global tokens introduced in Section3.2, we use zero camera features as placeholders [(Huang et al., 2026a)]. Text prompts are encoded and injected via cross-attention [(Rombach et al., 2022)].

    3.2 Hierarchical Communication for Multi-Player

    Effective multi-player generation requires structured information exchange across players. Let xᵢ∈ℝ^f_z×L×d denote the visual tokens of player i, where L denotes the number of spatial tokens per frame. All communication topologies below are implemented using self-attention masks that define the allowed token-to-token connections. We review prior mechanisms [(Savva et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a)] and their natural extensions before introducing our hierarchical design.

    Fully-Connected Communication. Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] concatenates the representations of all players along the sequence dimension and performs shared self-attention, allowing every player to communicate directly with all others:

    x_full=[x₁,x₂,…,x_N]_seq, xᵢ↔xⱼ, i,j=1,…,N.

    		(1)

    We denote this topology as “fully-connected communication” and illustrate it in Figure2(b).

    Centralized Communication. Recent work [(Liu et al., 2026a)] introduces shared global hub tokens h^G∈ℝ^f_z×k_G×d as a common communication interface across players, where k_G is the number of global tokens per latent frame. The communication sequence is

    x_cent=[x₁,…,x_N,h^G]_seq, xᵢ↔h^G, i=1,…,N.

    		(2)

    We denote this topology as “centralized communication” and illustrate it in Figure2(c).

    Group-Based Communication. As a straightforward extension, group-based communication introduces locality by restricting direct player-to-player communication to players within the same group. Let g(i) denote the group assignment of player i. The resulting communication is

    xᵢ↔xⱼ if g(i)=g(j), xᵢ↔h^G.

    		(3)

    We denote this topology as “group-based communication” and illustrate it in Figure2(d).

    Hierarchical Communication (Ours). To improve cross-player consistency and player-specific controllability while mitigating interference among unrelated local events, we introduce group tokens as intermediate group-level representations into self-attention. Let M denote the number of available group slots and g∈{1,…,M} denote a group index. For each group slot g, we instantiate k_L group tokens h^L_g∈ℝ^f_z×k_L×d between player- and global-level communication. Let h^L denote the collection of group tokens from all M group slots. For player i assigned to group g(i), the hierarchical communication is formulated as

    xₕᵢₑᵣ=[x₁,…,x_N,h^L,h^G]_seq, xᵢ↔h^L_g(i)↔h^G.

    		(4)

    Players within the same group can directly attend to one another. Players that are not assigned to a group communicate directly through the global tokens. We denote this topology as “hierarchical communication” and illustrate it in Figure2(a).

    To avoid binding group representations to fixed group identities, we learn a set of shared group-token parameters E^L∈ℝ^k_L×d. At runtime, E^L is replicated across the M group slots and broadcast over latent frames to instantiate h^L∈ℝ^f_z×M×k_L×d. Although all group slots share the same learnable parameters, their hidden representations evolve through hierarchical self-attention on the players assigned to each group, yielding group-specific representations. This design of shared group-token parameters makes the group slots exchangeable and enables the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players, without introducing new group-specific parameters or retraining the model. Appendix C.2 reports an ablation of shared group-token parameters.

    Comparison and Discussion. Our experimental results demonstrate the substantial advantages of hierarchical communication over fully-connected, centralized, and group-based alternatives, as illustrated in Figure3 and Figure5. We attribute these gains to the multi-granularity representations enabled by hierarchical communication. By introducing intermediate group-level representations between player- and global-level communication, our method allows locally related information to be aggregated before broader global exchange, reducing the direct mixing of heterogeneous information, such as actions, visual details, and unrelated local events, within a shared communication space. This facilitates more effective multi-player representation learning and improves cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness.

    3.3 Dynamic Grouping

    Hierarchical communication requires determining which players should share group-level representations. Treating all players as equally relevant for group communication introduces unnecessary information exchange and computation and can increase cross-event interference. We therefore introduce dynamic grouping, which estimates pairwise player relevance from recent camera trajectories [(Yu et al., 2025a)] and organizes relevant players into groups under a communication budget.

    Camera-Based Player Relevance. Building on the camera-based field-of-view (FoV) overlap in Context-as-Memory [(Yu et al., 2025a)], we estimate player relevance from recent camera trajectories. At each grouping update t, we compute a symmetric matrix R⁽ᵗ⁾∈[0,1]^N×N from observed camera histories: Rᵢⱼ⁽ᵗ⁾=Rel(Cᵢ^≤t,Cⱼ^≤t), where Rel measures spatial proximity and viewing-direction alignment using only past and current camera states to preserve causality. Higher scores indicate that the corresponding players are more likely to observe spatially related content and benefit from local exchange. Relevance determines only the communication topology, while feature exchange is learned through hierarchical self-attention. Details of computation are provided in Appendix B.

    Budget-Constrained Dynamic Grouping. Given N players, we determine the number of group slots M from the player count and derive the maximum group capacity K under a communication budget ℂₘₐₓ that matches the communication cost of the centralized baseline. At time t, the active groups G⁽ᵗ⁾ must satisfy |G⁽ᵗ⁾|≤M, |S|≤K for all S∈G⁽ᵗ⁾, and ℂ(G⁽ᵗ⁾)≤ℂₘₐₓ, where S is a set of players assigned to one group and ℂ measures the communication cost of the induced attention topology. Using R⁽ᵗ⁾, we select a feasible grouping that maximizes player coverage while preserving high-relevance player relations. Remaining group slots and budget are used to accommodate unassigned players; otherwise, they communicate only through global tokens. Details of the determination of M, budget calculation, and derivation of K are provided in Appendix B.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experiment Setting

    Implementation Details. We train Multics based on Wan2.2 TI2V 5B [(Wang et al., 2025)] using OpenCS2 [(Blanchon, 2026)], an open multiplayer dataset rendered from ten-player Counter-Strike 2 matches with camera trajectories and mouse/keyboard action annotations. We train separate models for N∈{4,6}, randomly selecting N of the ten players for each sample. Each sample contains N videos of 165 frames at 352×640 resolution. We adopt diffusion forcing training [(Chen et al., 2024)] and update the dynamic grouping topology every 48 video frames using causal camera trajectories. Additional details are provided in Appendix A.

    Baselines. Given the lack of existing open-source methods for evaluating more than 4 players, we adopt the following baselines. (1) Fully-Connected Communication: Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] pioneered multi-player video generation by concatenating all players’ tokens along the sequence dimension for shared self-attention. (2) Centralized Communication: γ-World [(Liu et al., 2026a)] introduces a set of shared hub tokens for information aggregation across players. For a fair comparison, we reimplement all baselines using the same base model and dataset, with identical training configurations and iterations.

    Evaluation Metrics. We employ 10 metrics across four key aspects: consistency, action accuracy, camera accuracy, and visual quality. (1) Consistency: following prior work [(Wang et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2026b)], we evaluate cross-view consistency with GeoKPM, which uses geometry-aware keypoint matching under epipolar-geometry filtering. Following [Liu et al. (2026a)], we also report the pixel-aligned metrics PSNR and SSIM [(Wang et al., 2004)] and the perceptual metric LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. (2) Action accuracy: following prior work [(Baker et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2026)], we use a trained Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM) to infer actions from generated videos. (3) Camera accuracy: we use RotErr, TransErr, and CamMC, following prior work [(Zheng et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026a)]. (4) Visual quality: following prior work [(Savva et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a)], we evaluate generation quality with FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)] and FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2018)]. For evaluation, following [Yu et al. (2025a)], we randomly select 200 held-out OpenCS2 samples, with 100 for each separately trained model. To assess cross-dataset applicability, we also train on EgoTeam’s training set [(Peng et al., 2026)], a dataset of multi-robot egocentric videos rendered in reconstructed real-world indoor environments, and evaluate on 100 test samples.

    4.2 Comparison with Previous Methods

    Quantitative Results. We compare Multics with Solaris and γ-World in Table1 (top). Our method outperforms the baselines on most evaluation metrics in both 4- and 6-player settings, demonstrating strong cross-player consistency, action/camera controllability, and visual quality. Despite unrestricted cross-player information exchange, Solaris underperforms Multics on most metrics while incurring substantial computational overhead, suggesting that dense communication does not necessarily translate into better multi-player generation. γ-World struggles with consistency and camera accuracy due to its reliance on the same shared global pathway, which aggregates heterogeneous player information, leading to degraded cross-player consistency and player-specific controllability under diverse concurrent interactions. We attribute Multics’s gains to hierarchical communication, which introduces intermediate group-level representations to effectively structure multi-player information exchange. As pixel-aligned metrics PSNR and SSIM compare pixel values or local image statistics at corresponding spatial locations, they are sensitive to small spatial deviations, whereas the consistent gains in GeoKPM and LPIPS indicate stronger geometric and perceptual cross-player consistency of our method.

    Qualitative Results. As shown in Figure3, Multics demonstrates stronger cross-player consistency, controllability, and interference robustness. Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] fails to preserve consistency across overlapping views of the same scene or one another, while γ-World [(Liu et al., 2026a)] is more susceptible to information mixing through its shared global pathway, causing inconsistent visual details and player-specific actions being affected by unrelated observations. Since all methods share the same video-generation backbone, the results highlight the effectiveness of hierarchical communication for robust multi-player generation.

    4.3 Scalability and Generalization Ability of Multics

    Computational Efficiency. Following [Liu et al. (2026a)], we compare communication methods using DiT latency, self-attention latency, and self-attention FLOPs. As shown in Figure6, fully-connected communication scales quadratically with player count, while Multics substantially reduces computation (9.6 vs. 69.1 TFLOPs with 10 players) and remains comparable to centralized and group-based methods. These results demonstrate the computational efficiency of our method for scalable multi-player world models.

    Generalization to More Player Counts. We apply models trained with 4 players to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining or introducing additional model parameters. The results in Table1 (middle) highlight Multics’s ability to generalize to larger player counts while achieving stronger consistency, controllability, and visual quality than Solaris and γ-World.

    Cross-Domain Applicability. Beyond game environments, we also evaluate Multics on EgoTeam [(Peng et al., 2026)]. As shown in Table1 (bottom), our method maintains robust multi-player generation performance, demonstrating its cross-domain applicability.

一句话：全连接随人数平方涨、全局表示又互相干扰；分层通信把无关事件隔在小组内。

要点：

  • 现有做法两难：全连接通信（如 Solaris）随玩家数带来平方级注意力开销；集中式（如 γ-World）让不相关事件在共享全局表示里互相干扰
  • Multics 在玩家、小组、全局三层组织信息交换：组 token 作为中间表示聚合局部相关玩家信息，再与全局 token 通信，拓扑天然限制了无关局部事件之间的直接混合
  • 组 token 参数在组槽间共享，因此同一套通信模块能吃不同玩家数而不引入新参数；作者另提了 budget-conscious 的预算分配

为什么值得看：多人交互是目前世界模型最没解的一块：两人还行，八人就崩。分层通信是分布式系统里的老办法（分区 + 聚合 + 全局同步），搬到世界模型上同样成立，对做多人游戏/协同仿真的团队是可借的结构。

中文摘要：多人交互世界模型要从多个玩家视角生成同一个共享环境，但随着玩家数增加，生成质量与可扩展性都难以维持。现有两条路各有硬伤：全连接通信（如 Solaris）随玩家数带来平方级注意力成本；集中式方案（如 γ-World）把所有事件塞进一个共享全局表示，导致不相关事件互相干扰。Multics 提出分层通信，把信息交换组织成玩家、小组、全局三层：组 token 作为中间表示聚合局部相关的玩家信息，再与全局 token 通信，这个拓扑限制了无关局部事件之间的直接混合；组 token 的参数在各组槽位间共享，因此同一套通信模块能适应不同玩家数而不新增组专属参数。作者还提出预算感知的容量分配，并在实验中验证了可扩展性。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心词（English）

原文发布：2026-10-12

本期推送：2026-10-28

Multics: Generative Multi-Player World Model with Hierarchical Communication

Abstract

Multi-player interactive world models aim to simulate shared environments from multiple players’ perspectives, but achieving robust generation while scaling to more players remains challenging. Existing approaches that rely on fully-connected communication (e.g., Solaris) incur quadratic attention costs as the number of players grows, while centralized approaches (e.g., γ-World) suffer from interference between unrelated events in a shared global representation. To address these challenges, we present Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures information exchange across player, group, and global levels. This hierarchy introduces group tokens into self-attention as intermediate group-level representations that aggregate locally relevant player information. These tokens connect to global tokens for cross-group communication, while the hierarchical topology limits direct mixing between unrelated local events. Group-token parameters are shared across group slots, allowing the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. We further propose budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories, which adaptively groups relevant players while limiting unnecessary communication. Experiments demonstrate that Multics achieves state-of-the-art performance in 4- and 6-player settings, with improved cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness. Moreover, Multics generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining, while reducing self-attention computation compared with fully-connected communication.

††footnotemark: ††footnotetext: † Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Multi-player interactive video world models aim to simulate shared environments from multiple players’ perspectives. They have broad applications in game entertainment [(Bruce et al., 2024)] and interactive simulation [(Ren et al., 2025; Fung et al., 2025)]. However, most video world models focus on single-player simulation [(Wang et al., 2026; HunyuanWorld, 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026)] and generate observations conditioned on a single player’s action, camera trajectory, and text prompt. Moving from single-player to multi-player simulation introduces two challenges: robust multi-player generation and scalability to more players (Figure1). Robust multi-player generation requires generated observations to maintain cross-player consistency across overlapping views, faithfully follow player-specific action and camera controls, and remain robust to interference from unrelated concurrent events. Scalability to more players requires the model to generalize to larger player counts without retraining and scale efficiently as the number of players increases.

Existing multi-player video generation methods adopt different communication mechanisms for inter-player information exchange, but remain limited in jointly supporting robust generation and scalability. Fully-connected communication methods [(Savva et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026a)] such as Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] enable unrestricted information exchange across players but incur quadratic computational cost as the player count grows. In contrast, centralized communication methods such as γ-World [(Liu et al., 2026a)] improve computational scalability through a shared global representation. However, routing heterogeneous interactions through the same communication pathway can mix information from unrelated events, increasing cross-event interference. This can further degrade cross-player consistency and player-specific controllability as concurrent interactions become more numerous and diverse. These limitations motivate structured local and global communication under a limited communication budget.

To address these challenges, we present Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures information exchange across the player, group, and global levels. Our key insight is that players vary in their relevance to one another, motivating a hierarchy that combines group-level aggregation of locally relevant information with global communication across groups. As shown in Figure2, the hierarchy incorporates group tokens into self-attention as intermediate group-level representations that aggregate locally relevant player information and connect to global tokens for cross-group communication. This topology limits direct mixing between unrelated local events. Group-token parameters are shared across group slots, allowing the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. To determine which players should share group-level representations, we propose budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories. This strategy adapts group assignments to player relevance while limiting unnecessary communication.

Experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in 4- and 6-player settings, with strong cross-player consistency, controllability, and interference robustness. Models trained with 4 players further generalize to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining. Efficiency comparisons show substantially reduced self-attention computation relative to fully-connected communication. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of our key designs. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures inter-player information exchange across player, group, and global levels. Group tokens provide intermediate group-level representations for local aggregation while preserving global communication for cross-group exchange.

  • •

    We propose shared group-token parameters across group slots, enabling the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. We further introduce budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories to organize relevant players while limiting unnecessary communication.

  • •

    Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in multi-player generation, with strong cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness.  Multics further demonstrates generalization to larger player counts without retraining and maintains computational efficiency.

    • 2 Related Work

    Video Generation and Video World Models. Recent advances in video generation span Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) [(Peebles & Xie, 2023; OpenAI, 2024)], next-token and masked-token prediction [(Villegas et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2023; Kondratyuk et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023a; Yu et al., 2023b; Chang et al., 2022)], and hybrid methods [(Chen et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025)], enabling high-quality video synthesis [(DeepMind, 2024; Kling, 2025; Kong et al., 2024; Runway AI, 2025; Wang et al., 2025)]. Conditioning on camera trajectories [(Bai et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b)], actions [(Yu et al., 2025b; Valevski et al., 2025)], and multimodal references [(MiniMax, 2026)] further enables controllable generation. Building on the world-model paradigm of predicting future states from past states and actions [(Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018)], video world models serve as visual simulators by generating future observations [(Bar et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023b)]. These models have been explored in robotics [(Li et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2023a; Ye et al., 2026a)], video games [(Fan et al., 2022; Alonso et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026; Valevski et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026)], autonomous driving [(Ren et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023)], and physical simulation [(Yuan et al., 2026)], demonstrating their potential as general-purpose visual simulators.

    Multi-Player World Models. Recent multi-player world models use different communication mechanisms to maintain cross-player consistency. Dense joint-generation methods [(Sun et al., 2026; Odyssey, 2026; Hu et al., 2026b)], including Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] and MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026a)], couple player streams through shared or cross-agent attention, enabling fine-grained interactions with increasing computational cost as player counts grow. Centralized methods, including γ-World [(Liu et al., 2026a)] and MultiWorld [(Wu et al., 2026)], improve scalability by aggregating information through sparse hubs or compact global visual representations [(Mo et al., 2026)]. Another line of work uses persistent or structured shared world states to decouple world-state evolution from per-player rendering [(Po et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a; Mo et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026b)]. These shared-state methods primarily address population scalability through state-rendering decomposition. Our work explores an orthogonal design dimension: scalable communication within learned visual representations, using a hierarchical player-group-global topology to structure information exchange across representation levels.

    Communication Topologies. Multi-agent communication includes dense exchange in CommNet [(Sukhbaatar et al., 2016)], selective or targeted communication in ATOC [(Jiang & Lu, 2018)] and TarMAC [(Das et al., 2019)], and hierarchical exchange across agent groups [(Zhao et al., 2026b)]. While these methods primarily support multi-agent decision making, we study communication within high-dimensional video representations for multi-player world modeling.

    3 Method

    Given N players in an environment, each player i has an initial image Iᵢ∈ℝ^c×h×w, a text prompt Pᵢ, an action sequence Aᵢ∈ℝ^(f-1)×dₐ, and a camera trajectory Cᵢ∈ℝ^f×3×4, where f,c,h,w,dₐ denote the frame count, number of channels, height, width, and action dimension, respectively. Our goal is to jointly generate videos V={Vᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, Vᵢ∈ℝ^f×c×h×w, conditioned on {Iᵢ,Pᵢ,Aᵢ,Cᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N. The videos should maintain cross-player consistency when players observe overlapping views of the same scene or one another, and follow player-specific action and camera controls. Thus, we introduce hierarchical communication across the player, group, and global levels, as shown in Figure2.

    3.1 Multi-Player Video Generation with Conditioning

    For each player i, the initial image Iᵢ serves as a clean anchor, while the action sequence Aᵢ, camera trajectory Cᵢ, and prompt Pᵢ condition the transformer blocks as detailed below. All players’ visual tokens are concatenated along the sequence dimension for inter-player communication (Section3.2).

    Action Conditioning. We decompose Aᵢ=(Dᵢ,Uᵢ) into discrete controls Dᵢ∈ℝ^(f-1)×23 and relative yaw/pitch changes Uᵢ∈ℝ^(f-1)×2[(Savva et al., 2026)]. Following GameFactory [(Yu et al., 2025b)], we condition each latent frame on rw_c action steps collected from a causal window spanning w_c latent intervals. Here, r is the video VAE’s temporal compression ratio and f_z=(f-1)/r+1 is the latent frame count. Discrete controls are projected to the transformer hidden dimension d, forming tokens in ℝ^f_z×rw_c×d that are injected into the visual tokens via cross-attention. Mouse controls are flattened into ℝ^f_z×2rw_c features and fused with visual tokens through a lightweight temporal module.

    Camera and Prompt Conditioning. Following ReCamMaster [(Bai et al., 2025)], we express all players’ camera rotations and translations in a shared coordinate system anchored at the first player’s initial frame, forming C∈ℝ^N×f×3×4. Learnable camera adapters project C to the transformer hidden dimension and inject the resulting features into the corresponding player tokens’ query and key features. For the group and global tokens introduced in Section3.2, we use zero camera features as placeholders [(Huang et al., 2026a)]. Text prompts are encoded and injected via cross-attention [(Rombach et al., 2022)].

    Effective multi-player generation requires structured information exchange across players. Let xᵢ∈ℝ^f_z×L×d denote the visual tokens of player i, where L denotes the number of spatial tokens per frame. All communication topologies below are implemented using self-attention masks that define the allowed token-to-token connections. We review prior mechanisms [(Savva et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a)] and their natural extensions before introducing our hierarchical design.

    Fully-Connected Communication. Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] concatenates the representations of all players along the sequence dimension and performs shared self-attention, allowing every player to communicate directly with all others:

    x_full=[x₁,x₂,…,x_N]_seq, xᵢ↔xⱼ, i,j=1,…,N.

    		(1)

    We denote this topology as “fully-connected communication” and illustrate it in Figure2(b).

    Centralized Communication. Recent work [(Liu et al., 2026a)] introduces shared global hub tokens h^G∈ℝ^f_z×k_G×d as a common communication interface across players, where k_G is the number of global tokens per latent frame. The communication sequence is

    x_cent=[x₁,…,x_N,h^G]_seq, xᵢ↔h^G, i=1,…,N.

    		(2)

    We denote this topology as “centralized communication” and illustrate it in Figure2(c).

    Group-Based Communication. As a straightforward extension, group-based communication introduces locality by restricting direct player-to-player communication to players within the same group. Let g(i) denote the group assignment of player i. The resulting communication is

    xᵢ↔xⱼ if g(i)=g(j), xᵢ↔h^G.

    		(3)

    We denote this topology as “group-based communication” and illustrate it in Figure2(d).

    Hierarchical Communication (Ours). To improve cross-player consistency and player-specific controllability while mitigating interference among unrelated local events, we introduce group tokens as intermediate group-level representations into self-attention. Let M denote the number of available group slots and g∈{1,…,M} denote a group index. For each group slot g, we instantiate k_L group tokens h^L_g∈ℝ^f_z×k_L×d between player- and global-level communication. Let h^L denote the collection of group tokens from all M group slots. For player i assigned to group g(i), the hierarchical communication is formulated as

    xₕᵢₑᵣ=[x₁,…,x_N,h^L,h^G]_seq, xᵢ↔h^L_g(i)↔h^G.

    		(4)

    Players within the same group can directly attend to one another. Players that are not assigned to a group communicate directly through the global tokens. We denote this topology as “hierarchical communication” and illustrate it in Figure2(a).

    To avoid binding group representations to fixed group identities, we learn a set of shared group-token parameters E^L∈ℝ^k_L×d. At runtime, E^L is replicated across the M group slots and broadcast over latent frames to instantiate h^L∈ℝ^f_z×M×k_L×d. Although all group slots share the same learnable parameters, their hidden representations evolve through hierarchical self-attention on the players assigned to each group, yielding group-specific representations. This design of shared group-token parameters makes the group slots exchangeable and enables the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players, without introducing new group-specific parameters or retraining the model. Appendix C.2 reports an ablation of shared group-token parameters.

    Comparison and Discussion. Our experimental results demonstrate the substantial advantages of hierarchical communication over fully-connected, centralized, and group-based alternatives, as illustrated in Figure3 and Figure5. We attribute these gains to the multi-granularity representations enabled by hierarchical communication. By introducing intermediate group-level representations between player- and global-level communication, our method allows locally related information to be aggregated before broader global exchange, reducing the direct mixing of heterogeneous information, such as actions, visual details, and unrelated local events, within a shared communication space. This facilitates more effective multi-player representation learning and improves cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness.

    Hierarchical communication requires determining which players should share group-level representations. Treating all players as equally relevant for group communication introduces unnecessary information exchange and computation and can increase cross-event interference. We therefore introduce dynamic grouping, which estimates pairwise player relevance from recent camera trajectories [(Yu et al., 2025a)] and organizes relevant players into groups under a communication budget.

Higher scores indicate that the corresponding players are more likely to observe spatially related content and benefit from local exchange. Relevance determines only the communication topology, while feature exchange is learned through hierarchical self-attention. Details of computation are provided in Appendix B.

At time t, the active groups G⁽ᵗ⁾ must satisfy |G⁽ᵗ⁾|≤M, |S|≤K for all S∈G⁽ᵗ⁾, and ℂ(G⁽ᵗ⁾)≤ℂₘₐₓ, where S is a set of players assigned to one group and ℂ measures the communication cost of the induced attention topology. Using R⁽ᵗ⁾, we select a feasible grouping that maximizes player coverage while preserving high-relevance player relations. Remaining group slots and budget are used to accommodate unassigned players; otherwise, they communicate only through global tokens. Details of the determination of M, budget calculation, and derivation of K are provided in Appendix B.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experiment Setting

    Implementation Details. We train Multics based on Wan2.2 TI2V 5B [(Wang et al., 2025)] using OpenCS2 [(Blanchon, 2026)], an open multiplayer dataset rendered from ten-player Counter-Strike 2 matches with camera trajectories and mouse/keyboard action annotations. Additional details are provided in Appendix A.

(1) Fully-Connected Communication: Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] pioneered multi-player video generation by concatenating all players’ tokens along the sequence dimension for shared self-attention. (2) Centralized Communication: γ-World [(Liu et al., 2026a)] introduces a set of shared hub tokens for information aggregation across players. For a fair comparison, we reimplement all baselines using the same base model and dataset, with identical training configurations and iterations.

(1) Consistency: following prior work [(Wang et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2026b)], we evaluate cross-view consistency with GeoKPM, which uses geometry-aware keypoint matching under epipolar-geometry filtering. Following [Liu et al. (2026a)], we also report the pixel-aligned metrics PSNR and SSIM [(Wang et al., 2004)] and the perceptual metric LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. (2) Action accuracy: following prior work [(Baker et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2026)], we use a trained Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM) to infer actions from generated videos. (3) Camera accuracy: we use RotErr, TransErr, and CamMC, following prior work [(Zheng et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026a)]. (4) Visual quality: following prior work [(Savva et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a)], we evaluate generation quality with FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)] and FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2018)]. For evaluation, following [Yu et al. (2025a)], we randomly select 200 held-out OpenCS2 samples, with 100 for each separately trained model. To assess cross-dataset applicability, we also train on EgoTeam’s training set [(Peng et al., 2026)], a dataset of multi-robot egocentric videos rendered in reconstructed real-world indoor environments, and evaluate on 100 test samples.

    4.2 Comparison with Previous Methods

    Quantitative Results. We compare Multics with Solaris and γ-World in Table1 (top). Our method outperforms the baselines on most evaluation metrics in both 4- and 6-player settings, demonstrating strong cross-player consistency, action/camera controllability, and visual quality. Despite unrestricted cross-player information exchange, Solaris underperforms Multics on most metrics while incurring substantial computational overhead, suggesting that dense communication does not necessarily translate into better multi-player generation. γ-World struggles with consistency and camera accuracy due to its reliance on the same shared global pathway, which aggregates heterogeneous player information, leading to degraded cross-player consistency and player-specific controllability under diverse concurrent interactions. We attribute Multics’s gains to hierarchical communication, which introduces intermediate group-level representations to effectively structure multi-player information exchange. As pixel-aligned metrics PSNR and SSIM compare pixel values or local image statistics at corresponding spatial locations, they are sensitive to small spatial deviations, whereas the consistent gains in GeoKPM and LPIPS indicate stronger geometric and perceptual cross-player consistency of our method.

    Qualitative Results. As shown in Figure3, Multics demonstrates stronger cross-player consistency, controllability, and interference robustness. Solaris [(Savva et al., 2026)] fails to preserve consistency across overlapping views of the same scene or one another, while γ-World [(Liu et al., 2026a)] is more susceptible to information mixing through its shared global pathway, causing inconsistent visual details and player-specific actions being affected by unrelated observations. Since all methods share the same video-generation backbone, the results highlight the effectiveness of hierarchical communication for robust multi-player generation.

    4.3 Scalability and Generalization Ability of Multics

    Computational Efficiency. Following [Liu et al. (2026a)], we compare communication methods using DiT latency, self-attention latency, and self-attention FLOPs. As shown in Figure6, fully-connected communication scales quadratically with player count, while Multics substantially reduces computation (9.6 vs. 69.1 TFLOPs with 10 players) and remains comparable to centralized and group-based methods. These results demonstrate the computational efficiency of our method for scalable multi-player world models.

    Generalization to More Player Counts. We apply models trained with 4 players to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining or introducing additional model parameters. The results in Table1 (middle) highlight Multics’s ability to generalize to larger player counts while achieving stronger consistency, controllability, and visual quality than Solaris and γ-World.

    Cross-Domain Applicability. Beyond game environments, we also evaluate Multics on EgoTeam [(Peng et al., 2026)]. As shown in Table1 (bottom), our method maintains robust multi-player generation performance, demonstrating its cross-domain applicability.

item.title: 字节押注的「实时空间视频」：人进去走，世界跟着变——但「用模型跑游戏」不等于「不用设计规则」 ｜ 颠覆传统游戏开发，张一鸣押注的世界模型：可直接预测生成画面
item.description:
一句话：把 Seedance 的生成推到实时交互，并点明 GameNGen 那类工作替代的是运行、不是设计。

要点：

  • 字节 9 月被披露的研发：以 Seedance 为基础做实时空间视频，把模型、云、内容平台与 Pico 硬件串起来，让人进入生成环境并持续操作
  • 对照最清楚的一段：GameNGen 用学习模型模拟《DOOM》的运行——传统引擎按规则更新坐标再渲染，它是从「画面+操作」记录里学映射，但仍是在模拟一款已有游戏
  • 作者给出的关键判断：把一段过程生成得像，和在任意操作下都准确延续规则，是两件事；记录没覆盖的动作、记不住的早期变化，都会让后续预测出错

为什么值得看：很多「世界模型取代引擎」的说法都跳过了一个区分：替代的是运行时，还是设计与内容生产。这篇把这个区分讲清楚了，还顺带把「多模态」「世界模型」「视频模型」几个被混用的词拆开，适合拿去校准内部讨论的措辞。

中文摘要：一篇把字节世界模型线索与技术概念一起梳理的长文。线索部分：2026 年 9 月张一鸣被报道协调多团队推进基于 Seedance 的实时空间视频，目标是人进入 AI 生成的环境、操作后环境继续变化，并把字节的模型、云、内容平台与 Pico 硬件串起来；Seedance 2.5 已支持最长 30 秒生成与片段延长，下一步是把生成推进到实时交互。技术部分以 GameNGen 为例拆开「引擎」与「世界模型」：传统引擎保存地图、坐标、血量，按规则更新再渲染；GameNGen 从游玩记录里学「画面+操作→下一帧」。作者强调两者不可混为一谈——用学出来的模型运行游戏，不等于开发者不再需要设计规则与制作内容；生成得像也不等于在任意操作下都能准确延续规则。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：知乎·放牛的星星（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-10-28

2026 年 9 月，张一鸣被报道正在协调字节跳动的多个团队与算力资源，推进一项基于 Seedance 的实时空间视频技术。它希望让人进入 AI 生成的环境，在其中行动，而环境会随着操作继续变化。这项研发试图把字节的 AI 模型、云计算资源、内容平台与 Pico 硬件串起来，生成能响应用户语音或动作的虚拟环境。项目当时计划最快在 10 月亮相，但完整产品与开放安排尚未公布。

Seedance 是字节的视频生成模型系列，已通过即梦面向创作者、通过火山方舟供开发者调用。2026 年 7 月 31 日发布的 Seedance 2.5 支持视频生成、片段延长与定向编辑：可用文字、图片、视频或声音作参考，生成最长 30 秒视频，也可在已有片段上延续、调整局部。9 月披露的研发，准备把这种生成推进到实时交互——用户不必等一段视频完成后修改，而是在过程里持续操作，模型随之生成后续环境。

世界模型 vs 游戏引擎：两种「向前走」

以《DOOM》为例：玩家向前走，墙壁逼近；开枪命中，敌人血量下降；转过街角，新通道进入画面。传统游戏里这些由程序计算——引擎保存地图、坐标、血量等状态，执行开发者写好的规则，再把结果画到屏幕上。

2024 年的 GameNGen 尝试用学习到的模型模拟这段过程：先让智能体在原版《DOOM》里游玩，收集画面与操作，训练生成模型按「之前的画面 + 当前动作」预测下一帧。于是同样一个「向前走」，传统引擎按规则更新坐标再渲染，GameNGen 则是从游玩记录里学会「操作→画面」的映射。

作者特别点出一句容易被忽略的话：用一个学出来的模型运行游戏，和让开发者不再需要设计规则、制作内容，是两件事。GameNGen 模拟的仍是已有游戏，训练依据也来自原游戏的运行。

「像」和「对」的差别

连续画面包含物体移动、遮挡与视角变化，大规模视频能提供学习世界规律的线索；加上操作记录后，模型还能学到某种行动通常带来什么后果。但把一段过程生成得像，和在任意操作下都准确延续规则，仍有距离：如果记录没覆盖某种动作，或模型记不住更早的变化，后面的预测就会出错。

谁在用：人进去玩，AI 进去练

在游戏里，最直接的使用者是创作者与玩家——创作者想试一个设计，玩家要在一套规则里持续操作。微软研究院与 Ninja Theory 在 2025 年 2 月公布 Muse 时，就把游戏构思列为一个用途：用《Bleeding Edge》的画面与控制输入（累计约七年的游玩记录），创作者可以从一个片段出发让模型继续生成，也可以在给定画面里加入角色，观察模型如何延续这个改变。

（延伸阅读节选，全文见原文链接。）

item.title: 世界模型会「演戏」：机械臂得分 78.8、被操作的物体只有 29.1，WorldOracle 用 335 条真机轨迹抓这个漏洞 ｜ WorldOracle 世界模型评测平台发布 用真机实测给行业「测谎」
item.description:
一句话：40% 考题是失败操作：抓空了必须预测抓空，把失败脑补成成功算幻觉。

要点：

  • 三重压力测试：因果服从（严格跟随给定动作，含失败操作）、分布迁移（要能吃策略自主执行带来的停顿与抖动）、时序耐力（120 秒后误差仍受控）
  • 335 条真机轨迹、约 40% 为失败或次优执行，覆盖刚体抓取、柔性毛巾、流体倒水、关节抽屉四种物理形态；评测按交互区域算分，避免背景稀释误差
  • 七模型横评最扎心的一条：把指标拆成机械臂与物体后，IRASim 是 78.8 vs 29.1、Cosmos 3 是 89.4 vs 45.4，最强 GE-Sim 2.0 也只有 100.0 vs 62.8——动作被复刻了，动作对世界的影响没看住

为什么值得看：如果要把世界模型接进引擎或机器人回路，验收就必须包含「失败样本」：只考成功片段的基准会系统性高估模型。这套「按交互区域算分 + 保留失败」的做法，可以直接借来做自家生成式内容的回归测试。

中文摘要：WorldOracle 是一个以真实执行为标尺的动作驱动世界模型评测平台，由智元、NVIDIA、普林斯顿、UT Austin、多伦多大学的研究者联合完成，10 月 16 日发布并开放提交。它要回答的问题很具体：给定一组动作，模型预测的未来与真实发生的过程差多少。为此设了三重压力测试——因果服从（包括失败动作，抓空就必须预测抓空）、分布迁移（动作来自人类遥操作或策略自主执行）、时序耐力（120 秒后误差是否受控）。考题是 335 条真机轨迹，约 40% 为失败或次优执行，覆盖刚体、柔性体、流体与关节体四类交互；标注用 VLM 生成物理判据、SAM3 分割交互区域，让评测只看真正发生交互的地方。七模型横评暴露的共性问题是：机械臂运动被精确复刻，但物体被操作后的结果没看住。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：知乎·单行科技（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-28

机器人明明抓空了，世界模型却预测它成功抓起了水果。这不是段子，而是行业普遍现象：给定完全相同的初始画面和动作序列，主流世界模型可以生成一段画面逼真、却与真实执行完全相反的视频。如果不把预测画面与真实执行逐帧对照，这次失败就被完美掩盖了。

10 月 16 日，首个以真实执行为标尺的动作驱动世界模型评测平台 WorldOracle 发布，由智元、NVIDIA、普林斯顿、UT Austin、多伦多大学的研究者联合完成。

三个压力测试

  • 因果服从：模型必须严格跟随给定动作序列，包括错误与失败的操作。现实抓空了，预测出抓空才是满分；把失败脑补成成功就是幻觉。
  • 分布迁移：动作可以来自人类遥操作，也可以来自策略自主执行（带停顿、抖动、临场修正），模型不能只会应付标准操作。
  • 时序耐力：不是前 10 秒像不像，而是连续操作 120 秒后误差是否还受控。

此前评测要么在仿真里跑，要么只考文本驱动视频生成；WorldOracle 是唯一同时做到「动作条件化 + 真实数据 + 含失败样本 + 长时序 + 多本体 + 多视角 + 策略自主执行分布」七项的基准。

考题本身

335 条真机轨迹（智元精灵 G2 100、YAM 75、人类第一视角手部 100、G2 策略自主 60），每条约 2 分钟；约 40% 是失败或次优执行，抓空、掉落、洒水完整保留。任务覆盖 4 种物理形态：刚体抓取、柔性体挂毛巾、流体倒水、关节体开合抽屉。标注管线也工业化：VLM 为每个交互片段的结果关键帧生成物理判据，SAM3 逐帧分割物体、机械臂与人手，评测聚焦在真正发生交互的区域，避免背景稀释误差。阅卷标准经 119 名参与者盲评校验，四项指标与人类判断一致率 88.1%–93.2%。

七个模型同台，最扎心的一条

把空间对齐指标拆成「机械臂」与「被操作物体」两部分后，所有模型出现巨大落差：G2 人工操作上 IRASim 机械臂 78.8、物体仅 29.1；Cosmos 3 是 89.4 对 45.4；最强的 GE-Sim 2.0 机械臂 100.0、物体 62.8。也就是说机械臂的运动被精确复刻，但它对世界造成的影响没看住——水果有没有被抓走、毛巾有没有滑落、水有没有进杯。

另一条：把预测窗口从 10 秒拉到 120 秒，多数模型分数出现断崖式衰减（GE-Sim 2.0 单视角综合分从 86.1 开始往下掉）。

（延伸阅读节选，全文见原文链接。）

为什么值得看：如果要把世界模型接进引擎或机器人回路，验收就必须包含「失败样本」：只考成功片段的基准会系统性高估模型。这套「按交互区域算分 + 保留失败」的做法，可以直接借来做自家生成式内容的回归测试。

中文摘要：WorldOracle 是一个以真实执行为标尺的动作驱动世界模型评测平台，由智元、NVIDIA、普林斯顿、UT Austin、多伦多大学的研究者联合完成，10 月 16 日发布并开放提交。它要回答的问题很具体：给定一组动作，模型预测的未来与真实发生的过程差多少。为此设了三重压力测试——因果服从（包括失败动作，抓空就必须预测抓空）、分布迁移（动作来自人类遥操作或策略自主执行）、时序耐力（120 秒后误差是否受控）。考题是 335 条真机轨迹，约 40% 为失败或次优执行，覆盖刚体、柔性体、流体与关节体四类交互；标注用 VLM 生成物理判据、SAM3 分割交互区域，让评测只看真正发生交互的地方。七模型横评暴露的共性问题是：机械臂运动被精确复刻，但物体被操作后的结果没看住。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：知乎·单行科技（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-28

机器人明明抓空了，世界模型却预测它成功抓起了水果。这不是段子，而是行业普遍现象：给定完全相同的初始画面和动作序列，主流世界模型可以生成一段画面逼真、却与真实执行完全相反的视频。如果不把预测画面与真实执行逐帧对照，这次失败就被完美掩盖了。

10 月 16 日，首个以真实执行为标尺的动作驱动世界模型评测平台 WorldOracle 发布，由智元、NVIDIA、普林斯顿、UT Austin、多伦多大学的研究者联合完成。

三个压力测试

  • 因果服从：模型必须严格跟随给定动作序列，包括错误与失败的操作。现实抓空了，预测出抓空才是满分；把失败脑补成成功就是幻觉。
  • 分布迁移：动作可以来自人类遥操作，也可以来自策略自主执行（带停顿、抖动、临场修正），模型不能只会应付标准操作。
  • 时序耐力：不是前 10 秒像不像，而是连续操作 120 秒后误差是否还受控。

此前评测要么在仿真里跑，要么只考文本驱动视频生成；WorldOracle 是唯一同时做到「动作条件化 + 真实数据 + 含失败样本 + 长时序 + 多本体 + 多视角 + 策略自主执行分布」七项的基准。

考题本身

335 条真机轨迹（智元精灵 G2 100、YAM 75、人类第一视角手部 100、G2 策略自主 60），每条约 2 分钟；约 40% 是失败或次优执行，抓空、掉落、洒水完整保留。任务覆盖 4 种物理形态：刚体抓取、柔性体挂毛巾、流体倒水、关节体开合抽屉。标注管线也工业化：VLM 为每个交互片段的结果关键帧生成物理判据，SAM3 逐帧分割物体、机械臂与人手，评测聚焦在真正发生交互的区域，避免背景稀释误差。阅卷标准经 119 名参与者盲评校验，四项指标与人类判断一致率 88.1%–93.2%。

七个模型同台，最扎心的一条

把空间对齐指标拆成「机械臂」与「被操作物体」两部分后，所有模型出现巨大落差：G2 人工操作上 IRASim 机械臂 78.8、物体仅 29.1；Cosmos 3 是 89.4 对 45.4；最强的 GE-Sim 2.0 机械臂 100.0、物体 62.8。也就是说机械臂的运动被精确复刻，但它对世界造成的影响没看住——水果有没有被抓走、毛巾有没有滑落、水有没有进杯。

另一条：把预测窗口从 10 秒拉到 120 秒，多数模型分数出现断崖式衰减（GE-Sim 2.0 单视角综合分从 86.1 开始往下掉）。

（延伸阅读节选，全文见原文链接。）

item.title: 一个想法要穿过好几个 agent 才到玩家手上：所以先定一份「怎么算做对了」的小协议 ｜ Making Games in the Age of Superintelligence: A First Playable Plan
item.description:
一句话：能产出更多文件，不代表游戏能玩；先写清玩家动作、目标、结束条件与验收方式。

要点：

  • 现状：一个想法在到达玩家之前可能穿过多个 agent——一个画关卡、一个写代码、第三个跑构建，产出文件的速度前所未有
  • 但它不回答两个问题：游戏到底能不能跑，以及有没有人想再玩一局
  • 给出的做法很朴素：先写一份关于「要做什么、怎么验证」的小协议，把玩家动作、目标、结束条件、视角、操作与首发平台固定成一份 Markdown brief 与一份 JSON plan

为什么值得看：当生产端从人变成 agent 群，先崩溃的不是产能而是验收标准。这份「先立小协议、再谈产出」的做法，可以直接搬成团队里 AI 参与的立项模板。

中文摘要：一篇短观点文，起点是当下的真实处境：一个想法在到达玩家之前可能穿过好几个 agent——一个画关卡、一个写代码、第三个跑构建。作者指出这种流水线很容易让人误判：它能以前所未有的速度产出文件，却不回答「游戏能不能跑」和「有没有人想再玩一局」。因此他们给出的起点不是更强的模型，而是一份关于「要做什么、怎么验证」的小协议：把玩家动作、目标、结束条件、视角、操作方式与首发平台固定下来，产出一份可分享的 Markdown brief 与一份给其他工具用的 JSON plan。文章也明确说，这两份文件都不是游戏本身——但它们让多个 agent 之间的协作有了验收基准。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：Blog·Summer Engine（English）

原文发布：2026-10-24

本期推送：2026-10-28

An idea can now pass through several agents before a player ever sees it. One agent may sketch a level, another may write code, and a third may test a build. That makes it easy to produce more files. It does not tell you whether the game works or whether anyone wants to play another round.

The practical starting point is a small agreement about what to build and how to check it. The free brief builder on this page asks for the player action, goal, end condition, view, controls, and first platform. It gives you a Markdown brief to share and a JSON plan to use in other tools. Neither file is a game.

What “superintelligence” means here

Superintelligence is a future possibility. It should not be confused with an AI assistant or agent working in a game project today. Calling a product an “SI game engine” does not establish that it can design, build, test, and ship a good game on its own. Ask what the current tool can read, change, run, and show you after each change.

Those capabilities vary. Godot documents command-line project runs and exports, which can support a repeatable build check. Unity documents an Assistant package with a read-only Ask mode and an Agent mode that can act on scene objects and assets, subject to permissions. Epic documents Unreal MCP as an experimental editor feature that exposes tools to compatible agents; Epic also warns that features and APIs can change. These are specific present-day workflows, not evidence of superintelligence.

Define the first playable version

Write the first build as one round, not a list of every feature the final game might have. State who the player is, what they do with the controls, what success looks like, what ends a run, and how to restart. Choose one space and one target platform. Leave shops, multiple levels, accounts, multiplayer, and a large story outside this first check unless one is essential to the core action.

Use a sentence a builder can act on: “Move through one street, collect three sparks, and reach the door before touching a cart.” Then add the missing decisions: side view, keyboard controls, browser build, success feedback, failure feedback, and restart. A visual direction can guide the work, but a beautiful still image cannot replace a playable round.

Example: Lantern Run

Imagine Lantern Run, a small side-view game about a courier crossing a rainy street. The player uses a keyboard to move around puddles and collect three sparks. Reaching the door with all three sparks wins. Touching a moving cart ends the run. The first build needs one street, one courier, three sparks, one cart, a visible spark count, and a restart action. It does not need a city map or a second level.

The handoff should include checks a person can observe:

  • Open the browser build. The first playable space loads without a blocking error.
  • Use the keyboard. The courier moves, avoids puddles, and collects sparks; the count changes.
  • Reach the door with fewer than three sparks. The game does not report a win.
  • Reach the door with three sparks. The game shows a clear success state.
  • Touch the cart. The run ends with clear feedback. Restart and play a fresh round.
  • Open the exported build outside the editor and ask a new player to finish one round without instructions.

    • These checks do not dictate code or engine. They say what must be true in the running game. If a result is missing, the builder has a concrete next change to make.

    Choose an engine for the build

    Choose from the requirements of this first game: view, input, target platform, export path, and access to project files. Test a tiny export before you commit to a long project. A browser target and a desktop target can have different setup and input needs. Confirm the current export instructions for the engine version you actually use.

    If you want to build with Summer, read the AI game engine guide, the Godot AI agent guide, and the MCP setup page. Those pages explain Summer's workflow; the brief on this page is engine-neutral. Keep the original project and the exported package in the handoff so another person can inspect what was built.

    Hand off work an agent can verify

    Give an agent the brief, one task at a time, with a result it can show you. “Make the courier move with the keyboard and show a running scene” is easier to review than “finish Lantern Run.” Ask for the changed files, the run or build result, and a short note about what remains broken. Play after each meaningful change. Do not accept “done” as evidence when the build has not been opened.

    Keep an asset list beside the brief. For every image, model, sound, and font added to the project, record its source and the license or terms you relied on. If you cannot identify the source or permitted use, replace the asset before release. The same habit applies whether a person made the asset, you bought it, or a tool generated it.

    Test, then ship the build you tested

    Run the acceptance checks in the editor, then repeat the round in the exported package on the target platform. Look for input that fails, missing files, unreadable feedback, audio problems, and a restart that keeps old state. Watch one new player without explaining the rules. Note what they try first and where they stop.

    If the build fails, narrow the next task to one observable fix and test again. If it passes, you have a first playable game and a clear basis for deciding what to add. Future AI may change how much an agent can build. The check that matters now is still simple: a person can open the game, understand the action, finish a round, and choose to play again.
